teile.einleitung: The Byzantine Iconoclasm was a long dispute in the Byzantine Empire in the 8th and 9th centuries. It was about the question whether Christians may venerate pictures of Christ, Mary and the saints.
wichtigste: Emperor Leo III started the dispute over images around 726 to 730.
The opponents of the veneration of images are called iconoclasts, that is, image breakers.
The opponents of images relied above all on the biblical ban on images.
John of Damascus defended the veneration of images in influential writings.
In 787 the Second Council of Nicaea allowed the veneration of images again.
The dispute over images finally ended in the year 843.
The Sunday of Orthodoxy still recalls the victory of the friends of images today.

abschnitte.text: In the churches of the Byzantine Empire there were many **icons**. These are painted pictures of Christ, Mary and saints. Many people kissed them, lit candles in front of them and prayed before them. Some thought this was wrong. They relied on the **biblical ban on images** in the Ten Commandments. They feared that people would worship the pictures themselves instead of God.

Around **726 to 730** Emperor **Leo III** turned against the veneration of images. With that the dispute began. The opponents of images are called **iconoclasts**, which means “image breakers”. Their opponents, the friends of images, are called iconodules. Under Leo III and his son Constantine V many pictures were removed or painted over. Whoever defended the pictures was often punished.

An important defender of images was the theologian **John of Damascus**. He lived outside the Byzantine Empire and wrote influential works. He distinguished between **worship**, which is due to God alone, and the **veneration** of a picture. According to his teaching, the honour shown to a picture belongs to the person depicted.

In **787** the **Second Council of Nicaea** allowed the veneration of images again. A council is a large assembly of bishops. But from 815 the dispute flared up again under later emperors. Only in the year **843** did it end **for good**, when Empress Theodora reintroduced the veneration of images. In the Orthodox churches the **Sunday of Orthodoxy** still recalls this today.

gewusst: Icons still play a very important part in the Orthodox Church today.
The word “iconoclast” is also used today for people who attack old ideas.

teile.einleitung: The Appenzell Wars were fights by the people of Appenzell against the Prince-Abbot of St Gallen at the beginning of the 15th century. In the end Appenzell became free and later joined the Swiss Confederacy.
wichtigste: From 1401, the people of Appenzell rose up against the Abbot of St Gallen.
They resisted high dues and the abbot's bailiffs.
Schwyz supported the people of Appenzell.
In 1405 they won the Battle of the Stoss.
Later Appenzell became a member of the Confederacy.

abschnitte.text: In the Middle Ages the land of **Appenzell** belonged to the territory of the **Prince-Abbot of St Gallen**. The abbot was both a churchman and a secular lord. The farmers had to pay him **dues**. His **bailiffs**, that is, administrators, made sure that his rights were respected. Many people of Appenzell found this unjust.

From **1401**, the people of Appenzell rose up against the abbot. They allied themselves with the town of St Gallen and received help from **Schwyz**. The abbot sought support from the Duke of Austria. In **1405**, the people of Appenzell won the **Battle of the Stoss**, a pass between Appenzell and the Rhine Valley. After that they marched with their allies through eastern Switzerland and the Lake Constance region.

After the wars, Appenzell was largely free of the abbot. The people of Appenzell made alliances with the Confederates. In **1513**, Appenzell became a full member of the **Confederacy**. Later the land split into today's cantons of **Appenzell Ausserrhoden** and **Appenzell Innerrhoden**.

gewusst: At the Stoss, a chapel recalls the battle of 1405.

teile.einleitung: Francisco Pizarro was a Spanish conqueror in the 16th century. With a small force he destroyed the great empire of the Incas in South America. He founded the city of Lima, the present-day capital of Peru.
wichtigste: Francisco Pizarro came from Trujillo in Spain.
In 1532 he marched into the Inca Empire with about 170 soldiers.
The captured Inca ruler Atahualpa offered a room full of gold as a ransom.
Although the ransom had been paid, Atahualpa was executed in 1533.
In 1535 Pizarro founded the city of Lima.
He fell out with his partner Diego de Almagro.
In 1541 Pizarro was murdered in Lima.

abschnitte.text: Pizarro came from the town of **Trujillo** in the Spanish region of Extremadura. He had no schooling and probably could not read. As a young man he went to America, where the Spanish were then conquering many regions. There he heard of a rich land in the south. Together with his partner **Diego de Almagro** he prepared the conquest of **Peru**.

abschnitte.titel: The march into the Inca Empire
abschnitte.text: In 1532 Pizarro marched into the empire of the **Incas** with **about 170 soldiers**. The empire was then weakened by a dispute over the throne. The Spanish had horses, steel armour and firearms that the Incas did not know. In the city of **Cajamarca** they took the Inca ruler **Atahualpa** prisoner. In the process many of his attendants were killed.

Atahualpa offered a **room full of gold** as a ransom. In addition, two rooms full of silver were to follow. From all over the empire the Incas brought golden objects. The Spanish melted down the works of art. Although the ransom had been paid, Atahualpa was **executed in 1533**.

After that the Spanish conquered the Inca capital Cusco. In **1535** Pizarro founded the city of **Lima** on the coast, which is today the capital of Peru. Soon he quarrelled with Almagro over the booty and the territories. There was fighting, and Almagro was executed in 1538. Almagro's followers took revenge: **in 1541 Pizarro was murdered in Lima**. For the peoples of the Andes the conquest brought great suffering, also through diseases from Europe.

gewusst: Pizarro first called Lima the “City of the Kings”.
With only about 170 men Pizarro overthrew one of the largest empires of America, also because it had been weakened by a dispute over the throne.

teile.einleitung: Feudalism, also called the fief system, was the order by which power and land were distributed in the Middle Ages. One lord gave land to another to use, and he promised loyalty and service in return. In this way a kind of pyramid arose with the king at the top.
wichtigste: A fief was borrowed land that one received in return for loyalty and service.
Whoever received a fief was called a vassal, whoever granted it was called a liege lord.
At the top of the feudal pyramid stood the king.
The vassal had to give his lord above all military service.
In return the liege lord promised his vassal protection.
In the course of the Middle Ages fiefs became hereditary.
At the very bottom of the order stood the peasants, who worked the land.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from the Latin **feudum**, which means fief. A **fief** was land, sometimes also an office, that one lord lent to another to use. The recipient was called a **vassal**, the giver the liege lord. The fief system arose in the Frankish Empire from the 8th century and shaped Europe throughout the whole of the Middle Ages.

In a solemn ceremony the vassal placed his hands in the hands of the lord and swore an **oath of loyalty**. The vassal promised loyalty, counsel and above all **military service** as a knight. In return the liege lord promised **protection** and gave him the fief. If either of them broke his promise, the fief could be taken away.

At the very top of the **feudal pyramid** stood the **king**. He granted large fiefs to dukes, counts, bishops and abbots, the tenants-in-chief. They passed on parts of their land to sub-vassals, mostly knights. At the very bottom stood the peasants, who farmed the land and paid dues but were not vassals themselves.

At the beginning a fief was valid only for the lifetime of the vassal. In the course of the Middle Ages, however, fiefs became **hereditary** and passed to the sons. As a result many noble families became very powerful and sometimes stronger than the king himself. They built castles and ruled over their territories almost like little kings.

In the area of present-day Switzerland too, noble families such as the **Habsburgs**, the Kyburgs and the Zähringens ruled over land and people. Many castles, for example Kyburg or Lenzburg, still recall this. In the late Middle Ages the Confederates resisted the power of the Habsburgs. Some feudal dues such as the tithe, however, were not completely abolished in Switzerland until the 19th century.

abschnitte.titel: The end of the fief system
abschnitte.text: In the late Middle Ages the fief system lost importance. Kings and towns now preferred to pay **mercenaries** with money rather than depend on vassals. The money economy and the growing towns made the old system unnecessary. With the **French Revolution** of 1789, feudal rights were abolished in France, and other countries followed later.

begriffe.erklaerung: Land or an office that a lord grants in return for loyalty and service.
Someone who has received a fief from a lord and serves him in return.
The lord who grants a fief.
A soldier who fights for money.

gewusst: A vassal could have several liege lords at the same time, which led to difficult conflicts of loyalty.
Bishops and monasteries too were liege lords and owned large estates.
The word “enfeoff” comes from fief and means to give someone a fief.

teile.einleitung: The Medici were a rich banking family from Florence. Over generations they steered the politics of the city and promoted art and science in the age of the Renaissance.
wichtigste: Giovanni di Bicci de' Medici founded the Medici Bank in Florence in 1397.
Cosimo the Elder is regarded as the founder of the family's power.
The most important customer of the bank was the papacy.
In 1478 Giuliano de' Medici was murdered in the Pazzi conspiracy.
With Leo X and Clement VII the family produced two popes.
From 1569 the Medici were grand dukes of Tuscany.

abschnitte.text: **Giovanni di Bicci de' Medici** moved the headquarters of his bank from Rome to **Florence** in **1397**. The **Medici Bank** soon had branches in many cities of Europe. Its most important customer was the **papacy**. The Medici collected Church dues from all over Europe. A large part of the profit came from the branch in Rome.

Giovanni's son **Cosimo** built the bank up into the most powerful in Europe. In **1434** he returned to Florence from exile. After that he steered the city without holding any official office. Later he was called “Father of the Fatherland”. He is regarded as the founder of the family's power.

Not everyone agreed with the power of the Medici. The banking family **Pazzi** wanted to overthrow them in **1478**. During a Mass in the cathedral the conspirators attacked the brothers **Lorenzo** and **Giuliano**. Giuliano died, and Lorenzo survived wounded. Lorenzo was later called “the Magnificent”.

Lorenzo's son **Giovanni** became pope in **1513** as **Leo X**. Later another Medici became pope as **Clement VII**. **Catherine de' Medici** married the later King Henry II and in **1547** became queen of France. As the mother of three kings she had great influence.

In **1569** Pope Pius V raised **Cosimo I** to **Grand Duke of Tuscany**. The Medici ruled the grand duchy until their extinction in **1737**. Under them Florence on the river **Arno** became the centre of the **Renaissance**. They supported artists such as Michelangelo and Botticelli.

gewusst: Over the Arno in Florence runs the famous bridge Ponte Vecchio with shops on it.
The last Medici, Anna Maria Luisa, bequeathed the family's art treasures to the city of Florence.

teile.einleitung: The Maya are a people in Central America who over a thousand years ago built great cities with pyramids, palaces and temples. They had a script of their own, an exact calendar and knew the number zero. The Maya still exist today, and millions of people still speak Mayan languages.
wichtigste: The Maya lived and still live in Central America, above all in Mexico, Guatemala and Belize.
They knew the number zero long before the Europeans.
Their number system was based on the base 20.
Maize was their most important food.
The Maya had a fully developed script, unlike the Incas.
Around the year 900 many great cities in the lowlands were gradually abandoned.
Today there are still millions of Maya.

abschnitte.text: The Maya region includes the south of **Mexico** with the **Yucatán** peninsula, as well as Guatemala, Belize and parts of Honduras and El Salvador. There are damp **rainforest**, dry limestone plains and volcanic mountains. The Maya were never a single empire. They lived in many **city states**, which often made war on one another or formed alliances.

The Maya had their golden age from about 250 to 900 AD, the so-called Classic period. One of the largest cities was **Tikal** in the rainforest of present-day Guatemala, with temple pyramids over 60 metres high. On Yucatán lies **Chichén Itzá** with the stepped pyramid “El Castillo”. Other well-known cities are Palenque and Copán. Around the year 900 many cities in the lowlands were abandoned, probably because of droughts, wars and overuse of the soil.

The Maya calculated with a **base-20 system**, that is, with the base 20. They wrote numbers with dots for one and bars for five. For **zero** they had a sign of their own, which often looked like a shell. With several calendars, including a year of 365 days, they observed the sun, the moon and Venus very exactly.

The Maya had a fully developed **hieroglyphic script** with hundreds of signs. They wrote on stone columns, on vessels and in folding books of bark paper. Spanish missionaries such as Diego de Landa had many of these books burnt in the 16th century. Today only four manuscripts survive, one of them the **Dresden Codex** in Dresden.

The most important food of the Maya was **maize**; in their myths people were even created from maize dough. They also grew beans, pumpkins and chilli. From early on they made a bitter drink from the beans of the **cocoa plant**. Cocoa beans were so valuable that they were also used as a means of payment.

The Maya have not vanished. Today several million **Maya** still live, above all in Guatemala and in the south of Mexico. They speak about 30 different **Mayan languages**, for example Yucatec or K'iche'. Many keep up old traditions such as colourful woven clothing, festivals and markets.

begriffe.erklaerung: A city that forms a small state of its own together with its surrounding land.
Written signs that often look like small pictures.
A number system that counts in steps of twenty instead of steps of ten.
An old book written by hand.

gewusst: Many people believed that the Maya calendar predicted the end of the world for 2012, but on that day only a new great period of time began.
The Maya played a ball game in which the heavy rubber ball was not allowed to be touched with the hands.
Because they counted with fingers and toes, the Maya probably arrived at the base 20.

teile.einleitung: From 1414 to 1418 bishops, princes and scholars from all over Europe met in Constance on Lake Constance. The Council of Constance was meant to end the split in the Church, in which three popes were ruling at the same time. It also had consequences for the Swiss Confederation.
wichtigste: The council met from 1414 to 1418 in Constance.
King Sigismund worked for the council.
With “Haec sancta” the council in 1415 declared itself above the pope.
In 1417 Martin V was elected pope, and with that the schism ended.
Jan Hus and Jerome of Prague were condemned and executed.
Because Duke Frederick IV helped a pope to escape, the Confederates conquered Aargau in 1415.

abschnitte.text: At the start of the 15th century there were **three popes** at the same time, who did not recognise one another. This is called the **Western Schism**. The Roman-German king **Sigismund** pressed for this quarrel to be ended. He invited people to a **council** in Constance. A council is a great assembly of the Church. For about four years bishops, princes and scholars met there.

In the year 1415 the council passed the decree **Haec sancta**. It states that a general council has its power directly from Christ and that even the pope must obey it. In 1417 followed the decree **Frequens**. It prescribed holding councils regularly: the next after five years, then after seven and after that every ten. In this way the Church was to be reformed lastingly. On 11 November 1417 **Martin V** was elected. It is regarded as the only papal election on German soil.

The council also dealt with teachings that it considered false. The Prague scholar **Jan Hus** sharply criticised the Church. He was condemned in 1415 and executed at the stake. A year later the same sentence struck his companion **Jerome of Prague**. In Bohemia this led to years of fighting, the Hussite Wars.

In March 1415 the Pisan pope **John XXIII** fled secretly and in disguise to **Schaffhausen**. He wanted to break up the council. He had been helped by **Duke Frederick IV of Austria**, a Habsburg. King Sigismund then put Frederick under the **imperial ban**. He called on the Confederates to occupy his territories. So Bern, Zurich, Lucerne and other places conquered the Habsburg **Aargau** in 1415.

Today a large statue in Constance recalls the council. The rotating figure **Imperia** by the artist **Peter Lenk** has stood at the harbour entrance since 1993. It mocks the powerful of that time. In her hands she holds two small figures representing an emperor and a pope.

gewusst: The election of Martin V in Constance in 1417 is regarded as the only papal election on German soil.
That Aargau came to the Confederation is connected with the flight of a pope.

teile.einleitung: Minnesang was a kind of love song in the Middle Ages. Poets and singers performed them at the courts of the nobles and in them mostly praised a noble lady.
wichtigste: “Minne” is an old German word for love.
A minnesinger composed songs and sang them himself.
He performed at the courts of the nobles.
Walther von der Vogelweide is regarded as the most famous minnesinger.
The Codex Manesse was made around 1300 in Zurich.
Today it lies in Heidelberg University Library.

abschnitte.text: The word **Minne** is an old German word for **love**. Minnesang therefore means love singing. A **minnesinger** composed his songs and performed them himself. He was poet and singer at once. The minnesingers travelled from court to court and sang before the nobles and their guests.

Usually the minnesinger sang for a **noble lady**. In **high love** he adored a high-ranking lady who was out of his reach. This love remained unfulfilled. It was meant to make the singer a better person. Loyalty, patience and good manners were important themes.

Probably the most famous minnesinger is **Walther von der Vogelweide**. He lived around **1200**. He wrote not only love songs but also songs about politics and life. Some of his verses schoolchildren still get to know today.

The **Codex Manesse** is the most famous song manuscript. It was written around **1300** in **Zurich**. It contains songs and colourful pictures of many minnesingers. Today it lies in **Heidelberg University Library**. That is why it is also called the “Great Heidelberg Song Manuscript”. The Zurich man **Johannes Hadlaub** wrote love songs himself and knew the Manesse family, who collected songs.

In the late Middle Ages **mastersingers** continued the art. They were mostly **craftsmen** in towns such as Nuremberg and Mainz. They practised in schools of their own according to strict rules. Their best-known representative is **Hans Sachs**.

gewusst: In the Codex Manesse almost every poet is shown with a full-page coloured picture.
Several nobles from present-day Switzerland are also represented in the Codex Manesse.

teile.einleitung: Averroes, in Arabic Ibn Rushd, was a philosopher, doctor and judge from Córdoba in al-Andalus. His commentaries on Aristotle shaped thinking at the universities of Europe.
wichtigste: Averroes was born in Córdoba in 1126.
He came from a respected family of legal scholars.
He wrote commentaries on almost all the works of Aristotle.
In the Latin Middle Ages he was simply called “the Commentator”.
Against al-Ghazali he wrote “The Incoherence of the Incoherence”.
He was a qadi, that is, a judge, and personal physician to the caliph.
He died in Marrakesh in 1198.

abschnitte.text: **Ibn Rushd** was born in **Córdoba** in the year **1126**. At that time the city lay in **al-Andalus**, the Muslim part of Spain. His family was famous for legal scholars, and his grandfather had already been chief judge. Ibn Rushd studied law, medicine and philosophy. In Europe his name became **Averroes**.

Averroes worked as a **qadi**, which is a judge, in **Seville** and Córdoba among other places. He was also **personal physician** to the caliph of the **Almohads**, a ruling family in North Africa and Spain. At times he fell out of favour and was banished. Later he was called back to the court in North Africa. He died in **Marrakesh** in 1198.

Averroes was concerned above all with the Greek philosopher **Aristotle**. He wrote short, medium and great **commentaries** on almost all his works. These explanations were translated into Latin. At the universities of Europe, Aristotle was called “the Philosopher” and Averroes simply **“the Commentator”**.

The scholar **al-Ghazali** had written a book with the title “The Incoherence of the Philosophers”. In it he attacked the philosophers. Averroes replied with **“The Incoherence of the Incoherence”** and refuted him point by point. He believed that reason and faith do not contradict each other. In Paris in the 13th century, **Latin Averroism** arose, represented for example by Siger of Brabant. The Church condemned some of these teachings, and Thomas Aquinas wrote against them.

gewusst: The painter Raphael shows Averroes in his famous picture “The School of Athens”.
A crater on the Moon is named after Ibn Rushd.

teile.einleitung: Kings and emperors showed their power with special signs. The most important were the crown, the sceptre and the orb. They are called regalia or insignia.
wichtigste: The crown is the most important sign of a king.
The sceptre is a decorated ruler's staff.
The orb is a golden ball with a cross.
Crowns were mostly made of gold and precious stones.
The king sat on a throne.
The old imperial crown lies in the Treasury in Vienna and has eight sides.

abschnitte.text: The **crown** is the most important sign of a king. He wears it on his head. Crowns were mostly made of **gold** and decorated with **precious stones** and pearls. In this way they showed wealth and power. When a new king took up office, he was solemnly **crowned**. The crown was placed on his head.

The **sceptre** is a decorated staff. The king holds it in his hand as a sign of his power. The **orb** is a golden ball with a cross on it. The ball stands for the world over which the ruler reigns. The cross shows that he is a Christian ruler. Crown, sceptre and orb are together called **regalia**.

The **throne** is the ruler's seat of honour. It often stands raised, so that everyone looks up to the king. Sitting on the throne the king received guests and gave judgement. By the crown, sceptre and throne everyone knew at once **who the ruler is**.

The emperors of the **Holy Roman Empire** had a special crown, the **imperial crown**. It is about 1000 years old. It consists of **eight plates** of gold and so has eight sides. On the plates sit many precious stones and pearls. Today it can be seen in the **Treasury in Vienna** together with other regalia.

gewusst: The imperial crown does not have a round but an octagonal shape.
The word “sceptre” comes from Greek and means staff.

teile.einleitung: After the voyage of Columbus in 1492 a great exchange began between the Americas and the rest of the world. Plants and animals, but also diseases, travelled across the Atlantic. This is called the Columbian Exchange.
wichtigste: The historian Alfred W. Crosby coined the term in 1972.
From America the tomato, maize, potato, cocoa and tobacco came to Europe.
The turkey also came from America to Europe.
Europeans brought wheat, pigs, cattle and horses to America.
On sugar cane plantations in America, enslaved people from Africa had to work.
Diseases from Europe killed very many native people of America.

abschnitte.text: The historian **Alfred W. Crosby** published the book “The Columbian Exchange” in 1972. The title became a technical term. It describes how, after the voyages of **Christopher Columbus**, two worlds that had long been separate came together. The Old World is Europe, Asia and Africa. The New World is America.

Many foods originally come from America. The **tomato** was grown in Central America and came to Europe in the 16th century. In Italy it became important only later. **Maize**, **potatoes** and **pumpkins** also came from America. The seeds of the **cocoa tree** were already made into a drink by the Maya and Aztecs. In the 19th century Swiss makers made **chocolate** world famous. Among animals, the **turkey** came from Mexico to Europe.

In the other direction Europeans brought **wheat** from western Asia to America. The Spanish brought **pigs** and **cattle**, which multiplied quickly there. Horses, chickens, sheep and goats also came newly to America. They changed farming and the landscape greatly. **Sugar cane** comes from Asia and was grown on large plantations in the Caribbean and in Brazil.

For the hard work on the sugar cane plantations, millions of people from Africa were taken away and **enslaved**. The Europeans also brought diseases such as **smallpox**. The native people of America had no protection against them, and very many died. So the Columbian Exchange brought new food, but also great suffering.

Already in 1492 Columbus and his men saw locals smoking **tobacco leaves**. In the 16th century tobacco came to Europe. At first it was even thought to be a **medicinal plant**. Today we know that smoking greatly harms health.

gewusst: Before Columbus there were no tomatoes in Italy and no potatoes in Switzerland.
The chocolate for which Switzerland is famous is based on a plant from America.

teile.einleitung: In the Middle Ages craftsmen made almost everything that people needed in daily life, from shoes through pots to houses. Most craftsmen lived in the towns and had their workshops there. They joined together in guilds, which had great influence in towns such as Zurich or Basel.
wichtigste: The smith made horseshoes and tools of iron, the potter pots and jugs of clay.
The miller made flour from grain, the shoemaker shoes and the tailor clothes.
Whoever learnt a craft was first an apprentice, after the apprenticeship a journeyman.
Only a master was allowed to run a workshop of his own.
The craftsmen of a town joined together in guilds.
In Zurich the Böögg is burnt at the Sechseläuten.
Many family names such as Müller, Schmid or Schneider come from crafts.

abschnitte.text: In the Middle Ages there were very many crafts. The **smith** made horseshoes, nails and tools of iron, the **potter** shaped pots and jugs of clay. The mason built houses of stone, the carpenter roof frames of wood. Bakers, butchers, tanners, weavers, tailors and shoemakers provided food and clothing.

A boy began at about twelve to fourteen years old as an **apprentice** with a master. He lived in the master's house and learnt the craft for several years. After the apprenticeship he became a **journeyman** and often went on his **travels**, to learn new things in other towns. Whoever made a **masterpiece** and had enough money could become a master himself and run a workshop.

The craftsmen of one trade joined together in **guilds**. The guild laid down how many masters there could be, how good the goods had to be and what prices applied. It also helped sick members and widows. In many towns the guilds even had a say in the government, in Zurich for example since the guild charter of **Rudolf Brun** in the year 1336.

Craftsmen of one trade often lived in the same lane. Street names such as Weavers' Lane or Tanners' Lane still bear witness to this today. The workshop was mostly on the ground floor of the house, and above it lived the family. Over the door there often hung a **guild sign**, so that even people who could not read recognised the trade.

The **Sechseläuten** is a spring festival of the Zurich guilds. The guild members parade through the town in historical costumes. In the evening the **Böögg** is burnt on the Sechseläutenplatz, a snowman made of cotton wool that is stuffed with fireworks. The faster his head explodes, the lovelier the summer is to be, or so people say.

Many family names recall old trades, for example **Müller** (miller), Schmid (smith), Schneider (tailor), Becker (baker) or Zimmermann (carpenter). In Switzerland there are still guild houses today, for example in Zurich, Basel and Bern, which often serve as restaurants. The training as an apprentice has survived to this day in the **vocational apprenticeship**. About two thirds of young people in Switzerland do an apprenticeship after school.

begriffe.erklaerung: An association of craftsmen of the same trade in a town.
A craftsman who has completed his apprenticeship but is not yet a master.
A particularly good piece of work with which a journeyman shows that he can become a master.
A snowman made of cotton wool that is burnt at the Zurich Sechseläuten.

gewusst: The name Sechseläuten comes from the fact that in summer the bell used to ring in the end of the working day at six in the evening.
On their travels, journeymen often were not allowed to come near their home town for a certain time.
Müller is the most common family name in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: The Lombards were a Germanic people who moved to Italy in the year 568 and founded a kingdom of their own there. To this day the name of the region of Lombardy recalls them.
wichtigste: The Lombards moved from Pannonia to Italy in 568 under King Alboin.
This migration is often seen as the end of the Migration Period.
Their capital was Pavia, south of Milan.
Lombardy is named after the Lombards.
In 643 King Rothari had the law of his people written down.
In the year 774 Charlemagne conquered the Lombard kingdom.

abschnitte.text: The Lombards lived first on the Elbe and later in **Pannonia**, an area in present-day Hungary. In the year **568** King **Alboin** led his people over the Alps into northern Italy. He conquered large parts of the north. Many experts see in this march the end of the **Migration Period**. Alboin himself was murdered in Verona in 572.

abschnitte.titel: A kingdom with Pavia as capital
abschnitte.text: The kingdom of the Lombards had its most important royal seat in **Pavia**. There the kings were elected and installed. The land they ruled was called “Langobardia”. From it came the name **Lombardy**. The capital of this region today is Milan.

In the year **643** King **Rothari** had the legal customs of his people written down. This **Edict of Rothari** is written in Latin. Before that the law was passed on only orally. Queen **Theodelinda**, a Bavarian prince's daughter, promoted the Catholic faith. She was in correspondence with Pope Gregory the Great and founded a church in **Monza**.

In the cathedral of Monza lies the famous **Iron Crown**. According to legend its inner band contains a piece of a nail from the Cross of Christ. With this crown several rulers were later crowned kings of Italy. It is still an important sign of the history of Italy today.

The last king of the Lombards was **Desiderius**. Charlemagne besieged Pavia, and the city had to surrender in **774**. Desiderius was taken prisoner and spent the rest of his life in a Frankish monastery. After that Charlemagne also called himself king of the Lombards. The kingdom thus became part of the Frankish Empire.

gewusst: According to a legend told by Paul the Deacon, “Langobarden” means something like “long beards”.
In Ticino too the Lombards ruled for a time, so traces from their period can be found there.

teile.einleitung: The Hagia Sophia is a huge domed building in Istanbul in Turkey. It was built in the 6th century as a church, later it was a mosque and then a museum. Its mighty dome was for a long time a wonder of architecture.
wichtigste: The name Hagia Sophia means “Holy Wisdom”.
Emperor Justinian had it built.
The building took about five years and was finished in 537.
The master builders were called Anthemius and Isidore.
It is famous for its huge dome.
After 1453 it became a mosque, in the 1930s a museum.
Today four minarets stand beside it.

abschnitte.text: The city of Istanbul used to be called **Constantinople** and was the capital of the Byzantine Empire. There Emperor **Justinian** had a new, splendid church built. Its name is Greek and means **“Holy Wisdom”**. It was planned by the two master builders **Anthemius and Isidore**. The building went very fast: after **about five years** the church was finished in **537**.

Most famous is the **huge dome**. It has a diameter of over 30 metres and seems to float above the space. At the foot of the dome many windows sit in a circle. As a result it looks as if the dome rests on light. After earthquakes the first dome partly collapsed and was rebuilt higher. For almost a thousand years the Hagia Sophia was the largest church in the world.

In the year **1453** the Ottomans under Sultan Mehmed II conquered Constantinople. After that the Hagia Sophia became a **mosque**. Towers from which people are called to prayer, the **minarets**, were built round it. Today **four minarets** stand there. Many Christian mosaics were covered over, and large panels with Arabic writing were added.

After the end of the Ottoman Empire, Turkey became a republic. Its founder **Atatürk** had the Hagia Sophia made into a **museum** in the **1930s**. The old mosaics were uncovered again. In the year 2020 it was declared a mosque again. Visitors may still look round it, however. It is part of the **UNESCO World Heritage Site** of the old town of Istanbul.

gewusst: For almost a thousand years the Hagia Sophia was the largest church in the world.
Many later mosques in Istanbul, for example the Blue Mosque, were built on the model of the Hagia Sophia.

teile.einleitung: Kublai Khan was a grandson of Genghis Khan and one of the most powerful rulers of the Middle Ages. He became Great Khan of the Mongols and founded the Yuan dynasty in China.
wichtigste: Kublai was a grandson of Genghis Khan and a son of Tolui.
In 1260 he became Great Khan of the Mongols.
In 1271 he founded the Yuan dynasty in China.
His capital Dadu lay on the site of present-day Beijing.
His summer residence Shangdu became famous as “Xanadu”.
Two attacks on Japan in 1274 and 1281 failed, partly because of storms.
The lama Phagpa created a new script for him.

abschnitte.text: **Kublai** was a son of **Tolui**, the youngest son of **Genghis Khan**. So he was his grandson. In the year 1260 he had himself proclaimed **Great Khan** of the Mongols. A Great Khan was the supreme ruler of all Mongols. After that Kublai first had to assert himself against his brother **Ariq Böke**, who also wanted to be Great Khan.

In the year 1271 Kublai gave his rule in China the name **Yuan**. In this way he founded the **Yuan dynasty** and ruled as Chinese emperor. From 1267 he had the new capital **Dadu** laid out according to plan. The Mongols called it Khanbaliq, “city of the Khan”. It lies in present-day **Beijing**. The merchant **Marco Polo** of Venice later described Kublai's splendid court.

The city of **Shangdu** north of Beijing served as a summer residence. The English poet Coleridge made it, as **Xanadu**, a symbol of splendour. Kublai wanted a single script for his great empire. The Tibetan lama **Phagpa** created in 1269 an alphabet for Mongolian, Chinese and other languages. This **Phagspa script**, however, did not catch on in everyday life.

Kublai tried twice to conquer **Japan**, in 1274 and 1281. Both times his fleets failed. Japanese warriors put up resistance, and **typhoons** destroyed large parts of the ships. The Japanese interpreted the storms as **kamikaze**, which means “divine wind”.

The Yuan divided the population into four groups. At the very top stood the **Mongols**. After them came the **Semu**, people from central and western Asia. Then followed the northern Chinese, called Han. At the very bottom stood the **southern Chinese**, who had been conquered last. They had the fewest rights.

gewusst: The word “Xanadu” for a place full of splendour goes back to Kublai's summer residence Shangdu.
The Japanese word “kamikaze” originally means “divine wind”.

teile.einleitung: The Gothic is a style of building from the Middle Ages. It arose around 1140 in France and then spread across the whole of Europe. Typical are tall churches with pointed arches and large, colourful windows.
wichtigste: The Gothic arose in France.
The typical feature is the pointed arch.
Gothic churches are tall and have large windows.
Flying buttresses on the outside carry the pressure of the vaults away.
Gargoyles lead rainwater away from the roofs.
Bern Minster has the tallest church tower in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: Before the Gothic, churches were built with thick walls, small windows and round arches. This older style is called **Romanesque**. In the Gothic people wanted to reach **high** and bring a lot of **light** into the churches. The new churches were meant to look like a picture of heaven. The Gothic arose around 1140 in **France**, at the church of Saint-Denis near Paris.

The most important feature of the Gothic is the **pointed arch**. It comes to a point at the top. A pointed arch carries the weight downwards better than a round arch. So it was possible to build higher. The ceilings consist of **rib vaults**, in which stone ribs cross like a net.

On the outside of Gothic churches there are often **buttresses** with **flying buttresses**. They support the tall walls and **carry the pressure of the vaults outwards**. In this way the walls needed less stone and had room for huge windows. On the roof there are often stone figures with rainwater running from their mouths. They are called **gargoyles** and often look like fabulous creatures.

Gothic churches have **large windows** with coloured glass. The windows show pictures from the Bible. A large round window is called a **rose window**. The fine stone patterns in the windows are called **tracery**. When the sun shines, the space is full of coloured lights.

abschnitte.titel: The Gothic in Switzerland and in Europe
abschnitte.text: In Switzerland **Bern Minster** is the best-known Gothic church. Its tower is about 100 metres high and so the **tallest church tower in Switzerland**. In Lausanne stands the **Cathedral of Notre-Dame**, a large Gothic cathedral above the town. Famous in Germany is **Cologne Cathedral** with its two very tall towers. It was begun in 1248 and finished only in 1880.

gewusst: The word “Gothic” was at first meant as an insult: the style was thought to be as crude as the Goths.
In Lausanne Cathedral, a tower watchman still calls out the hours every night.

teile.einleitung: In the Middle Ages not every place could simply hold a market. For that it needed market rights, a special right that a king or territorial lord granted.
wichtigste: Market rights were originally granted by the king, later also by territorial lords.
A market brought the lord customs duties and stall fees.
During the market the market peace applied.
Cloth was measured with the ell.
Cheats were put on show in the pillory.
Zurzach in Aargau was known for its fairs.

abschnitte.text: **Market rights** were a privilege. Originally the **king** granted them, later also princes and other **territorial lords**. A place with market rights was allowed to hold a market regularly. This was valuable, because a market brought traders, buyers and money to the place.

For the lord of a place a market was worthwhile. Traders had to pay **stall fees** for their stalls. On goods **customs duties** were often charged. This income flowed to the **market lord**. So many lords sought market rights for their places.

During the market the **market peace** applied. It guaranteed special protection from violence and quarrels. Anyone who used violence at the market was punished especially severely. A **market cross** or another sign often showed that this peace applied.

Cloth was measured with the **ell**. It corresponded roughly to the length of a forearm and differed from town to town. Often a measuring ell hung at the town hall or the church, so that nobody cheated. Dishonest traders were put on public show in the **pillory** as a punishment. The shame in front of everyone was part of the punishment.

Large markets often took place on church feast days, when many people came to the church service. That is why a large trade fair is still called a **Messe** in German, the same word as for the church Mass. The **Chilbi** in Switzerland also goes back to a church festival, the **Kirchweih**, the dedication feast of a church. In the late Middle Ages the **Zurzach fairs** on the Rhine in the present canton of Aargau were known far and wide. They attracted traders from many countries.

gewusst: The word “Chilbi” comes from “Kirchweih”, the festival of the consecration of a church.
On some old town halls one can still see units of length carved in stone today.

teile.einleitung: The House of Wisdom was a famous library and a place of learning in Baghdad. Here in the Middle Ages scholars translated many books into Arabic and carried on research themselves.
wichtigste: The House of Wisdom stood in Baghdad, the capital of the Abbasid caliphs on the river Tigris.
It was a large library in which scholars read, researched and learnt.
The most important task was translating scientific books into Arabic.
Many works came from Greek, others from Persian and Indian.
The caliphs supported the House, especially Caliph al-Mamun, who ruled from 813 to 833.
Mathematics, astronomy and medicine were especially important.
In 1258 the Mongols conquered Baghdad and destroyed many books.

abschnitte.text: Baghdad lies on the **Tigris** in present-day Iraq. In the 8th century the **Abbasids** made the city their capital. It soon became one of the largest and richest cities in the world. In the **House of Wisdom** the rulers collected books from many countries. Scholars came there to read, to write and to discuss with one another.

The scholars translated books from other languages into **Arabic**. Many works came from the ancient **Greeks**, for example on philosophy, medicine and geometry. In addition there were books from Persia and India. Through this work a lot of old knowledge was preserved that might otherwise have been lost. Later it also reached Europe by way of Spain and Italy and was translated into Latin there.

A **caliph** was the ruler of the Islamic empire. The caliphs in Baghdad paid translators and scholars and had valuable manuscripts collected. The House of Wisdom had its **golden age** under Caliph **al-Mamun**, who ruled from 813 to 833. He himself was very interested in science. Scholars of different religions and origins worked together.

In the circle of the House of Wisdom the mathematician **al-Khwarizmi** worked. From the title of his book on calculation came the word **algebra**, and from his name the word **algorithm**. He also spread the Indian numerals with the zero, which we know today as “Arabic numerals”. Other scholars observed the stars and measured the Earth.

In the year **1258** the **Mongols** conquered Baghdad. In the process the city was badly destroyed, and many books and libraries were lost. The end of the caliphate of Baghdad was a great turning point. But the knowledge lived on, because many writings had already been copied and taken to other cities.

gewusst: The numerals 0 to 9 that we use today came from India to Europe by way of Arabic scholars.
The word “algorithm” goes back to the name of the mathematician al-Khwarizmi.

teile.einleitung: Building a castle was an enormous task in the Middle Ages. Many craftsmen often worked together for years, and almost everything was done with the sheer muscle power of people and animals.
wichtigste: The building of a large castle often took many years.
The stones were mostly fetched from near the building site.
Oxen pulled the heavy carts with stones and timber.
Stonemasons shaped the stones with hammer and chisel.
Mortar made of lime, sand and water joined the stones.
Carpenters built scaffolding and roof frames from wood.

abschnitte.text: First the builder looked for a good site, for example on a rock or hill. Stones were heavy and hard to transport. So they were mostly quarried **very close by**. Often a lot of stone was already produced when digging the **moat**. Timber for scaffolding and roofs came from the woods nearby.

For heavy loads **oxen** were used. They are very strong and have great stamina. They pulled carts with stones, timber and sand to the building site. On the site itself, **cranes** lifted the stones up. Some of these wooden cranes were driven by a **treadwheel**, in which people walked as in a hamster wheel.

A **stonemason** is a craftsman who dresses stones. With **hammer and chisel** he knocked the rough lumps into shape. He worked especially carefully on corners, windows and gates. Many stonemasons scratched a sign of their own into their stones, the **mason's mark**. In this way it could later be seen who had made which stone and how much he had worked.

For the walls to hold, **mortar** was needed. It was mixed from burnt **lime**, sand and water and hardened over time. Castle walls were often several metres thick. Often they consisted of two shells of dressed stones, with rubble stones and mortar filled in between.

Nothing could be done without wood. The **carpenter** built **scaffolding**, stairs, floors and **roof frames**. In old walls one can still see small holes today in which the beams of the scaffolding were fixed. Because everything was done by hand, the building of a large castle often took **many years** or even decades. Many castles were later rebuilt and extended again and again.

gewusst: In Guédelon in France, craftsmen have been building a castle since 1997 using only the tools and methods of the Middle Ages.
In Switzerland there are hundreds of castles and castle ruins, many of them on hills and rocks.

teile.einleitung: The Carolingian Renaissance is the name given to the upswing in education, script and art under Charlemagne and his successors. Monasteries and bishops' seats became centres of knowledge.
wichtigste: Around 800 Charlemagne promoted education, script and the Church.
The Admonitio generalis of 789 is regarded as the programmatic document of this reform.
Scholars from all over Europe worked at Charlemagne's court, for example Alcuin.
The Plan of St Gall shows the ideal layout of a monastery.
Hrabanus Maurus was praised as the “teacher of Germany”.
Many ancient texts survive only in Carolingian copies.

abschnitte.titel: A reform for Church and school
abschnitte.text: **Renaissance** means rebirth. Charlemagne wanted clergy to be better educated and the texts of the Church to be free of errors. In the year 789 he issued the **Admonitio generalis**. Such a decree is called a **capitulary**. Among other things it demanded schools at monasteries and bishops' seats. Important books were also to be carefully corrected.

Charlemagne brought clever men from many countries to his court. The most important was **Alcuin** from England. His pupil **Hrabanus Maurus** later made the monastery school of Fulda famous and became archbishop of Mainz. He was praised as “Praeceptor Germaniae”, teacher of Germany. **Theodulf of Orléans** came from the Visigothic kingdom in Spain. He wrote the “Libri Carolini”, in which the Frankish court took a position against a Byzantine council of 787 on the **veneration of images**.

A special treasure lies in the **Abbey Library of St Gall**. It is the **Plan of St Gall**. It was made around 820 to 830 in the monastery of Reichenau on Lake Constance. The plan shows the ideal layout of a whole monastery complex with church, school, gardens and workshops. It is the earliest surviving drawing of a monastery complex from the Middle Ages.

In the scriptoria of the monasteries monks copied books by hand. For this a new, easily readable script arose, the **Carolingian minuscule**. Our lower-case letters today go back to it. The monks copied not only the Bible but also works by Roman authors. For many **ancient texts** these Carolingian copies are the oldest surviving evidence.

gewusst: Without the copies made by Carolingian monks many works of Roman writers would be lost.
The Plan of St Gall is over 1200 years old.

teile.einleitung: The Little Ice Age is the name given to a cooler period that lasted from about the 14th to the 19th century. It was not cold all the time, but there were many hard winters, wet summers and growing glaciers.
wichtigste: The Little Ice Age lasted from about the 14th to the 19th century.
From 1315 to 1317 the Great Famine struck northern Europe.
The St Mary Magdalene's flood of 1342 is regarded as the worst flood in central Europe.
The Maunder Minimum from about 1645 to 1715 was a time with very few sunspots.
The volcano Samalas erupted in 1257 and may have helped trigger the cooling.
Around 1850 the Alpine glaciers reached their last high point.

abschnitte.text: The **Little Ice Age** was not a real ice age. On average it was only somewhat cooler than before and after. But even small differences had great consequences. There were more hard winters and more rainy summers. Harvests often turned out badly, and people suffered from hunger and rising prices.

From 1315 to 1317 it rained almost without a break in northern Europe. The grain rotted in the fields. This **Great Famine** cost millions of people their lives, even before the Black Death came. In July 1342 days of rain led to the **St Mary Magdalene's flood** on the Rhine, Main and Danube. It is regarded as the worst flood in central Europe in thousands of years. The soil was washed away so heavily that the traces can still be found today.

Why it became cooler is not entirely clear. One cause was probably great **volcanic eruptions**. Their ash and gases in the air block sunlight. In the year 1257 the volcano **Samalas** erupted on the island of Lombok in Indonesia. It was one of the strongest eruptions in thousands of years. Its traces can be found in **ice cores** from Greenland and Antarctica.

The sun, too, was at times somewhat less active. This can be seen from the **sunspots**, dark places on the sun. From about 1645 to 1715 there were very few of them. This time is called the **Maunder Minimum**, after the astronomer Edward Walter Maunder. It fell in an especially cold phase of the Little Ice Age.

In the Alps the **glaciers** grew strongly. Some threatened Alpine pastures and villages. Around 1850 they reached their last **high point**. The **Rhône Glacier** in the Valais then reached far down into the valley. Since then the glaciers have been melting back strongly. In old pictures one can see well how big they once were.

gewusst: Traces of the eruption of 1257 can still be found today in the ice of Greenland and Antarctica.
Since the high point around 1850 the Alpine glaciers have lost a large part of their ice.

teile.einleitung: In the Middle Ages there were Jewish communities in many cities of Europe. They had a rich culture and learning, but were often put at a disadvantage, excluded and persecuted.
wichtigste: Speyer, Worms and Mainz formed the SchUM communities, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2021.
The scholar Rashi of Troyes wrote commentaries on the Bible and Talmud that are still important today.
Jews were regarded as “servants of the chamber” of the emperor and had to pay taxes for his protection.
In 1215 the Fourth Lateran Council demanded that Jews distinguish themselves by their clothing.
In 1290 King Edward I expelled all Jews from England.
Many trades were forbidden to Jews, so some worked in trade or moneylending.

abschnitte.text: On the Rhine lay three especially important Jewish communities: **Speyer**, **Worms** and **Mainz**. They are called the **SchUM communities**. The name is put together from the Hebrew initial letters of the city names: Shpira, Warmaisa and Magenza. They were centres of Jewish **learning**. Synagogues, ritual baths and cemeteries are preserved there to this day. Since **2021** they have been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

In the 11th century the scholar **Rashi** lived in **Troyes** in France. His name is an abbreviation of Rabbi Shlomo ben Yitzhak. He studied in Worms and Mainz. Rashi wrote **commentaries** on the Bible and on the **Talmud**, an important work of Jewish law and teaching. His commentaries are still printed in almost every edition of the Talmud.

In the Middle Ages Jews had a special legal position. In the empire they were regarded as “**servants of the chamber**” and came directly under the imperial chamber. The emperor was supposed to protect them, and in return they had to pay **taxes**. The emperor often pledged this income to cities or princes. Many trades and the guilds remained closed to Jews. So some worked in trade or **moneylending**.

The **Fourth Lateran Council** of **1215** laid down that Jews had to distinguish themselves from Christians by their **clothing**. From this came, for example, the pointed **Jewish hat** or a yellow ring on the garment. In many cities Jews had to live in lanes of their own. Again and again they were wrongly accused and attacked.

Some rulers expelled the Jews from their country altogether. King **Edward I** of **England** issued an edict of expulsion in **1290**. Only in the 17th century were Jews allowed to settle in England again. Jews were also expelled from France and later from Spain. In Switzerland Jews were for a long time later allowed to live only in **Endingen** and **Lengnau** in the canton of Aargau.

gewusst: The ritual bath in Speyer, the mikveh, is over 900 years old and can still be visited today.
In the Middle Ages many Jews in central Europe used a language of their own in everyday life, which later became Yiddish.

teile.einleitung: Frederick Barbarossa was a powerful emperor in the Middle Ages. His nickname means “Red Beard”. Legends cling to him to this day, especially well known in Germany.
wichtigste: Barbarossa is Italian and means “Red Beard”.
Frederick belonged to the ruling family of the Staufer.
In 1152 he was elected king, later he became emperor.
He marched several times with his army to Italy.
On a crusade he drowned in a river in 1190.
According to the legend he sleeps in the Kyffhäuser mountain.

abschnitte.titel: An emperor with a red beard
abschnitte.text: Frederick was born around 1122 and belonged to the family of the **Staufer**. In Italy he was called **Barbarossa**, which means **“Red Beard”**. In the year **1152** the princes elected him Roman-German king. In 1155 he was crowned **emperor** in Rome. He ruled over a large empire that included Germany, parts of Italy and also regions of present-day Switzerland.

Barbarossa marched several times with his army **to Italy**. There he wanted to enforce his power over the rich towns in the north. At the **Diet of Roncaglia** in 1158 he had it written down which **royal rights** belonged to him. These rights are called **regalia**, and they included tolls and the minting of coins. Many towns resisted this, and long wars followed.

As an old man Barbarossa set out on a **crusade** to the Holy Land. The route led through Asia Minor, present-day Turkey. In the year 1190 he **drowned in a river**. Whether he died while bathing or while crossing is not quite certain. His death was a great shock for the army.

Many people could not believe that the emperor was dead. So a **legend** arose. Barbarossa is said to sleep in the **Kyffhäuser** mountain in Thuringia. He sits at a table of stone, and **his beard grows through the table**. **Ravens** fly around the mountain. When one day they no longer fly, the emperor is to wake up and save his empire. Originally this legend was probably told of his grandson Frederick II.

gewusst: At the Kyffhäuser today there stands a large monument with a figure of the sleeping Barbarossa.
In the legend the emperor's beard must grow three times round the table before he wakes.

teile.einleitung: The castle chapel was the room in a castle in which people prayed and held services. In the Middle Ages faith was very important, so many castles had a little church of their own.
wichtigste: In the castle chapel people prayed and held services.
The services were mostly held by a chaplain.
In the small tower on the roof there was often a bell.
In double chapels the lord and lady sat upstairs, the household staff downstairs.
Celebrations such as a baptism could also take place in the chapel.
The altar mostly faced east.
The chapel was often in the palas or in a tower.

abschnitte.text: The way to the nearest village church was often long, and in times of danger people did not want to leave the castle. So many lords of the castle built a **castle chapel**. It was often in the **palas**, the residential building, or in a **tower**. Sometimes it stood as a small building of its own in the courtyard. A small tower on the roof often carried a **bell**, which called people to prayer.

The services were held by a **chaplain**. This is a priest who is responsible for a chapel or a family. Often he was one of the few people in the castle who could read and write well. So he sometimes also wrote letters and deeds for the lord of the castle. In the chapel masses were celebrated, and celebrations such as a **baptism** could take place.

The **altar** of a chapel mostly faced **east**. That is where the sun rises, and for Christians this was a sign of Christ and the Resurrection. This alignment is called **orientation**. In a chapel in a tower this was not always easy. Sometimes a small **oriel** was then built facing east, in which the altar had room.

Some castles had a **double chapel** with two storeys one above the other. In the middle there was an opening, so that one could look from the top down to the bottom. **Upstairs sat the lord and lady**, downstairs the household staff. A well-known double chapel stands in the Imperial Castle of Nuremberg. The walls of many castle chapels were decorated with coloured **wall paintings** that showed stories from the Bible.

gewusst: Because only a few people could read, the pictures on the walls told the stories of the Bible.
Many castle chapels are better preserved than the rest of the castle, because they continued to be used as churches.

teile.einleitung: The Franciscans are a Catholic order founded by Francis of Assisi in the 13th century. The brothers live simply, own nothing and care for the poor and the sick. In Switzerland too they and their branches have left many traces.
wichtigste: The official name is Ordo Fratrum Minorum, “Order of Friars Minor”.
In 1223 Pope Honorius III confirmed the rule of the order, the Regula bullata.
The Franciscans belong to the mendicant orders.
In the 16th century the reform branch of the Capuchins arose.
The Capuchins were very widespread in Catholic Switzerland.
From 1309 Queen Elisabeth founded the double monastery of Königsfelden.

abschnitte.text: The official Latin name of the order is **Ordo Fratrum Minorum**, abbreviated OFM. That means “Order of Friars Minor”. By this Francis of Assisi wanted to show that the brothers should feel small and modest. **Pope Honorius III** confirmed their rule in **1223** with a document, a **bull**. That is why it is called the **Regula bullata**.

The Franciscans wear a simple brown or grey habit with a cord as a belt. The cord has three knots that recall the three vows: poverty, chastity and obedience. As a **mendicant order** the brothers used to live on donations. They went into the **towns**, preached and helped the poor and the sick. Because many went barefoot or in sandals, they were also called **Barefoots**.

In the **16th century** some Franciscans wanted to live more strictly and more poorly again. In this way the reform branch of the **Capuchins** arose. The name comes from the pointed hood on their habit. The Capuchins were very widespread in **Catholic Switzerland**, for example in Central Switzerland and in the Valais. They preached, helped people in everyday life and were popular with the people.

In 1308 King **Albert I** was murdered near Windisch in the present-day canton of Aargau. At the place of the deed his widow, Queen **Elisabeth**, founded the monastery of **Königsfelden** from **1309**. It was a **double monastery** for Franciscans and Poor Clares. The monastery church is famous today for its coloured stained-glass windows from the 14th century. In Basel the Barfüsserkirche recalls the Franciscans, and today it houses a museum.

gewusst: The Franciscans' cord has three knots, one for each of their vows.
The drink cappuccino is said to be named after the brown colour of the Capuchin habits.

teile.einleitung: After the First Crusade, European knights founded four states of their own on the eastern coast of the Mediterranean. These Crusader States lasted for almost 200 years, until in 1291 the last great city, Acre, fell.
wichtigste: There were four Crusader States: Edessa, Antioch, Jerusalem and Tripoli.
The County of Tripoli was founded last, in 1109.
In French they were called together Outremer, “beyond the sea”.
In 1144 Zengi conquered Edessa, which triggered the Second Crusade.
The Krak des Chevaliers is regarded as the best-preserved Crusader castle.
The Teutonic Order arose in 1190 during the siege of Acre.
Sultan Baibars conquered Antioch in 1268.

abschnitte.text: In the **First Crusade** knights from Europe conquered territories in the Near East. In 1098 the **County of Edessa** and the **Principality of Antioch** arose. In 1099 they conquered Jerusalem and founded the **Kingdom of Jerusalem**. The last state to be added, in 1109, was the **County of Tripoli** in present-day Lebanon. The French called these territories together **Outremer**, which means “beyond the sea”.

The Crusader States were small and surrounded by Muslim rulers. In the year 1144 **Imad ad-Din Zengi**, the atabeg of Mosul and Aleppo, conquered the city of Edessa. An atabeg was a powerful prince. The loss shook Europe. So a **Second Crusade** was called, which however failed.

For protection the Crusaders built strong **castles**. The best known is the **Krak des Chevaliers** in Syria. From 1142 the **Hospitallers**, an order of knights, extended it. It is regarded as the best-preserved Crusader castle and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. In 1190 citizens from Bremen and Lübeck founded a field hospital during the siege of **Acre**. From this in 1198 the **Teutonic Order** arose, which later ruled in the Baltic.

In the 13th century the **Mamluks** in Egypt became very powerful. Their sultan **Baibars** conquered Antioch in 1268 and so ended the principality. He also took many castles from the Crusaders. In 1291 **Acre**, the last great city of the Crusaders, fell. With this the time of the Crusader States came to an end.

gewusst: The Krak des Chevaliers is so well preserved that one can still walk through its halls today.
The Teutonic Order began as a field hospital for sick Crusaders.

teile.einleitung: The Corpus iuris civilis is a great collection of Roman law. Emperor Justinian had it compiled in Constantinople in the 6th century. It shapes the law in Europe to this day.
wichtigste: In the 6th century, Emperor Justinian had Roman law collected.
The commission for this was led by the jurist Tribonian.
The most extensive part is the Digest, with extracts from the writings of classical jurists.
The Institutes were intended as a textbook for the teaching of law.
The Novels are new laws that Justinian issued after 534, most of them in Greek.
From the late 11th century the collection was taught scientifically in Bologna.
The name “Corpus iuris civilis” has been in general use only since the 16th century.

abschnitte.text: In the Roman Empire, over the centuries, countless laws and writings by jurists had accumulated. Nobody could keep an overview any more. So Emperor **Justinian I** decided to put everything in order. From **528** a commission worked on it. It was led by the jurist **Tribonian**. Within a few years a huge collection of law was produced.

The collection consists of four parts. The **Code** contains the laws of the emperors. The **Digest** is the most extensive part, with extracts from the writings of **classical Roman jurists**. The **Institutes** were a **textbook** for the teaching of law. Later came the **Novels**, that is, new laws that Justinian issued after 534. Most of the Novels survive in the original in **Greek**, because Greek was spoken in the east of the empire.

In the west of Europe the work was almost forgotten for a long time. From the late **11th century**, scholars in **Bologna** in Italy began to teach it scientifically. They wrote explanations in the margins of the texts. Students from all over Europe came to Bologna to learn Roman law. From this school one of the oldest universities in Europe developed.

The name **“Corpus iuris civilis”**, that is, “body of civil law”, has been in general use only since the **16th century**. At that time printed editions appeared under this title. Roman law influenced the law codes of many countries. In **Swiss civil law** too one finds terms and ideas that go back to Roman law, for example in contracts and property.

gewusst: The Digest consists of 50 books.
Those who study law often still learn Latin legal terms from Roman law today.

teile.einleitung: From the 9th to the 15th century the Khmer Empire was the most powerful empire in South-East Asia. Its centre lay at Angkor in present-day Cambodia, where huge temples are preserved to this day.
wichtigste: Jayavarman II is regarded as the founder of the Khmer Empire in the year 802.
The centre of the empire was Angkor in present-day Cambodia.
Huge water reservoirs, the barays, stored water for the rice fields.
Around 1200 Jayavarman VII had Angkor Thom built with the Bayon temple.
The most famous temple is Angkor Wat.
In 1431 the kingdom of Ayutthaya conquered the capital Angkor.

abschnitte.text: In the year 802 **Jayavarman II** had himself proclaimed universal ruler. In this way he made himself independent of Java. With him the time of **Angkor** begins. The Khmer are the people who still form the majority in **Cambodia** today. Their kings ruled over a large area in South-East Asia.

The Khmer built artificial water reservoirs several kilometres long. They are called **barays**. In them the rainwater of the rainy season was stored. In this way the **rice fields** could be irrigated even in the dry months. The reservoirs also had a religious meaning. Thanks to the abundant rice, very many people could live in the area of Angkor.

The Khmer kings had mighty temples built. The best known is **Angkor Wat** from the 12th century. Around 1200 **Jayavarman VII**, who was a Buddhist, ruled. He had the city of **Angkor Thom** built. In its centre stands the **Bayon**. This temple is famous for its towers with huge stone faces.

In the west the Thai kingdom grew ever stronger. In the year 1431 the kingdom of **Ayutthaya** in present-day Thailand took the capital Angkor. After that the Khmer kings moved their seat further south, to the area of today's capital Phnom Penh. The temples of Angkor are now a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

gewusst: Angkor Wat is shown on the flag of Cambodia.
Angkor Wat is regarded as one of the largest religious buildings in the world.

teile.einleitung: A helmet protects the head. In the Middle Ages knights wore various helmets of metal, which changed greatly over the centuries.
wichtigste: Early knights' helmets had a strip of metal over the nose at the front, the nasal.
The great helm covered the whole head and looked like an upturned pot.
Through narrow eye slits the knight could look out, small holes helped with breathing.
The visor is a part in front of the face that can be flipped up.
Helmets were mostly of iron or steel, and padding was worn underneath.

abschnitte.text: In the early Middle Ages warriors often wore a pointed or round helmet of iron. At the front it had a vertical strip of metal that protected the nose. This strip is called the **nasal**. The face otherwise stayed free, so the warrior could see and breathe well. Such helmets can be seen, for example, on the famous **Bayeux Tapestry**.

Later the **great helm** came into use. It covered the whole head and looked like an upturned pot. At the front it had narrow **eye slits** through which the knight looked out. Small holes helped with breathing. The great helm protected well, but one could see and hear little in it. Because the face could no longer be recognised, coats of arms on shield and clothing became important.

In the later Middle Ages many helmets got a **visor**. This is a movable part in front of the face. In battle the knight flipped it down to protect his face. At rest he flipped it up to see and breathe better. Well-known helmet shapes with a visor are the **bascinet** with its pointed snout and later the closed helmet of plate armour.

Helmets were made by an **armourer** or smith from iron or steel. He hammered the metal into the right shape. Under the helmet a padded cap was worn so that blows were cushioned. Often a mail covering for the throat and neck belonged with it. A good helmet was expensive, so only rich warriors could afford one.

gewusst: At tournaments knights often wore a large decoration of feathers or figures on the helmet, the crest.
Many knights' helmets from the Middle Ages can be seen in museums today, for example in the Swiss National Museum in Zurich.

teile.einleitung: Ibn Battuta was a traveller from Morocco in the 14th century. He was on the road for almost 30 years and visited countries from West Africa to China. His travel account is still famous today.
wichtigste: Ibn Battuta was born in 1304 in Tangier in Morocco.
In 1325 he set out to make the pilgrimage to Mecca.
He travelled through North Africa, Arabia, Asia and parts of Europe.
For some years he lived in India and travelled on as far as China.
On his last journey he crossed the Sahara and came to Timbuktu.
In all he was on the road for almost 30 years.
After his return a scribe set down his stories in a travel account.

abschnitte.text: Ibn Battuta was born in **1304** in **Tangier**. Tangier lies in **Morocco** in the north of Africa, very close to Spain. He was a **Muslim** and as a young man studied Islamic law. In 1325 he set off. He wanted to make the **pilgrimage to Mecca**, which is very important for Muslims. At that time he had no idea that he would be on the road for almost 30 years.

After Mecca Ibn Battuta travelled on and on. He visited **Egypt**, Syria, Persia and East Africa. He travelled with caravans, on ships and on horseback. Because he was learned, he was received kindly at many courts and was given presents. On his travels, however, he also ran into storms and was attacked by robbers.

For some years Ibn Battuta lived in **India**. There he worked as a judge for the Sultan of Delhi. Later he visited the Maldives and travelled across the sea as far as **China**. In all he covered very many tens of thousands of kilometres on his travels. This makes him one of the greatest travellers of the Middle Ages.

After his return to Morocco, Ibn Battuta set out once more. On his last journey he crossed the **Sahara**. He came to the empire of **Mali** and to the famous desert city of **Timbuktu**. Mali was then very rich through the trade in gold. Around 1354 he came home for good.

A **travel account** is a book about a journey. Ibn Battuta did not write his own. He told everything, and a scribe called **Ibn Juzayy** set it down. In this way the **Rihla** arose, the Arabic word for journey. The book describes cities, rulers, foods and customs of many countries. For historical research it is an important source.

gewusst: Ibn Battuta travelled further than Marco Polo, who was on the road about 50 years before him.
A crater on the Moon is named after Ibn Battuta.

teile.einleitung: Leif Eriksson was a Viking who sailed to North America around the year 1000. He is regarded as one of the first Europeans to set foot in America, some 500 years before Columbus.
wichtigste: Leif Eriksson lived in Greenland and sailed from there to the west.
Around the year 1000 he reached North America.
He called the land Vinland.
On the way he saw Helluland and Markland.
His epithet was “the Lucky”.
Remains of a Viking village were found at L'Anse aux Meadows in Canada.

abschnitte.text: Leif was the son of **Erik the Red**. The name **Eriksson** therefore means “son of Erik”. The family lived in **Greenland**. According to the saga, **Bjarni Herjólfsson** had already seen an unknown coast in the west around 986 but had not gone ashore. Leif later bought his ship and followed his report.

On his voyage Leif found first **Helluland**, the “land of flat stones”, probably Baffin Island. Next came **Markland**, the “forest land”, probably Labrador. Finally he reached **Vinland**. The name probably means wine land, because according to the saga wild grapes grew there. Where exactly Vinland lay is still not certain.

Our knowledge comes above all from the **sagas**, old tales from Iceland. They also report on the people whom the Vikings met in America. The Vikings called them **Skraelings**. There was trade, but also fighting. So the Vikings did not stay long.

For a long time nobody knew whether the sagas were true. In the 1960s remains of Viking houses were found at **L'Anse aux Meadows** on **Newfoundland**. Newfoundland belongs to **Canada**. The find shows that Vikings really were in America. The site is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

gewusst: Leif is said to have rescued sailors from distress at sea on one voyage, which is why he was called “Leif the Lucky”.
Columbus reached America only in 1492, so about 500 years after Leif.

teile.einleitung: In the Middle Ages houses had no water pipes. Water was fetched at the fountain, which was also an important meeting place. In Swiss towns such as Bern, many old fountains still stand today.
wichtigste: Most townspeople fetched their water at the fountain.
Often maids and children carried the water home in buckets.
At the fountain people met neighbours and swapped news.
In a fire, fountain water was needed for putting it out.
In a running fountain the water flows constantly.
The troughs were mostly made of stone.
Bern is famous for its painted figure fountains from the 16th century.

abschnitte.text: In the Middle Ages there were no **water pipes** in the houses. Whoever needed water had to fetch it at the **fountain**. It was carried home in **buckets**. This daily job was often done by **maids** or the family's **children**. Water was needed for drinking, cooking, washing and for the animals.

abschnitte.titel: The fountain as a meeting place
abschnitte.text: Every day many people met at the fountain. While they waited, they told each other the **news** of the town. So the fountain was also a place for a chat. Fountain masters, who looked after the fountain, kept order. Whoever fouled the water could be punished.

In a **running fountain** the water comes through **pipes** from a **spring**, often from outside the town. In the past the pipes were made of hollowed tree trunks. The water flows **day and night** from the pipe into the **trough**. The troughs were mostly made of **stone**, because stone is strong and lasts long. That is why many old fountains still stand today.

The houses were often made of wood and stood close together. A **fire** was therefore very dangerous. When a fire broke out, people formed a **chain**. They passed **buckets** of water from the fountain from hand to hand. So it was important that the fountains always had water.

In the old town of **Bern** there are many fountains with brightly painted **figures** from the **16th century**. The old town is a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**. On the **Zähringer Fountain** stands a **bear** in knight's armour holding a flag. The bear is the heraldic animal of Bern. Another well-known fountain is the Kindlifresser Fountain, the “Child Eater” Fountain.

gewusst: In Basel there are very many public fountains, and from almost all of them drinking water flows.
Many of the figures on the Bern fountains were made by the sculptor Hans Gieng.

teile.einleitung: A moat is a wide, deep ditch in front of the castle wall. It was one of the most important means of protecting a castle, because it kept enemies at a distance.
wichtigste: A moat protected the castle because enemies could hardly reach the wall.
Moats could be filled with water or be dry.
A ditch without water is called a dry moat.
A neck ditch separates a castle on a ridge from the rest of the hill.
Attackers often tried to fill the ditch with earth and wood.

abschnitte.text: A moat made it very hard for attackers to reach the **castle wall**. Ladders, battering rams and siege towers could not simply be pushed up. Whoever wanted to cross the ditch was defenceless against the defenders on the wall. Over the moat there was usually a **drawbridge**, which could be pulled up in danger.

For castles on flat land, the moat was often filled with **water** from a stream or river. Such castles are called **water castles**. A well-known example in Switzerland is **Hallwyl Castle** in the canton of Aargau. On mountains this was hardly possible. There a **dry moat** was dug, that is, a ditch without water, but deep and steep.

Many castles stand on a narrow **ridge** or rocky spur. On three sides they are protected by steep slopes. Only on one side is the approach flat. Exactly there a deep ditch was dug right across the hill. It is called a **neck ditch**, because it cuts the castle off from the rest of the hill as if at the neck. The stones that were broken out were often used straight away for building the walls.

Attackers knew how important the ditch was. So they often tried to **fill it with earth, stones and wood**. For this they also used bundles of branches. Once the ditch was full, they could bring ladders and equipment up to the wall. The defenders tried to prevent this with arrows and stones.

gewusst: At many castle ruins in Switzerland the neck ditch can still be seen well today, even if hardly anything is left of the castle.
In some castle moats animals were later kept, for example deer or bears.

teile.einleitung: From the 13th to the 15th century the Mali Empire was a powerful empire in West Africa. It became rich and famous through the trade in gold and salt.
wichtigste: The Mali Empire lay in West Africa on the river Niger.
