According to tradition, Sundiata Keita founded the empire.
Around 1235 he won the battle of Kirina.
Gold from the south was exchanged for salt from the Sahara.
Ibn Battuta visited the empire in 1352.
In the 15th century the Songhai Empire replaced Mali as the strongest power.

abschnitte.text: The Mali Empire lay in the west of **Africa**. It stretched from the Atlantic coast far into the interior. Today the states of **Mali**, **Senegal** and **Guinea**, among others, lie there. Through the empire flowed the **Niger**, a long river. On it boats carried goods.

According to tradition, **Sundiata Keita** founded the empire. He lived almost 800 years ago. Around **1235** he defeated King **Sumanguru** of Sosso in the battle of **Kirina**. After that Mali became the greatest power in West Africa. The story of Sundiata is still told today.

In the south of the empire there was a lot of **gold**. In the desert, by contrast, there was **salt**, for example at **Taghaza**. There salt was broken out of the ground in large slabs. **Caravans** brought it south, where salt was scarce. Traders exchanged the two goods, and the empire earned from this.

Much knowledge about the Mali Empire comes from the **griots**. These are singers and storytellers in West Africa. They learnt the history of their people by heart. Over many generations they passed on songs and stories **orally**. In this way the memory of Sundiata stayed alive.

The traveller **Ibn Battuta** from Morocco visited the empire in **1352**. He travelled for almost 30 years through the world of the time. He described the king's court and the safety on the roads. In the **15th century** the **Songhai Empire**, with its capital at Gao, grew ever stronger and took over many cities of Mali.

gewusst: The present-day state of Mali is named after the old empire.
Salt was so valuable in West Africa that it was sometimes worth almost as much as gold.

teile.einleitung: Stained glass is the name for pictures made of coloured glass, such as one sees in church windows. In the Middle Ages splendid windows arose in many churches. When the sun shines through them, the colours inside glow like precious stones.
wichtigste: The pictures in church windows are made of coloured glass.
The pieces of glass were held together with lead.
In the Middle Ages glass was coloured with metal powder.
The windows showed stories from the Bible, because many people could not read.
A large, round window like a flower is called a rose window.
Famous are the windows of Königsfelden and those by Marc Chagall in the Fraumünster in Zurich.

abschnitte.text: For a church window many small pieces of **coloured glass** were needed. The glass was coloured as it was made. For this, **metal powder** was mixed into the hot molten glass. Cobalt gave a deep blue, copper green or red. Faces and folds were painted onto the glass with a dark paint and fired in.

The pieces of glass were put together like a jigsaw puzzle. Between them went narrow strips of **lead**. Lead is soft and bends well. So it could be laid round every piece of glass and soldered. The dark lines of lead frame the figures like the strokes in a drawing.

In the Middle Ages **many people could not read**. So the windows showed **stories from the Bible**, for example the birth of Jesus or pictures of saints. In this way everyone could understand the stories. Especially in the tall churches of the **Gothic** period there were huge windows. A large, round window that looks like a flower is called a **rose window**.

From outside the windows look rather dark. Only from inside can one see their full splendour. They glow most beautifully **when the sun shines**. Then coloured patches of light fall on the floor and walls. People were meant in this way to think of the light of God.

In the monastery church of **Königsfelden** in Aargau there are famous stained-glass windows from the 14th century. They are among the most beautiful medieval windows in Europe. In the **Fraumünster** in Zurich the artist **Marc Chagall** created five large, coloured windows around 1970. In **Romont** in the canton of Fribourg there is even a museum of its own for stained glass. In Switzerland small painted heraldic panes in windows were also popular.

gewusst: Some church windows from the Middle Ages are over 800 years old and still glow today.
Marc Chagall was already over 80 years old when he created the windows for the Fraumünster in Zurich.

teile.einleitung: Boniface was an English monk who spread Christianity in Germania in the 8th century. He founded bishoprics and monasteries and is therefore called the “Apostle of the Germans”.
wichtigste: Boniface was really called Winfrid and came from England.
In 719 Pope Gregory II gave him the task of mission work in Germania.
Before that he worked for some years with Willibrord, the “Apostle of the Frisians”.
In 723 he felled the Donar Oak at Geismar in Hesse.
His pupil Sturmi founded Fulda Abbey in 744.
In the end he led the Archbishopric of Mainz.
In 754 he was killed among the Frisians and buried in Fulda.

abschnitte.text: Boniface was born around **673** in the south-west of **England**. His original name was **Winfrid**. He became a monk and teacher in a monastery. But he wanted to spread the faith on the Continent. For some years he worked with **Willibrord**, the Archbishop of Utrecht, who did mission work among the Frisians and is called the “Apostle of the Frisians”.

In the year **719** Winfrid travelled to **Rome**. Pope **Gregory II** gave him the task of **mission work** in Germania. At that time he received the Latin name **Boniface**, which means roughly “benefactor”. He went above all to **Hesse** and **Thuringia**. There he founded churches and monasteries.

In the year **723** Boniface felled a great oak at **Geismar** in Hesse. It was consecrated to the Germanic god **Donar**. Boniface wanted to show that the old gods were powerless. When nothing happened to him, many people had themselves baptised. He is said to have built a chapel from the wood.

Boniface reorganised the **Church in the Frankish Empire**. He founded bishoprics and became Bishop of **Mainz**. As archbishop he had great influence. In the year **744** his pupil **Sturmi**, also called Sturmius, founded **Fulda Abbey** on his instructions. Sturmi became the first abbot, and the abbey became an important centre of learning.

Already over 80 years old, Boniface travelled once more to the **Frisians**. In the year **754** he was killed by robbers near **Dokkum** in the north of the present-day Netherlands. His body was taken to **Fulda**. His grave is today in **Fulda Cathedral**. Because of his work he is called the **“Apostle of the Germans”**.

gewusst: In Fulda the Catholic bishops of Germany meet regularly at the grave of Boniface.
The feast day of Boniface is 5 June.

teile.einleitung: The three-field system was the most important way of farming fields in the Middle Ages. The arable land of a village was divided into three large fields, and how each was used changed every year.
wichtigste: The arable land was divided into three large fields.
On one field winter grain grew, on one summer grain such as oats.
The third field lay fallow for a year so that the soil could recover.
The cattle grazed on the fallow and manured it with their dung.
The use of the three fields changed every year.
A peasant often owned a narrow strip of land in each field.
Because of the compulsory crop rotation, all peasants had to sow and harvest at the same time.

abschnitte.text: In the **three-field system** the arable land of a village was divided **into three** large fields. On the first, **winter grain** was sown in autumn, for example rye or wheat. On the second, **summer grain** was sown in spring, often **oats** or barley. The third field stayed without seed for a year. Such a field is called **fallow**.

The use of the three fields changed **every year**. Where winter grain had stood last year, summer grain now came. Where there had been summer grain, there was now fallow. So every field had a rest every three years. In this time the **soil could recover**. On the fallow the cattle grazed. Their **dung** fertilised the soil for the next year.

A peasant mostly did not own a whole field, but in each of the three fields a **narrow strip** of land. There were often no paths between the strips. So all peasants had to plough, sow and harvest at the same time. This rule was called the **compulsory rotation**. Otherwise, when working, one would have trampled the neighbours' crops.

Earlier the land was divided into only two parts. This **two-field system** let half of the fields lie fallow every year. With three fields only a third lay fallow. So more could be harvested and more people fed. In Switzerland the three fields were called **Zelgen**. Only in the 18th and 19th centuries was the three-field system replaced by new methods, for example by growing clover and potatoes on the fallow.

gewusst: Many field names in Switzerland still contain the word “Zelg” today.
Oats were important as feed for the horses.

teile.einleitung: The Byzantine Empire was the eastern part of the Roman Empire, which lasted almost 1000 years after the end of the West. Its capital was Constantinople, present-day Istanbul.
wichtigste: The Eastern Roman Empire in the Middle Ages is mostly called the Byzantine Empire.
The name comes from Byzantion, an old Greek settlement.
In its place the capital Constantinople arose.
In daily life and in the administration, Greek became established.
With Greek fire the Byzantines set enemy ships alight.
In 1054 the Church split, in the East-West Schism.
From the Church of the empire the Orthodox Church developed.

abschnitte.text: In the 4th century the Roman Empire was divided into a western and an eastern part. The West fell in the 5th century. The East, however, lived on. The people there still called themselves **Romans**. Only scholars of a later time called the empire the **Byzantine Empire**, after **Byzantion**, an old Greek settlement on the Bosporus.

Emperor **Constantine** built Byzantion up into a splendid new capital and dedicated it in the year 330. It was named after him **Constantinople**. The city lay between Europe and Asia and for a long time was one of the largest and richest cities in the world. Mighty walls protected it. Under Emperor Justinian the huge church **Hagia Sophia** was built in the 6th century.

At the beginning **Latin** was the language of administration and law. But most people in the East spoke **Greek**. In time Greek became established in daily life and administration. The scholars of the empire preserved many works of the ancient Greeks. Later many of these texts reached Italy and Western Europe.

The empire had many enemies and often had to defend itself. A feared weapon was **Greek fire**. It was a burning liquid that was sprayed through tubes onto enemy **ships**. It could hardly be put out with water. Exactly how Greek fire was made was a closely guarded secret and is still not known for certain today.

Faith was very important in the empire. In the 8th and 9th centuries there was the **dispute over images** about holy pictures. In the year **1054** the Church of the East and the Church of Rome separated. This split is called the **East-West Schism**. In the East the **Orthodox Church** developed. In 1453 the Ottomans conquered Constantinople, and the Byzantine Empire came to an end.

gewusst: The Byzantine Empire lasted for more than 1000 years, counting from the founding of Constantinople to 1453.
From the 7th century the Byzantine emperors bore the Greek title Basileus, which means king.
The number of Orthodox Christians in the world runs into hundreds of millions.

teile.einleitung: Cocoa comes from Central and South America. The Aztecs made a bitter drink from cocoa beans and even paid with them. The Spanish brought cocoa to Europe, and later milk chocolate was invented in Switzerland.
wichtigste: The Aztecs ground cocoa beans and made a drink from them.
The drink was bitter and spicy, because it was prepared without sugar and often with chilli.
Cocoa beans were so valuable that one could pay with them at the market.
Cocoa was drunk mainly by the ruler, nobles and warriors.
After the conquest of Mexico the Spanish brought cocoa to Europe.
Daniel Peter invented milk chocolate in Vevey in 1875.

abschnitte.text: Cocoa grows on the **cocoa tree**. It thrives only in warm, damp regions near the equator. Its large fruits grow directly on the trunk. Inside them are many **cocoa beans**. The **Maya**, and later the **Aztecs**, in Central America already used these beans. Today cocoa is grown mainly in West Africa.

The Aztecs ground the cocoa beans and mixed them with **water**. In this way a **drink** was made. They did not know sugar. So they often flavoured the drink with **chilli** and vanilla. It therefore tasted **bitter and spicy**. Cocoa was expensive. Above all the **ruler**, nobles and **warriors** were allowed to drink it.

Among the Aztecs cocoa beans were very **valuable**. One could pay with them at the **market**, for example for fruit or animals. So cocoa beans served as **money**. Even taxes to the ruler were partly paid in cocoa. Large quantities of it were kept in the rulers' storehouses.

After the conquest of **Mexico** in the 16th century the **Spanish** brought cocoa to **Spain**. There it was mixed with **sugar**, and now it tasted sweet. From Spain the drink spread across the whole of Europe. For a long time **drinking chocolate** was an expensive drink for rich people and nobles.

In the 19th century **Switzerland** became a famous chocolate country. **Daniel Peter** from **Vevey** on Lake Geneva was the first, in **1875**, to mix cocoa with **condensed milk**. In this way **milk chocolate** was created. In 1879 **Rudolf Lindt** in Bern invented **conching**. In this process the chocolate mass is stirred for a long time until it is especially fine and melts smoothly.

gewusst: The scientific name of the cocoa tree, Theobroma, means “food of the gods”.
People in Switzerland eat as much chocolate per head as hardly any other people.

teile.einleitung: A chinampa is an artificial garden in a shallow lake. The Aztecs laid out many such beds in the Valley of Mexico and so could grow a great deal of food for their large cities.
wichtigste: A chinampa is an artificial garden in a lake.
The Aztecs built chinampas from mud and plants.
Maize, beans and squash grew on them.
The plants thrived because they always had enough water.
At the edge, willows were planted so that the beds stayed firm.
Today chinampas can still be seen in Xochimilco near Mexico City.

abschnitte.text: The capital of the Aztecs, **Tenochtitlan**, lay on an island in a lake. There was little firm land there for fields. So people laid out long, narrow beds in the shallow water, the **chinampas**. Between them **canals** were left open, along which people travelled by boat. In this way a landscape of gardens and waterways arose.

First a rectangle was marked out with posts and twigs were woven between them. Then it was filled layer by layer with **mud** from the lake bottom and with **plant remains**, until the bed rose above the water. At the edge **willows** were planted. Their roots grew into the ground and held the chinampa fast, so that it did not slip away.

On the chinampas grew mainly **maize, beans and squash**, as well as chilli, tomatoes and flowers. The plants got **enough water** from below at all times. The mud from the canals was very fertile and fed the beds. So several harvests a year were possible. The chinampas helped to feed the many people in Tenochtitlan.

The great lake has almost disappeared today, and **Mexico City** stands in its place. But in **Xochimilco** on the southern edge of the city there are still canals and chinampas. Farmers there still grow vegetables and flowers. Visitors travel through the canals in colourful boats. Xochimilco, together with the old town of Mexico City, is a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

gewusst: The name Xochimilco means roughly “place of the flower fields” in the language of the Aztecs.
In the canals of Xochimilco lives the axolotl, a rare salamander that occurs in the wild only there.

teile.einleitung: The Golden Bull is an important law from the year 1356. In it Emperor Charles IV laid down how the king of the Holy Roman Empire is elected. It remained in force for about 450 years, until the end of the empire in 1806.
wichtigste: The Golden Bull was issued in 1356 by Emperor Charles IV.
It gets its name from the golden seal.
It was proclaimed at imperial diets in Nuremberg and Metz.
Seven electors chose the king.
The election took place in Frankfurt am Main, by a majority of the votes.
The Archbishop of Mainz invited the other electors to the election.
The secular electorates were not allowed to be divided.

abschnitte.titel: A law with a golden seal
abschnitte.text: A **bull** is an important document with a round seal. In the Golden Bull this seal was made of **gold**, which is where its name comes from. It was issued by **Emperor Charles IV** in the year **1356**. It was proclaimed at two **imperial diets**, that is, great assemblies: first in **Nuremberg**, then in **Metz**. It was the most important basic law of the empire.

The Golden Bull laid down that **seven electors** choose the king. The German word for electing, “küren”, is an old one. Three electors were clergymen: the archbishops of **Mainz**, **Cologne** and **Trier**. Four were secular princes: the **King of Bohemia**, the Count Palatine of the Rhine, the Duke of Saxony and the Margrave of Brandenburg. Other princes were not allowed to vote.

The **Archbishop of Mainz** had to invite the other electors to the election. The election was held in **Frankfurt am Main**. **Majority voting** applied: whoever got the most votes of the electors was king. Before that there could easily be disputes when two candidates both regarded themselves as elected. Afterwards the king was crowned in Aachen.

Each secular elector held an honorary office at court, a so-called **arch-office**. The King of Bohemia, for example, was **Arch-Cupbearer**. At feasts he handed the king the first cup. In addition, the Golden Bull laid down that the secular electorates were **not to be divided**. They always went to the **eldest son**. In this way the electors stayed powerful and their number stayed the same.

gewusst: Of the Golden Bull there are several originals, one of which lies in Frankfurt am Main.
The Golden Bull is part of the UNESCO Memory of the World.

teile.einleitung: In many villages there used to be a large linden tree in the middle of the place. Under the village linden people met, celebrated festivals and sometimes even held court.
wichtigste: The linden was the typical tree in the middle of the village.
Under the village linden people met and chatted.
Sometimes court was held under a linden.
A linden under which people danced is called a dance linden.
Linden leaves have the shape of a heart.
Tea can be made from linden blossoms.
Lindens can live to be several hundred years old.

abschnitte.titel: The tree in the middle of the village
abschnitte.text: The **village linden** usually stood on a square in the middle of the village, often by the church or the fountain. Its broad crown gave plenty of **shade** in summer. So it was a favourite **meeting place**. Here people met, chatted and swapped news. Often there was a bench under the tree.

In the Middle Ages, **court** was sometimes held in the open air. For this a linden was often chosen. It is called a **court linden**. Under the tree, disputes were settled and judgements pronounced. Meetings of the villagers also took place there when important things had to be discussed.

At festivals people danced under the linden. Such a tree is called a **dance linden**. On some dance lindens the branches were drawn out horizontally and a **wooden platform** was even built in them. In this way people could dance and make music in the crown of the tree. A few such dance lindens still exist today, mainly in Germany.

The leaves of the linden are **heart-shaped**. In early summer the linden blooms and smells sweet. Then many **bees** hum in the crown. From the dried blossoms one can make **linden blossom tea**, which is popular for colds. Lindens grow slowly and can live to be **several hundred years** old. Their soft wood is well suited to **carving**.

One of the best-known lindens in Switzerland stands in the hamlet of **Linn** in the canton of **Aargau**. It is several hundred years old and has an enormous trunk. The tree stands on a rise and can be seen from far away. Old **legends** twine around the linden of Linn. It is one of the mightiest trees in Switzerland.

gewusst: Many place names such as Linden, Lindau or Linn recall the linden.
Medieval wooden figures of saints were often carved from linden wood.

teile.einleitung: Mansa Musa was king of the Mali Empire in West Africa some 700 years ago. He is famous for his huge wealth and his pilgrimage to Mecca in the year 1324.
wichtigste: Mansa Musa ruled over the Mali Empire.
“Mansa” means something like king.
In 1324 he made a pilgrimage to Mecca.
He took a great deal of gold with him.
Because of him the value of gold fell in Cairo.
The Catalan Atlas of 1375 shows him with a ball of gold.

abschnitte.text: In the 14th century Mansa Musa ruled over the **Mali Empire**. The word **mansa** was the title of the rulers and means something like king or emperor. Mali was very rich through the trade in **gold**. Many experts regard Mansa Musa as one of the richest people who ever lived.

Mansa Musa was a **Muslim**. So in **1324** he set out on a long pilgrimage to **Mecca**. According to Arab reports, **many thousands of people**, servants and soldiers, accompanied him. The exact numbers are probably exaggerated, but the journey was enormous. **Camels** carried the heavy loads through the desert.

On the way Mansa Musa came through **Cairo**. There he spent so much gold and gave away so much that gold was worth less for years afterwards. Arab historians reported this. When there is suddenly a great deal of something, its price falls.

From his journey Mansa Musa brought scholars and artists back with him. One of them was the architect and poet **Al-Sahili** from **Granada** in Spain. He is said to have designed mosques and a palace in Mali. Cities such as **Timbuktu** became places of learning.

In Europe too people heard of Mansa Musa. The **Catalan Atlas** of **1375** was made on Majorca. It shows Mansa Musa on a throne with a crown and a ball of gold in his hand. In this way the king from Africa also became known to European merchants.

gewusst: How much gold Mansa Musa exactly owned nobody knows, so his wealth cannot be converted into francs.
The mud mosque Djinguereber in Timbuktu goes back to his time.

teile.einleitung: After the arrival of Christopher Columbus in 1492, European states began to conquer and settle the Americas. This is called the colonisation of the Americas. It changed two continents for ever and brought great suffering to the indigenous peoples and to millions of Africans taken away by force.
wichtigste: In 1494 the Treaty of Tordesillas divided the newly discovered territories between Spain and Portugal.
The Spanish conquerors in America were called conquistadors.
Because Brazil was a Portuguese colony, Portuguese is spoken there.
With the encomienda, Spanish settlers were allowed to force indigenous people to work and pay tribute.
Diseases from Europe such as smallpox killed very many indigenous people.
Millions of people from Africa were taken to America as slaves.
England, France and the Netherlands founded colonies above all in North America.

abschnitte.text: In 1492 **Christopher Columbus**, on behalf of Spain, reached islands in the Caribbean. He believed he was in Asia. Already in 1494 Spain and Portugal divided the new world with a line in the **Treaty of Tordesillas**. What lay to the west of it was to belong to Spain, and what lay to the east, to Portugal. That is why Brazil became a Portuguese colony, and Portuguese is spoken there to this day.

Spanish conquerors, the **conquistadors**, pushed far into the land with small forces. Hernán Cortés conquered the empire of the Aztecs by 1521, and Francisco Pizarro the empire of the Incas from 1532. They had horses, steel weapons and cannon, and found allies among peoples who were enemies of the Aztecs. Most people, however, died of imported **diseases** such as smallpox, against which the population of America had no protection.

With the **encomienda** indigenous people were assigned to Spanish settlers and had to work for them. In the mountain of **Potosí** in present-day Bolivia, huge amounts of silver were found from 1545. Thousands of indigenous people had to toil there in terrible conditions. Because the indigenous population shrank greatly, the colonial powers took millions of people from Africa to America as slaves, above all for sugar and tobacco plantations.

Not all Europeans thought this treatment was right. The Spanish cleric **Bartolomé de las Casas** witnessed the violence himself and afterwards campaigned all his life for the rights of the indigenous population. He wrote reports to the Spanish king and described the crimes of the conquerors. His writings are now among the most important sources about this time.

In the north it was mainly the English, French and Dutch who settled. In 1607 the English founded **Jamestown**, the first lasting English settlement in North America. In 1620 the Pilgrim Fathers arrived on the **Mayflower**, seeking freedom for their faith. The Dutch founded New Amsterdam, which became English in 1664 and has been called **New York** ever since. In 1608 France founded Québec in present-day Canada.

Through colonisation plants and animals travelled between the continents. From America the **tomato**, potato, maize, cocoa and tobacco came to Europe. In the opposite direction the Europeans brought horses, cattle, pigs, wheat and sugar cane. There were no horses in America at that time, and later they became very important for many indigenous peoples of the prairie.

begriffe.erklaerung: A territory that is ruled and exploited by a foreign state.
Spanish word for conqueror, the name given to the Spanish conquerors in America.
A Spanish system under which settlers were allowed to force indigenous people to work.
The first inhabitants of a territory and their descendants.

gewusst: Without colonisation there would be neither chocolate nor rösti in Switzerland, because cocoa and potatoes come from America.
Coins were minted from the silver of Potosí that travelled as far as China.
The name “America” goes back to the seafarer Amerigo Vespucci, not to Columbus.

teile.einleitung: Mendicant orders are religious communities that arose in the 13th century. Their members gave up all possessions, lived on donations and worked mainly in the towns.
wichtigste: Mendicant orders gave up property even as a community.
They lived on donations and settled in the growing towns.
In this they differed from older orders such as the Benedictines.
Well-known mendicant orders are the Franciscans, Dominicans, Carmelites and Augustinian Hermits.
The Carmelites are named after Mount Carmel in the Holy Land.
Martin Luther was a monk with the Augustinian Hermits.

abschnitte.text: Older orders such as the **Benedictines** lived in monasteries in the countryside. The individual monks owned nothing, but the monastery often owned a lot of land. The **mendicant orders** went further: the **community** too was to have no property. The brothers lived on **donations** and wanted to live as poorly as Jesus and the apostles. Instead of withdrawing, they moved into the **towns**, preached and helped the poor and the sick.

In the 13th century several mendicant orders arose. The **Franciscans** go back to Francis of Assisi, the **Dominicans** to Dominic, and they were mainly preachers. To these were added the **Carmelites** and the **Augustinian Hermits**. The Augustinian Hermits arose from several groups of hermits. In Swiss towns such as Zurich, Bern and Basel too there were houses of the mendicant orders.

The **Carmelites** are named after **Mount Carmel** near Haifa in the Holy Land. Hermits lived there in the 12th century. Later they moved to Europe and became a mendicant order. **Martin Luther** belonged to the order of the **Augustinian Hermits**. He entered their monastery in **Erfurt** in 1505, before he became a reformer.

gewusst: Many mendicant order churches have no tall tower, only a small roof turret, because they were meant to be plain.

teile.einleitung: Frederick I Barbarossa of the house of Staufer ruled the Holy Roman Empire from 1152 to 1190. He fought for a long time for his power in Italy and quarrelled with the Welf duke Henry the Lion. He died on the Third Crusade.
wichtigste: In 1155 Barbarossa was crowned emperor in Rome.
In 1162 he had the city of Milan destroyed.
In 1164 the bones of the Three Kings came from Milan to Cologne.
In 1176 he lost the Battle of Legnano against the Lombard League.
He got into a serious quarrel with Henry the Lion.
In 1184 he celebrated a huge Whitsun festival in Mainz.
In 1190 he drowned in the river Saleph on the Third Crusade.

abschnitte.text: In 1152 Frederick was elected king. Three years later, in **1155**, the pope crowned him emperor in **Rome**. Frederick wanted to strengthen the power of the emperor, above all in Italy. There towns such as Milan had become very rich and largely governed themselves. This led to many conflicts.

Milan resisted the emperor especially stubbornly. After a long siege Frederick had the city **destroyed in 1162**. After that his chancellor Rainald of Dassel brought the **bones of the Three Kings** from Milan to **Cologne** in **1164**. For them the splendid Shrine of the Three Kings was later built, which today stands in Cologne Cathedral. Cologne thereby became an important place of pilgrimage.

Many towns in northern Italy joined together against the emperor. This alliance is called the **Lombard League**. In **1176** Frederick lost the **Battle of Legnano** against it. After that he had to make peace. The towns recognised the emperor but were allowed to go on governing themselves.

abschnitte.titel: The quarrel with Henry the Lion
abschnitte.text: **Henry the Lion** of the house of the **Welfs** was Duke of Saxony and Bavaria and very powerful. For a long time he and Frederick worked together. When Henry refused the emperor help for an expedition to Italy, a serious quarrel broke out. In 1180 Frederick took his duchies away from him. Henry had to go to England for some years.

In **1184** Frederick celebrated a huge **Whitsun festival** in **Mainz**. Thousands of knights came from all over the empire, and his sons were knighted. A few years later he set out on the **Third Crusade** to reconquer Jerusalem. In Asia Minor he drowned in June 1190 in the river **Saleph**. The river is today called the Göksu and lies in Turkey.

gewusst: The Whitsun festival at Mainz in 1184 was regarded as one of the greatest festivals of the whole Middle Ages.
The bones of the Three Kings still lie today in a golden shrine in Cologne Cathedral.

teile.einleitung: The heliocentric worldview says that the Sun is at the centre and the Earth and the other planets circle round it. For a long time people believed the opposite, namely that everything turns round the Earth. The change to the new worldview in the 16th and 17th centuries was one of the greatest upheavals in the history of science.
wichtigste: In the geocentric worldview the Earth is at the centre, in the heliocentric one the Sun.
The geocentric worldview of the ancient scholar Ptolemy held throughout the Middle Ages.
In modern times Nicolaus Copernicus established the heliocentric worldview, his main work appeared in 1543.
From 1609 Galileo Galilei pointed a telescope at the sky and discovered four moons of Jupiter.
Johannes Kepler recognised that the planets circle the Sun on ellipses.
Kepler worked with the exact observations of the Dane Tycho Brahe.
In 1633 Galileo had to answer before the court of the Inquisition.

abschnitte.text: With the naked eye it looks as if the Sun, Moon and stars wander round the Earth. So most scholars of antiquity believed in the **geocentric worldview**, in which the Earth stands in the middle. The Greek scholar **Ptolemy** described it very exactly around the year 150 AD. His model held throughout the Middle Ages and also fitted the teaching of the Church at that time.

The astronomer **Nicolaus Copernicus** lived in the region of present-day Poland. Around the time when Christopher Columbus reached America in 1492, he began to study in Kraków. Copernicus came to the conclusion that the movements of the planets can be explained more simply if the **Sun** stands at the centre and the Earth turns daily on its own axis. His main work on the revolutions of the heavenly bodies appeared in 1543, the year of his death.

From 1609 **Galileo Galilei** in Italy pointed a **telescope** that he had built himself at the sky. He discovered craters on the Moon, countless stars in the Milky Way and **four moons** that circle Jupiter. With that it was clear that not everything turns round the Earth. Galileo became a well-known defender of the heliocentric worldview.

The Church at that time saw the new worldview as a contradiction of the Bible. In 1633 Galileo came before the court of the **Inquisition** and had to renounce his teaching. He spent the rest of his life under house arrest. The sentence “**And yet it moves**” is attributed to him but is probably a legend.

The Dane **Tycho Brahe** observed the positions of the planets very exactly for decades, still without a telescope. With his measurements **Johannes Kepler** found out that the planets run round the Sun not in circles but on **ellipses**. From this he formulated Kepler's laws. Later Isaac Newton explained with gravity why the planets circle the Sun in this way.

The heliocentric worldview changed how people saw their place in the universe. The Earth was now one planet among many. Today we know that the Sun too is only one of billions of **stars** in our Milky Way. In 1992 Pope John Paul II declared that the Church had done Galileo an injustice.

begriffe.erklaerung: With the Earth at the centre, from the Greek word “Ge” for Earth.
With the Sun at the centre, from the Greek word “Helios” for Sun.
A shape like a circle stretched lengthwise.
A Church court that took action against teachings regarded as false.

gewusst: Even in antiquity the Greek Aristarchus of Samos suspected that the Earth turns round the Sun.
The four large moons of Jupiter that Galileo discovered are today called the Galilean moons.
Tycho Brahe had an artificial nose made of metal, because he had lost the tip of his real nose in a duel.

teile.einleitung: The Investiture Controversy was a great conflict between pope and king in the 11th and early 12th centuries. It was about the question of who may install bishops and abbots in their office.
wichtigste: Investiture means installation into an office, from the Latin “investire”, to clothe.
Pope Gregory VII quarrelled with King Henry IV.
In 1075 Gregory VII forbade the installation of bishops by laymen.
In the Dictatus Papae the pope set out his supremacy in 1075.
Important impulses came from the reform movement of the monastery of Cluny in Burgundy.
The Concordat of Worms of 1122 ended the dispute.
It was concluded between Henry V and Pope Callixtus II.

abschnitte.text: **Investiture** comes from the Latin “investire”, to clothe. It means the solemn **installation** of a bishop or abbot in his office. A bishop received **ring and staff**, the signs of his spiritual office. But bishops were also powerful lords of the land with estates and rights. So kings wanted a say in who became bishop.

From the **monastery of Cluny** in Burgundy, founded in 910, an important **reform movement** spread. It wanted to free the Church from the influence of secular lords. The reformers fought **simony**, that is, the buying and selling of Church offices. The term comes from **Simon Magus**, who in the Bible wanted to buy spiritual powers. They also fought **Nicolaitism**, the marriage of priests, and demanded strict celibacy.

**Pope Gregory VII** wanted only the Church to install bishops. In 1075 he forbade **lay investiture**, that is, installation by non-clergy such as the king. In the **Dictatus Papae** he stated that the pope could even depose emperors. **King Henry IV** resisted. The pope then laid him under the **ban** and excluded him from the Church. In 1077 Henry went in winter to **Canossa** in Italy and asked there for the ban to be lifted.

Henry IV also had opponents in his own realm. In 1073 the **Saxons** rose against him. Among other things they felt threatened by his castles in the **Harz**, such as the Harzburg. This **Saxon War** weakened the king even before the conflict with the pope. Later princes even elected rival kings, and the dispute dragged on for decades.

Only in **1122** did **Henry V**, the son and successor of Henry IV, and **Pope Callixtus II** agree in the **Concordat of Worms**. A concordat is a treaty between Church and state. The Church now installed the bishops in their spiritual office with ring and staff. The emperor granted them their secular rights with the **sceptre**. In this way spiritual and secular installation were separated.

gewusst: The expression “to go to Canossa” today means having to humble oneself and ask for forgiveness.
The word “investment” for putting money into something comes from the same Latin word.

teile.einleitung: Haithabu, also called Hedeby, was one of the most important trading places of the Vikings. The settlement lay on the Schlei near the present-day town of Schleswig in the north of Germany. Since 2018 it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
wichtigste: Haithabu was a trading place of the Vikings.
It lies in Germany, near the town of Schleswig.
The settlement lay on the Schlei, a long inlet of the Baltic Sea.
On land a large rampart protected the settlement.
Traders often paid with silver and checked it with scales.
Since 2018 Haithabu has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

abschnitte.text: Haithabu arose in the 8th century on the **Schlei**. This is a long, narrow inlet of the Baltic Sea. Today the place lies in the north of **Germany**, near the town of **Schleswig**. At that time the area belonged to the kingdom of the Danes. From here it was not far to the North Sea. So in Haithabu traders from the north, the west and the east met.

On land a **great rampart** of earth protected the settlement. It enclosed it in a semicircle, and the other side lay on the water. The rampart was connected to a long border wall, the **Danevirke**. In the settlement stood houses of wood, and wooden roads led through the lanes. Craftsmen made jewellery, combs, glass beads and tools.

Traders often paid with **silver**. For this, coins and jewellery were sometimes chopped into pieces, which is called **hack silver**. What mattered was not the shape but the weight. So the traders used a small pair of **scales** to check how much silver they received. Archaeologists have found many such scales and weights in Haithabu.

In the 11th century Haithabu was attacked and destroyed several times. The inhabitants then moved to the other side of the Schlei, where the town of Schleswig grew. For a long time Haithabu lay hidden under earth. Archaeologists later dug it up and even found an old shipwreck. Since **2018** Haithabu and the Danevirke have been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**. Today a museum with rebuilt houses shows how the people lived there.

gewusst: Because the ground in Haithabu is damp, many things made of wood and leather survived there for over a thousand years.
In Haithabu, coins of its own were minted as early as the 9th century.

teile.einleitung: Frederick II of the house of Staufer was one of the best-known emperors of the Middle Ages. He was very well educated, spoke several languages and was interested in science. His contemporaries called him “Stupor mundi”, the wonder of the world.
wichtigste: Frederick II was born in 1194 in Jesi near Ancona.
His grandfather was Emperor Frederick Barbarossa.
He grew up on the island of Sicily.
In 1220 he was crowned emperor in Rome.
In 1229 he won back Jerusalem by negotiation.
In 1240 he issued a charter of freedom to the valley of Schwyz.

abschnitte.text: Frederick was born in **1194** in **Jesi near Ancona** in Italy. His father was Emperor Henry VI, and his mother Constance came from the royal house of Sicily. His grandfather was **Frederick Barbarossa**. Because his father died early, Frederick grew up on the island of **Sicily**, above all in Palermo. There Christians, Muslims and Jews lived together, and he learnt many languages.

Frederick became King of Sicily and later also Roman-German king. In **1220** the pope crowned him emperor in **Rome**. With the popes, however, he kept falling out, because both wanted to rule Italy. Several times he was therefore excluded from the Church, which is called **excommunication**. He died in 1250 in southern Italy.

Frederick undertook a crusade to the Holy Land. Unlike other rulers he hardly fought. He negotiated with the Sultan of Egypt and in **1229** won Jerusalem back for the Christians **by a treaty**. Many people in Europe were amazed at this. Others thought it wrong to negotiate with a Muslim ruler.

Frederick loved science. He wrote a famous book about **hunting with falcons**, in which he observed and described birds closely. In **1224** he founded a university in **Naples**. In **1231** he issued a law code for Sicily, the **Constitutions of Melfi**. Because of his many interests he was called **“Stupor mundi”**, the wonder of the world.

abschnitte.titel: The charter of freedom for Schwyz
abschnitte.text: Frederick II is also important for the history of Switzerland. In **1240** he issued a **charter of freedom** to the valley of **Schwyz**. In it he took the people of Schwyz under the direct protection of the empire. So they did not have to obey any other prince. This **imperial immediacy** was very important for the later Confederation.

gewusst: Frederick's book on falconry describes birds so exactly that it is still valued today.
The University of Naples, which Frederick founded in 1224, still exists today and bears his name.

teile.einleitung: Llamas are animals from the Andes in South America. For the Incas they were very important, because they carried loads over steep mountain paths. Today one can also hike with llamas in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Llamas and alpacas come from the Andes in South America.
The Incas kept them as domestic animals.
Llamas served above all for carrying loads.
Llamas and alpacas belong to the camel family.
When llamas get annoyed, they spit.
In Switzerland there are hikes with llamas.

abschnitte.text: **Llamas** and **alpacas** come originally from the **Andes**. This is a long, high mountain range in South America. There the air is thin and the weather is often harsh. Llamas cope well with this. They have a thick coat and are very undemanding.

Llamas and alpacas belong to the **camel family**. But they have no hump. Like camels they have soft feet with two toes and long necks. Llamas are larger and are used above all as pack animals. Alpacas are smaller and are kept for their fine **wool**.

The **Incas** kept llamas as domestic animals. Above all they used the llamas for **carrying loads**. The animals carried goods over the steep mountain paths of the Inca Empire. There were no horses or cattle in South America at that time. In addition, llamas supplied wool, meat and dung.

When llamas get annoyed or quarrel, they **spit**. Mostly, however, they spit at other llamas, not at people. Otherwise they are calm and curious animals. In **Switzerland** there are farms with llamas. There one can hike with them, and they carry the luggage.

gewusst: A llama has no hump, but is still related to the camel.
When a llama is loaded too heavily, it often simply lies down and does not walk on.

teile.einleitung: The Interregnum is the name given in the Holy Roman Empire to the time from about 1250 to 1273. In these years there was no king who was recognised everywhere and able to assert himself.
wichtigste: Interregnum literally means “period between reigns”.
The time began after the death of Frederick II in 1250 or of Conrad IV in 1254.
In 1257 the prince-electors, in a double election, chose Richard of Cornwall and Alfonso X of Castile.
In 1268 the last Staufer, Conradin, was executed in Naples.
In 1254 the Rhenish League of Cities arose to protect trade and peace.
The imperial princes used the weak royal power to build up their own power.
With the election of Rudolf of Habsburg in 1273 the Interregnum ended.

abschnitte.titel: An empire without a strong king
abschnitte.text: The word **Interregnum** means “**period between reigns**”. In the Holy Roman Empire it refers to the time from about **1250 to 1273**. In 1250 Emperor **Frederick II** of the **Staufer** family died, and in 1254 his son Conrad IV. After that there was no king whom everyone recognised. Even before this, **William of Holland** had appeared from 1247 as anti-king of the papal party. He died in 1256 fighting the Frisians.

The princes who elected the king are called **prince-electors**. In 1257 they were divided and chose two foreign candidates at once: **Richard of Cornwall** from England and **Alfonso X of Castile** from Spain. Alfonso never came to the empire. Richard was there only a few times, and briefly. So there was no power to keep order in the empire.

The young **Conradin** was the last Staufer. He wanted to win back the Kingdom of Sicily. In 1268 he was defeated at **Tagliacozzo** by **Charles of Anjou**. After that he was executed in the market square of **Naples**. With this the Staufer family, which had shaped the empire for a long time, came to an end.

Without a strong king, many had to help themselves. In 1254 Mainz and Worms joined together to form the **Rhenish League of Cities** to protect trade and the **public peace**. Soon about 60 cities belonged to it, among them **Basel**, as well as some princes. The **imperial princes** used the situation and took over imperial property and royal rights. In this way the empire was broken up even further into many separate territories.

In 1273 the prince-electors chose **Rudolf of Habsburg** as king. The Habsburgs came originally from the area of present-day Switzerland, and their ancestral castle stands in the canton of Aargau. The poet **Friedrich Schiller** called the Interregnum, in his 1803 ballad “The Count of Habsburg”, “**the time without an emperor, the terrible time**”. Today's research, however, considers the term **misleading**. There were elected kings after all; what was missing was above all a central power able to enforce its will.

gewusst: Habsburg Castle, the ancestral seat of the Habsburgs, stands near Brugg in the canton of Aargau.
Schiller's ballad “The Count of Habsburg” tells how Rudolf gave his horse to a priest so that he could ride to a sick person.

teile.einleitung: The great indigenous civilisations of America are mainly the Maya, the Aztecs and the Incas. Long before Europeans came to America, these peoples built large cities, temples and roads and developed calendars, writing and a sophisticated agriculture. In the 16th century the empires of the Aztecs and Incas were conquered by the Spanish.
wichtigste: The most important civilisations of America were the Maya, the Aztecs and the Incas.
The Aztec capital Tenochtitlan lay on islands in Lake Texcoco in the Valley of Mexico.
The Aztec Triple Alliance was formed by Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan.
The Inca Empire was called Tawantinsuyu in Quechua, Empire of the Four Parts.
With quipus, knotted cords, the Incas recorded numbers and data.
The classic Maya lived in many city states competing with one another.
Spanish missionaries had Maya writings burnt, and only parts of four manuscripts survive.

abschnitte.text: In **Central America** the Maya lived on the Yucatán peninsula and in the rainforests of present-day Guatemala. In the 15th century the **Aztecs** ruled the Valley of Mexico. The **Incas** built up the largest empire in America in the Andes of South America. Long before them there were other civilisations such as the Olmecs in Mexico.

The Maya never had a single united empire, but many **city states** that competed with one another and often made war. Large cities were Tikal, Palenque and Chichén Itzá. The Maya developed a fully formed **script** and an exact calendar and knew the number zero. Because Spanish missionaries such as Diego de Landa had their books burnt, only parts of four Maya manuscripts survive.

The capital **Tenochtitlan** lay on islands in Lake Texcoco. According to the founding legend, the Aztecs saw there an eagle on a cactus fighting a snake. Together with Texcoco and Tlacopan, Tenochtitlan formed the **Triple Alliance**, which subjugated many peoples. In the centre stood the **Templo Mayor**, which was dedicated to the war god Huitzilopochtli and the rain god Tlaloc.

The Inca Empire was called **Tawantinsuyu**, which means Empire of the Four Parts. Under the ruler **Pachacuti**, its great expansion began from about 1438. Instead of paying taxes in money, people performed the **mit'a**, a labour duty for the state, for example in building roads and terraces. Numbers and data were recorded with **quipus**, cords with knots.

All three cultures were masters of agriculture. The Aztecs laid out **chinampas**, artificial growing areas in the shallow lake water. The Incas built terraces on steep mountain slopes for potatoes and maize. Many foods that we know today, such as maize, potatoes, tomatoes, beans and cocoa, come from America.

In 1521 Hernán Cortés, with indigenous allies, conquered Tenochtitlan. The Inca Empire had been weakened before the arrival of Francisco Pizarro by a **war of succession** between the brothers Atahualpa and Huáscar. In addition there were diseases such as **smallpox**, against which the people in America had no resistance. But the descendants of these peoples live on to this day, and millions of people still speak Maya languages, Nahuatl or Quechua.

begriffe.erklaerung: A culture with cities, writing or records, a state and great buildings.
Originally native to a region, the first inhabitants of a country.
A city that, together with its surrounding land, forms a small state of its own.
A knotted cord with which the Incas recorded numbers and data.
The labour duty in the Inca Empire, performed for the state as a tax.

gewusst: The Incas had no writing in the usual sense and yet ran their huge empire with knotted cords.
One of the four surviving Maya manuscripts lies today in Dresden.
The Templo Mayor was rediscovered only in 1978, when workers in Mexico City found a large block of stone.

teile.einleitung: In 1381 many peasants and craftsmen in England rose up against high taxes and against serfdom. It was one of the biggest uprisings in medieval England.
wichtigste: The trigger was a poll tax, a tax on each head.
Every adult had to pay the same amount, which hit the poor especially hard.
The tax was meant to pay for the war against France.
The preacher John Ball asked who was the nobleman when Adam dug and Eve spun.
The leader was Wat Tyler, who was killed at Smithfield.
King Richard II was only 14 years old at the time.

abschnitte.text: In the 14th century England fought a long war against France. To pay for it, the government demanded a **poll tax**. Every adult had to pay the **same amount**, whether rich or poor. For poor people this was very hard. Many peasants were also **unfree** and had to work for their lords.

The preacher **John Ball** spoke of the original **equality** of all people. His question is famous: “When Adam delved and Eve span, who was then the gentleman?” By this he meant that at the beginning there was no nobility. His sermons gave many people courage. After the uprising he was executed.

In June **1381** large groups from Kent and Essex marched to **London**. Their best-known leader was **Wat Tyler**. The rebels demanded an end to serfdom and the punishment of the king's advisers. In London there was looting and violence. The king met them several times.

King **Richard II** was born in 1367 and so was only **14 years** old. At a meeting at **Smithfield** outside London, a quarrel broke out, and the Mayor of London fatally wounded Wat Tyler. Richard rode out to the rebels and promised them concessions. After that the uprising quickly collapsed, and the king took back his promises.

gewusst: In 1381 the poll tax was being collected for the third time within a few years.

teile.einleitung: The rock-hewn churches of Lalibela lie in the highlands of Ethiopia in Africa. The eleven churches were not built of masonry but cut out of the rock. They are still a holy place for Christians in Ethiopia today.
wichtigste: The rock-hewn churches of Lalibela lie in Ethiopia.
There are eleven churches, all cut out of the rock.
They were made around the year 1200 under King Lalibela of the Zagwe dynasty.
Lalibela was meant to be a “New Jerusalem”.
Seen from above, the Church of St George has the shape of a cross.
The churches are still used for services today.

abschnitte.text: The place is named after **King Lalibela**. He belonged to the **Zagwe dynasty**, a ruling family in Ethiopia. Around **1200** he had the churches built. In the year 1187 **Saladin** had conquered Jerusalem. This event is said to have inspired the building. Lalibela was to become a **New Jerusalem**, so that the faithful no longer had to travel so far.

The churches were not put together from stones. The workers cut them out of the **rock** from the top downwards. First they dug a deep trench round a large block. Then they hollowed out the block inside and shaped doors, windows, pillars and rooms. So each church is made from a single piece of rock.

In Lalibela there are **eleven rock-hewn churches**. The best known is the **Church of St George**. Seen from above, it has the **shape of a cross**. It stands free in a deep, cut-out pit. It is reached through a passage in the rock.

The churches are not ruins but are still in use today. Priests and faithful of the **Ethiopian Orthodox Church** pray there. At great festivals such as Christmas very many pilgrims come to Lalibela. Since 1978 the rock-hewn churches have been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

gewusst: Each rock-hewn church of Lalibela was cut out of a single piece of rock.
A small stream in Lalibela bears the name Jordan, like the river in the Holy Land.

teile.einleitung: In the Middle Ages women mostly had fewer rights than men. Even so, they worked in many trades, led monasteries, wrote books and ran craft businesses. Some of them are still known today.
wichtigste: Most women worked in the countryside, in the house, in the stable and in the field.
In towns such as Cologne there were women's guilds of their own, for example of the silk makers.
Beguines lived in religious communities without a lifelong vow.
Abbesses led monasteries and were often very well educated.
In the 12th century Herrad of Landsberg created the “Hortus deliciarum”.
In 1405 Christine de Pizan defended the dignity of women.

abschnitte.text: Most people in the Middle Ages lived in the countryside, women too. They cooked, baked bread and looked after the children and the animals. They worked in the garden and helped with the harvest. In addition they spun wool and wove cloth. Without the work of women no farm would have functioned.

In the towns women worked as traders, bakers, innkeepers or in crafts. Often widows carried on the business of their dead husband. In **Cologne** in the late Middle Ages there were even **women's guilds** of their own. A guild was an association of craftsmen. Among them were the **silk makers** and the **yarn makers**. In law, however, women mostly stood under the guardianship of a father or husband.

Many women lived in **monasteries** as nuns. There they could learn to read and write, which was rare at that time. An **abbess** led a monastery and had a lot of power. Besides there were the **Beguines**. These were women who lived in communities without a lifelong vow. They prayed together, nursed the sick and earned their money with handwork.

In the 12th century the abbess **Herrad of Landsberg** led a monastery in Alsace. She created the **“Hortus deliciarum”**, which means “Garden of Delights”. It was a kind of encyclopaedia with many pictures for her nuns. Also well known is **Hildegard of Bingen**, who wrote about medicine and composed music. The writer **Christine de Pizan** lived in France. In 1405, in the **“Book of the City of Ladies”**, she defended the dignity and cleverness of women.

Some noble women too had great power. Queens sometimes governed for their young sons. Noble women managed castles and estates when their husbands were away at war. In Switzerland, Queen **Agnes of Hungary**, together with her mother, helped to found the monastery of Königsfelden and lived there for many years. Such women, however, were exceptions.

gewusst: Christine de Pizan is regarded as one of the first women in Europe who could make a living from writing.
The “Hortus deliciarum” burned in 1870, and today it is known only from copies and tracings.

teile.einleitung: A herald in the Middle Ages was a messenger and crier of a ruler. He delivered messages, announced news and knew coats of arms especially well.
wichtigste: A herald delivered messages from his lord and cried news in public.
Often he announced the ruler's orders in the market square.
Beforehand trumpeters often blew so that everyone listened.
He wore a tabard with the coat of arms of his lord.
A herald was regarded as inviolable, even the enemy was not allowed to harm him.
At the tournament he introduced the knights and called out their names.
From the heralds comes the word heraldry for the study of coats of arms.

abschnitte.text: In the Middle Ages many people could not read. So a ruler needed someone to announce his **orders** and **news** aloud. This was the **herald**. He went where many people came together, for example to the **market square**. Before he spoke, **trumpeters** often blew. In this way everyone knew that something important was now coming.

Over his clothes the herald wore a **tabard**. On it the coat of arms of his lord could be seen. So everyone recognised at once on whose behalf he came. The herald did not speak for himself, then, but for the king, the prince or the town that had sent him.

Sometimes a herald took a message to the **enemy**, for example a declaration of war or an offer to negotiate. In doing so he was regarded as **inviolable**. Nobody was allowed to harm him, not even the opponent. This rule was important so that messages arrived safely and people could talk to each other even in war.

At a **tournament** the herald had a lot to do. He introduced the knights and called out their **names**. Because the knights wore helmets, he had to recognise them by their **coats of arms**. He also made sure that the rules were kept. On the battlefield too, the herald knew from the coats of arms who was there.

Because the heralds knew so much about coats of arms, the **study of coats of arms** is still called **heraldry** today. Heralds compiled books of arms in which many coats of arms were collected. In some countries there are still heralds today. They look after coats of arms above all and appear at ceremonial occasions.

gewusst: In England there is still a College of Arms today that looks after coats of arms.
Many newspapers are called “Herald”, the English word for herald, because they announce news.

teile.einleitung: The Jacquerie was a great peasant uprising in the north of France in the year 1358. The peasants rose against the nobility because they were suffering from war, taxes and hardship.
wichtigste: The Jacquerie broke out in 1358 in the north of France.
The name comes from the nickname “Jacques Bonhomme”, with which nobles referred to the peasants.
After the defeat at Poitiers in 1356 the nobility was seen as incompetent.
The most important leader was Guillaume Cale.
The uprising was put down after a few weeks.

abschnitte.text: In the middle of the 14th century life was hard for peasants in France. The **Hundred Years' War** against England brought plundering, and shortly before, the plague had killed many people. In 1356 the French lost the battle of **Poitiers**, and King **John II** fell into English captivity. The **nobility** was now seen as unable to protect the country. Even so, the peasants had to bear high **ransoms** and taxes.

In early summer **1358** peasants in the north of France rose up. Nobles mockingly called the peasants “**Jacques Bonhomme**”, and from this came the name **Jacquerie**. The rebels attacked castles and noble residences. The most important leader was **Guillaume Cale**. He tried to organise the peasant bands militarily.

The nobility quickly gathered troops against the rebels. **Guillaume Cale** was captured during negotiations and executed. After that the uprising was put down after only a few weeks. Many peasants lost their lives in the process. In French the word “Jacquerie” still stands today for a peasant uprising.

gewusst: At about the same time there was an uprising of the townspeople in Paris under the merchant Étienne Marcel.

teile.einleitung: Francis of Assisi was a monk from Italy who was born around 1181 and died in 1226. He gave up his wealth in order to live as poorly as Jesus. He founded the order of the Franciscans and is one of the best-known saints.
wichtigste: Francis of Assisi came from Italy.
His father was a rich cloth merchant.
At the centre for him and his brothers was a life of poverty.
In the Canticle of the Sun he praises God for the sun, moon and water.
His feast day on 4 October is also World Animal Day.
His companion Clare founded the women's order of the Poor Clares.

abschnitte.text: Francis was born in **Assisi**, a town in central Italy. His father was a **rich cloth merchant**. As a young man Francis lived merrily and spent a lot of money. He wanted to become a knight and went off to a war, but was taken prisoner and later fell ill. After that he changed his life.

Francis gave up all his property. He wanted to live as **poorly** as Jesus and his disciples. He looked after the sick and preached to the people. Soon other men joined him, whom he called **brothers**. From this the order of the **Franciscans** arose. His companion **Clare** founded an order for women, the **Poor Clares**.

Francis loved nature and saw God's work in everything. In his famous **Canticle of the Sun** he praises God for “Brother Sun”, “Sister Moon”, water, fire and earth. The song is regarded as one of the first poems in the Italian language. According to a legend, Francis even preached to the birds. That is why his feast day on **4 October** is also **World Animal Day**.

The Franciscans belong to the **mendicant orders**. Their members owned no property and lived on donations. The **Dominicans** too count among the mendicant orders. Older monasteries often lay remote in the countryside. The mendicant orders, by contrast, mostly settled **in the towns**, where they preached and helped the poor. Francis was canonised as early as 1228, two years after his death.

gewusst: The Canticle of the Sun by Francis of Assisi is among the oldest poems in the Italian language.
Because Francis loved animals, his feast day on 4 October is World Animal Day.

teile.einleitung: The Dominicans are a Catholic order founded in the 13th century. Their official name is the Order of Preachers, because preaching and study are at the centre for them.
wichtigste: The founder of the order was Dominic, who came from Castile in Spain.
Dominic first preached in southern France against the teaching of the Cathars.
In 1216 Pope Honorius III confirmed the order.
The Dominicans belong to the mendicant orders and live in poverty.
Besides poverty, preaching and study are at the centre.
A Latin pun interpreted their name as “Domini canes”, the Lord's hounds.

abschnitte.text: **Dominic** was born around 1170 in **Castile**, a kingdom in present-day Spain. He became a priest and travelled through Europe with his bishop. In **southern France** he met the **Cathars**. This was a religious movement that departed from the teaching of the Catholic Church. Dominic wanted to win people for the Catholic faith through **preaching** and a simple life.

Dominic gathered companions around him who, like him, wanted to preach. In the year **1216** Pope **Honorius III** confirmed the community as an order. The official name is the **Order of Preachers**, in Latin Ordo Praedicatorum. That is why the letters **OP** often follow the name of a Dominican. Dominic died in 1221 in Bologna and was later canonised.

The Dominicans belong to the **mendicant orders**. They were to own no property of their own and to live on donations. Unlike many older orders, they did not live secluded in the countryside but in the **towns**. There they preached to the people. So that they could preach well, they placed great value on **study**. Well-known scholars such as **Thomas Aquinas** and **Albertus Magnus** were Dominicans.

The name Dominican comes from their founder Dominic. A Latin **pun** interpreted it as **“Domini canes”**, which means **“hounds of the Lord”**. What was meant was that, like faithful watchdogs, they defend the faith. In the Middle Ages Dominicans were often put in charge of the **Inquisition**, that is, of investigations against people regarded as heretics. Today they work in pastoral care, education and science.

gewusst: The Predigerkirche in Zurich belonged in the Middle Ages to a monastery of the Dominicans.
Dominicans wear a white habit with a black cloak.

teile.einleitung: Michelangelo Buonarroti was an Italian sculptor, painter and architect of the Renaissance. He created the marble statue “David” and painted the huge ceiling of the Sistine Chapel in Rome. Many regard him as one of the greatest artists of all time.
wichtigste: Michelangelo Buonarroti was born in 1475 and died in 1564 in Rome.
His marble statue “David” stands in its original form in Florence.
From 1508 to 1512, commissioned by Pope Julius II, he painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel.
The best-known scene on the ceiling is the Creation of Adam.
Later he painted the huge picture “The Last Judgement” on the altar wall.
The Pietà in St Peter's is the only work he signed.
For St Peter's in Rome he designed the mighty dome.

abschnitte.text: Michelangelo was born in 1475 in Caprese in Tuscany and grew up in **Florence**. Even as a boy he learnt in the workshop of the painter Domenico Ghirlandaio. After that he was allowed to study ancient statues in the garden of **Lorenzo de' Medici**, the most powerful man in Florence. There he discovered his great love, working with **marble**.

From 1501 to 1504 Michelangelo created the statue **David** from a single large block of marble. It is over five metres high and shows the young shepherd from the Bible just before he fights the giant **Goliath**. The David became a symbol of the city of Florence, which held its own against powerful enemies. The original stands today in the Galleria dell'Accademia in Florence, and a copy stands in the square in front.

At only about 24 years old Michelangelo completed the **Pietà** in Rome. The marble figure shows Mary holding the dead Jesus on her lap. It stands today in **St Peter's Basilica**. It is the only work that Michelangelo signed: his name is on a band across Mary's chest.

Pope **Julius II** commissioned Michelangelo to paint the ceiling of the **Sistine Chapel** in the Vatican. From 1508 to 1512 he worked on a high scaffold, often with his head stretched upwards. He painted scenes from the Bible, from the creation of the world to Noah's Ark. Most famous is the **Creation of Adam**, in which the fingers of God and Adam almost touch.

More than twenty years later Michelangelo returned to the chapel. From 1536 to 1541 he painted the huge picture **The Last Judgement** on the altar wall. It shows how Christ judges people at the end of the world. Many nude figures disturbed some churchmen at the time, so later some were painted over with cloths.

In old age Michelangelo also became an important **architect**. He designed the Capitoline Square in Rome and in 1546 took over the direction of the building of **St Peter's**. For it he designed the mighty dome, which was completed only after his death. Michelangelo died in 1564 at the age of 88 in Rome.

begriffe.erklaerung: An artist who shapes figures from stone, wood or metal.
Wall painting in which the paint is applied to plaster that is still damp.
A depiction of Mary with the dead Jesus on her lap.
A hard, often white stone from which statues and buildings are made.

gewusst: Michelangelo saw himself above all as a sculptor and painted the Sistine ceiling only reluctantly.
He also wrote poems, including hundreds of sonnets.
The marble for the David had already been begun by other sculptors before him and then abandoned.

teile.einleitung: Before printing existed, books were written by hand and often richly painted. This art is called manuscript illumination. It arose above all in monasteries.
wichtigste: A large, decorated first letter is called an initial.
Small pictures in manuscripts are called miniatures.
Wafer-thin gold leaf made the pages shine.
A brilliant blue was obtained from the expensive stone lapis lazuli.
In the margin, painters drew tendrils, leaves and animals.
The “Book of Kells” from Ireland was made around the year 800.
Painted manuscripts were very valuable.

abschnitte.text: In the Middle Ages there was no **printing** yet. Every book was written by hand, mostly by **monks** in monasteries. Many books were also decorated with pictures. This art is called **manuscript illumination**. Writing was often done on **parchment**, which is treated animal skin.

The first letter of a section was often large and colourfully decorated. It is called an **initial**. Sometimes whole scenes or animals are hidden in it. Small painted pictures in manuscripts are called **miniatures**. The word comes from **“minium”**, a red colour. In the **margin** the illuminators painted tendrils, leaves and often funny animals too.

For splendid books the illuminators stuck wafer-thin **gold leaf** onto the pages, which still shines today. The colours were made from **plants**, earths and ground **stones**. They were mixed, for example, with **egg white**. A particularly expensive blue was obtained from the stone **lapis lazuli**. It came from far away, from present-day **Afghanistan**.

One of the most famous painted books is the **“Book of Kells”** from **Ireland**. It was made around the year **800** and is therefore about 1200 years old. It contains the **four Gospels**. Its pages are painted with intertwined patterns, animals and figures. Today it lies in a library in Dublin.

A painted book needed a lot of **time**, **gold** and expensive **colours**. Sometimes scribes and painters worked for years on a single book. That is why such manuscripts were very **valuable**. Only monasteries, churches, kings and rich people owned them. In Switzerland the **Abbey Library of St Gallen** owns many famous manuscripts from the Middle Ages.

gewusst: The Abbey Library of St Gallen, together with the abbey district, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
For one large book made of parchment, the skins of many animals were needed.

teile.einleitung: Erasmus of Rotterdam was one of the best-known scholars of his time. He lived around 1500, belonged to the movement of humanism and worked for many years in Basel, where he is also buried.
wichtigste: Erasmus was born in Rotterdam in the present-day Netherlands.
He was a priest and a great scholar.
He belonged to the intellectual movement of humanism.
In 1511 his well-known satire “In Praise of Folly” appeared.
With the “Adagia” he published a large collection of ancient proverbs.
Hans Holbein the Younger painted famous portraits of him.
Today a student exchange programme in Europe is named after him.

abschnitte.text: Erasmus was born around **1466** in **Rotterdam**. He went into a monastery and became a **priest**. But above all he was interested in learning. He studied in Paris and later travelled through France, England and Italy. He wrote in **Latin**, the language of scholars all over Europe. So his books could be read everywhere.

Erasmus belonged to **humanism**. This movement of the Renaissance wanted to read and understand the texts of **antiquity** anew. The humanists learnt Latin and Greek in order to study the old writings in the original. With the **“Adagia”** Erasmus published a large collection of **ancient proverbs** with explanations. He also published the New Testament in Greek.

In the year **1511** his best-known work appeared, **“In Praise of Folly”**. In it Erasmus lets Folly, that is, foolishness, speak for herself. She praises herself and tells how many people follow her. In this way Erasmus made witty fun of the faults of his time, including abuses in the Church. Erasmus wanted to improve the Church, but remained Catholic when the Reformation began.

For many years Erasmus lived in **Basel**. There he worked closely with the printer **Johann Froben**, who printed many of his works. In Basel he also got to know the painter **Hans Holbein the Younger**. Holbein painted several famous **portraits** of Erasmus. Erasmus died in **1536** in Basel and is buried in **Basel Minster**.

gewusst: The European exchange programme Erasmus for students has existed since 1987.
Erasmus wrote thousands of letters to scholars all over Europe.

teile.einleitung: The Aztecs were a people in the highlands of present-day Mexico who ruled a powerful empire in the 15th and early 16th centuries. Their capital Tenochtitlan lay in the middle of a lake and was one of the biggest cities in the world at the time. In 1521, the Spanish under Hernán Cortés conquered the city.
wichtigste: The capital of the Aztecs was called Tenochtitlan.
According to tradition, the Aztecs founded Tenochtitlan around 1325.
According to the legend, an eagle on a cactus with a snake showed them the place for the city.
Today Mexico City stands on the ruins of Tenochtitlan.
The Aztecs spoke Nahuatl.
Hernán Cortés conquered the empire when Moctezuma II was ruling.
In 1521, Tenochtitlan fell to the Spanish and their allies.

abschnitte.text: The Aztecs called themselves **Mexica**, which is where the name Mexico comes from. According to their legend, they wandered for a long time until they saw a sign: an **eagle on a cactus** with a snake. There, on an island in Lake Texcoco, they founded their city around 1325. This image can be seen today on the flag of Mexico.

abschnitte.titel: Tenochtitlan, the city in the lake
abschnitte.text: **Tenochtitlan** was joined to the shore by causeways and bridges and crossed by canals. Probably well over 100,000 people lived there, more than in almost any city in Europe at that time. In the centre stood the **Templo Mayor**, a huge double pyramid. At the great market, maize, beans, cloth, feathers and cocoa were traded.

To make sure enough food grew, the Aztecs built **chinampas**, artificial beds in the shallow lake water. On them they grew maize, beans, squashes and chilli. Cocoa beans were also used as money. Children went to schools, where they learnt history, religion and fighting.

The Aztecs worshipped many gods, for example the sun and war god **Huitzilopochtli** and the rain god Tlaloc. **Quetzalcoatl** was worshipped as the “Feathered Serpent”. The Aztecs believed that the gods needed sacrifices so that the sun would keep rising. That is why they also made human sacrifices, mostly of prisoners of war.

In 1519, Hernán Cortés landed in Mexico with a few hundred soldiers. The ruler **Moctezuma II** received the Spanish in Tenochtitlan, but was taken prisoner and died in 1520. Many conquered peoples, especially the **Tlaxcalans**, fought with the Spanish against the Aztecs. A **smallpox epidemic** killed many people in the city, and in 1521 Tenochtitlan fell after a long siege.

On the ruins of Tenochtitlan arose **Mexico City**, the present-day capital of Mexico. Archaeologists have dug up the remains of the Templo Mayor there. Even today more than a million people in Mexico speak Nahuatl. Words such as chocolate, tomato and avocado originally come from this language.

begriffe.erklaerung: The language of the Aztecs, which is still spoken today.
An artificial bed in shallow lake water on which vegetables and maize grew.
The Spanish word for conqueror, used for the Spaniards who conquered America.
Payments such as maize, cloth or gold that defeated peoples had to deliver to the Aztecs.

gewusst: In the canals of Xochimilco in Mexico City, you can still see remains of the old chinampas today.
The famous Aztec Sun Stone is a round block of stone with a diameter of over three metres.
The word chocolate comes from the Nahuatl word for a drink made of cocoa.

teile.einleitung: Porridge was one of the most important dishes in the Middle Ages, especially for peasants. It was cooked every day from grain with water or milk.
wichtigste: Porridge was mostly cooked from grain such as oats, barley or millet.
The grains were boiled with water or milk.
It was cooked in a cauldron over the open fire.
It was sweetened with honey, because sugar was expensive.
Simple peasants rarely ate meat.
The potato was not yet known in Europe.

abschnitte.text: For many people in the Middle Ages, **porridge** was the daily meal. It was cooked from **grain** such as **oats**, **barley** or **millet**. The grains were boiled in **water or milk** until a soft porridge was made. Cooking was done in a **cauldron** that hung over the open fire. Soups were also prepared in it.

**Millet porridge** was especially widespread. Millet is a grain with small, round seeds. In the Brothers Grimm fairy tale **“The Sweet Porridge”**, a little pot cooks so much millet porridge that the whole town fills up. A soft mash made of fruit is called a **purée**. Stewed apples become **apple purée**.

**Sugar** was very expensive and rare in the Middle Ages. So food was sweetened with **honey**. Many peasants kept bees. There was also fruit such as apples, pears and berries. **Meat** was expensive, and simple peasants ate it **rarely**, for example on feast days.

Many plants that we eat every day today were not yet known in Europe. **Potatoes**, **tomatoes**, **maize** and **peppers** came to Europe only after the discovery of America. In the farm garden, **turnips**, cabbage, onions, beans and peas grew instead. From these people cooked soups and stews.

gewusst: Even today's Birchermüesli from Switzerland is a kind of grain dish, invented around 1900 by Maximilian Bircher-Benner.

teile.einleitung: Voyages of discovery is the name for the great sea journeys with which Europeans explored unknown seas and lands in the 15th and 16th centuries.
