Sailors such as Christopher Columbus, Vasco da Gama and Ferdinand Magellan sailed across the oceans in small wooden ships. Their voyages changed the picture of the world for ever.
wichtigste: The explorers' ships were driven by the wind.
Many explorers sailed in nimble ships, the caravels.
Besides Spain, it was above all Portugal that sent many explorers to sea.
In 1498 Vasco da Gama found the sea route round Africa to India.
The ships of Ferdinand Magellan were the first to sail round the whole world, but Magellan died on the way.
Of Magellan's fleet only a single ship came back.
Many explorers were looking for spices such as pepper, for gold and for new trade routes.

abschnitte.text: In Europe **spices** such as pepper, cinnamon and cloves were in great demand and expensive. They came from Asia and were brought to Europe through many middlemen. The sailors wanted to find a **sea route to India** of their own, in order to buy there directly. In addition there was the search for gold, for fame and the wish to spread the Christian faith.

Many explorers sailed in **caravels**, small and nimble sailing ships. The ships were driven by the **wind** alone. The **compass** showed the direction, and with the astrolabe or the cross-staff the sailors used the sun and the stars to work out how far north or south they were. Even so, every voyage into the unknown was very dangerous.

**Christopher Columbus** sailed west in 1492 on behalf of Spain and reached America, but believed he was in India. The Portuguese **Vasco da Gama** sailed round Africa and reached India in 1498. In 1519 **Ferdinand Magellan** set out with five ships to find a way to the Spice Islands in the west. Magellan died in 1521 in the Philippines, and in 1522 only one ship, the Victoria, came back to Spain.

The voyages often lasted months, and the sailors lived crowded close together. They ate ship's biscuit, salted meat and beans, and the drinking water soon turned foul. Without fresh fruit and vegetables, many sailors got **scurvy**, an illness caused by a lack of vitamin C. Teeth fell out and wounds no longer healed, and many sailors died of it.

With the discoveries, new plants came to Europe, for example **potatoes**, maize, tomatoes and cocoa. In the other direction the Europeans brought horses, cattle and wheat to America. For the people in America and Africa, however, the voyages had terrible consequences: conquest, diseases and slavery. The Europeans began to rule large parts of the world as **colonies**.

The Swiss Confederation sent no ships on voyages of discovery, because it is **not on the sea**. Even so, the consequences were felt here too, for example through new foods and spices. The **potato** became an important food in Switzerland in the 18th century. Swiss scholars in Basel printed books and maps that spread the new knowledge about the world.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small, nimble sailing ship that the explorers often used.
An instrument with a magnetic needle that always points north.
An illness caused by too little vitamin C, from which many sailors suffered in the past.
A region that is conquered and ruled by a foreign country.

gewusst: Because Columbus believed he had arrived in India, the Europeans called the people of America “Indians”.
Of the roughly 240 men who set out with Magellan, only 18 returned on the Victoria.
The name America comes from the Italian navigator Amerigo Vespucci.

teile.einleitung: The Teutonic Order is a religious order of knights from the time of the Crusades. It arose in the Holy Land, later ruled a large territory on the Baltic Sea and still exists today as a Church order.
wichtigste: The order grew out of a hospital community that arose in Acre in 1190.
Around 1226, Duke Conrad of Masovia called on the order for help against the heathen Prussians.
Emperor Frederick II's Golden Bull of Rimini confirmed the order's rights in Prussia.
In 1309 the Marienburg on the Nogat became the seat of the Grand Master.
In 1242 an army of the order lost on the ice of Lake Peipus against Alexander Nevsky.
In 1525 Albert of Brandenburg-Ansbach turned the Order's State into a secular duchy.
In Hitzkirch in the canton of Lucerne the order had a commandery.

abschnitte.text: During the Third Crusade, merchants from Bremen and Lübeck founded a **field hospital** near **Acre** in the Holy Land in the year **1190**. From it a community arose that cared for the sick. A few years later it became an **order of knights**. Its members were monks and knights at the same time. They wore a white cloak with a black cross. At its head stood the **Grand Master**.

Around **1226** Duke **Conrad of Masovia** in Poland called on the order for help against the **Prussians**. They were a heathen people on the Baltic Sea. Emperor **Frederick II** confirmed the order's rights in this region with the **Golden Bull of Rimini**. In long wars the order conquered the land of the Prussians and founded a state of its own. In 1309 the mighty **Marienburg** on the Nogat became the seat of the Grand Master.

The order also tried to win territory further east. In the year **1242** an army of the order lost on the ice of **Lake Peipus** against the Russian prince **Alexander Nevsky**. The greatest defeat the order suffered was in 1410 at Tannenberg against Poland and Lithuania. After that it gradually grew weaker.

At the time of the Reformation, Grand Master **Albert of Brandenburg-Ansbach** turned to the new Protestant faith. In the year **1525** he turned the Order's State of Prussia into a **secular duchy**. The order itself continued in other places. It had many **commanderies**, that is, houses, also in Switzerland. One of them was in **Hitzkirch** in the canton of Lucerne. Today the Teutonic Order is a religious order with its seat in Vienna.

gewusst: The Marienburg in present-day Poland is regarded as one of the largest castles in the world and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Another commandery of the order in Switzerland was in Köniz near Bern.

teile.einleitung: The keep is the tall, strong main tower of many castles. It served as a lookout and, in danger, as a last refuge.
wichtigste: The keep often stood on the side from which attacks came.
Its walls were very thick, sometimes several metres.
The entrance was high above the ground.
People climbed up by a ladder or wooden stairs and pulled them in when in danger.
From the top one could see far across the land.
At the very bottom there was often a room used as a store or dungeon.

abschnitte.titel: The main tower of the castle
abschnitte.text: Many castles in Switzerland and Germany have a **keep**. This is a tall, strong tower. Often it stood on the side from which an **attack** was most likely to come. In this way it protected the rest of the castle like a **shield**. Usually nobody lived in the keep permanently, it was mainly a defensive tower.

The keep had very **thick walls**, some of them several metres thick. So it withstood stones and **battering rams** for a long time. The **entrance** was often several metres up above the ground. One got in by a **ladder** or a wooden staircase. In danger it was simply pulled in, and enemies could hardly get inside.

If enemies had already broken into the **courtyard**, the inhabitants could flee into the keep. It was then the **last refuge**. How often this really happened is **disputed** among researchers. Many experts think the tower was also meant to show how powerful the lord of the castle was.

From the top of the keep a watchman could **look far across the land**. So he noticed enemies early. A watchman at the top of the tower is called a **tower watchman**. If he saw enemies or fire, he raised the alarm. At the very bottom of the tower there was often a room without a door. It mostly served as a **store**, sometimes as a **dungeon**, that is, a dark prison.

gewusst: The dungeon could often be reached only through a hole in the ceiling, which is called the “fear hole”.
In many towns there were tower watchmen until well into the 20th century, who kept a lookout for fires.

teile.einleitung: The Kamakura Shogunate was a military government in Japan from about 1185 to 1333. In this period it was not the emperor who ruled but military leaders, the shoguns, and their regents from the city of Kamakura.
wichtigste: The shogunate arose after the Genpei War, which ended in 1185 with the naval battle of Dan-no-ura.
The shogun's government was called the bakufu, which means “tent government”.
From the early 13th century the Hojo family, as regents, held the real power.
In 1221 the shogunate won the Jokyu War against the retired Emperor Go-Toba.
In 1232 the law code Goseibai Shikimoku was created.
Many samurai turned to Zen Buddhism.
In 1333 Emperor Go-Daigo overthrew the Kamakura Shogunate.

abschnitte.text: In the 12th century two powerful warrior families fought for power in Japan: the **Minamoto** and the **Taira**. This war is called the **Genpei War**. It ended in **1185** with the naval battle of **Dan-no-ura**. There the Taira fleet was destroyed, and the child emperor Antoku drowned. The victor was **Minamoto no Yoritomo**. In 1192 he was appointed **shogun**, supreme military commander.

Yoritomo ruled from the city of **Kamakura**, far from the imperial court in **Kyoto**. His government was called the **bakufu**, which means “**tent government**”. The name recalls the field camp of a military leader and shows its military origin. The **emperor** stayed in office but had hardly any power left. After Yoritomo's death the **Hojo**, the family of his widow, seized power. As regents, called **shikken**, they steered the country, and the shoguns became puppets.

In 1221 the retired Emperor **Go-Toba** tried to overthrow the shogunate. In this **Jokyu War** the troops from Kamakura quickly took Kyoto. The shogunate won, and Go-Toba was **banished**. After that the shogunate watched over the imperial court with an authority of its own. In 1232 the government issued the **Goseibai Shikimoku**. This first law code of the warrior nobility regulated above all land ownership and disputes among warriors.

In this period **Zen Buddhism** gained many followers among the **samurai**. Zen stresses **meditation**, self-discipline and calm. These values suited the ideal of the warrior well. The **Great Buddha** of Kamakura, the **Daibutsu**, also dates from the middle of the 13th century. The bronze statue is about 13 metres high including its base. It stands in the open air today because its hall was destroyed by tidal waves.

In 1274 and 1281 the **Mongols** tried to conquer Japan. Both times they were repelled, partly because storms hit their fleets hard. The Japanese later called these storms “**kamikaze**”, divine wind. The defence cost a great deal of money, however. In **1333** Emperor **Go-Daigo** overthrew the Kamakura Shogunate. He was supported by warriors such as **Ashikaga Takauji**. The restoration of imperial power lasted only a short time, though.

gewusst: The Great Buddha of Kamakura is hollow inside, and visitors can go into it.
After the Kamakura Shogunate, shoguns still ruled in Japan until 1868.

teile.einleitung: Genghis Khan was a ruler of the Mongols. In the 13th century he united the Mongol tribes and created an empire that after his death became the largest continuous land empire in history.
wichtigste: Genghis Khan led the people of the Mongols.
As a child he was called Temüjin, which was his birth name.
In 1206 Temüjin was proclaimed Genghis Khan.
The Mongols lived in tents, the yurts, because they often moved about.
The warriors rode on horses and were especially good with bow and arrow.
The empire of the Mongols became huge.
The land of the Mongols is today called Mongolia.

abschnitte.text: Genghis Khan was born around **1162**. His **birth name** was **Temüjin**. His father was a tribal leader but died early. After that the family had a very hard time and lived in great poverty. In time Temüjin won friends and allies. With their help he became more and more powerful.

The **Mongols** lived as **nomads** on the wide steppes of Central Asia. They moved with their herds from pasture to pasture. So they lived in **yurts**. These are round tents made of wooden poles and felt that can be taken down quickly and carried along. Horses were the most important thing for them. Even small children learnt to ride.

At that time the Mongols were divided into many tribes, which often fought each other. Temüjin defeated his rivals and united the tribes. In the year **1206** the leaders proclaimed him **Genghis Khan** at a great assembly. The title means roughly “ruler as wide as the ocean” or “mighty ruler”. He gave his people laws and a strict order.

The warriors of the Mongols rode on small, hardy **horses**. They were especially skilled with **bow and arrow** and could even shoot at full gallop. Genghis Khan led many campaigns, including to China and Central Asia. Many towns were destroyed in the process. The conquests cost very many people their lives.

Genghis Khan died in the year **1227**. His sons and grandsons conquered even more territory. The empire of the Mongols became **huge** and stretched from China to Eastern Europe. Within the empire, traders could travel fairly safely on the **Silk Road**. Today the land of the Mongols is called **Mongolia**. There Genghis Khan is revered as a national hero.

gewusst: Where Genghis Khan lies buried is still unknown today.
Even today many people in Mongolia live in yurts.

teile.einleitung: The German Eastward Settlement is the name for the settling of regions east of the Elbe and Saale in the High Middle Ages. Peasants, craftsmen and merchants from the west moved there and founded new villages and towns.
wichtigste: The Eastward Settlement took place mainly in the 12th to 14th centuries.
A locator recruited settlers on behalf of a territorial lord and laid out new villages.
When forest was cleared in the uplands, forest-strip villages often arose.
The Cistercians were important carriers of clearing and land development east of the Elbe.
In 1147 the Wendish Crusade against Slavic tribes east of the Elbe took place.
The Culm Charter of the Teutonic Order regulated the rights of Culm and Thorn in 1233.

abschnitte.text: In regions east of the Elbe, **Slavic** peoples had long lived. In the 12th century, princes and bishops there, and also Slavic rulers, brought new settlers into the land. They came from Saxony, Franconia, the Rhineland and Flanders, among other places. The rulers wanted more land to be farmed and higher incomes. The settlers received land for this and often better rights than in their old homeland. In many places settlers and the native population lived side by side and mixed in time.

An important part was played by the **locator**. He was an entrepreneur who recruited settlers on behalf of a **territorial lord**. He shared out the land and laid out the new village. As his reward he often got more land and became the **village headman**, the head of the village. In the uplands, **forest-strip villages** often arose when forest was **cleared**: the farms stood in a row, and behind each farm lay a long strip of land.

The monks of the **Cistercians** founded many monasteries in the new regions. They cleared forests, laid out fields and were regarded as important carriers of **land development**. The expansion did not always go peacefully. In the year **1147** princes led a campaign against Slavic tribes east of the Elbe, the **Wendish Crusade**. But it brought hardly the results that had been hoped for.

Besides villages, many **towns** arose. They often received a fixed **town law**, for example on the model of Magdeburg. In the territory of the **Teutonic Order**, the **Culm Charter** of **1233** regulated the rights of the towns of **Culm and Thorn**. It later became a model for many other places. The consequences of the Eastward Settlement shaped language and culture in Central Europe for many centuries.

gewusst: Many place names in eastern Germany have Slavic roots, for example names ending in “-itz” or “-ow”.
Thorn is today called Toruń and lies in Poland.

teile.einleitung: The Maori are the original people of New Zealand. Their ancestors came some 700 to 800 years ago in large canoes from Polynesia across the Pacific.
wichtigste: The Maori live in New Zealand.
Their ancestors sailed in large canoes from Polynesia.
New Zealand is called Aotearoa in their language.
The haka is a famous dance of the Maori.
With the hongi they greet one another, nose to nose.
The early Maori hunted the giant moas.

abschnitte.text: The ancestors of the Maori lived on islands in **Polynesia**. In large **canoes** they sailed across the Pacific. They steered by stars, waves and birds. Some **700 to 800 years ago** they reached New Zealand. With this New Zealand is among the last large countries to be settled by humans.

In the language of the Maori New Zealand is called **Aotearoa**. That means roughly “land of the long white cloud”. The language **Te Reo Maori** is today, alongside English, an official language of the country. Many place names in New Zealand come from this language.

When the Maori arrived, giant birds lived in New Zealand, the **moas**. They were **flightless birds with no wings**, some over three metres tall. The Maori hunted them. A few hundred years ago the moas died out. Today they are known only from bones and finds.

The **haka** is a powerful dance with shouts, stamping and grimaces. The rugby team of New Zealand performs it before their matches. In greeting, Maori traditionally press nose and forehead together. This is called the **hongi**. In doing so one symbolically shares the breath of life.

The traditional tattoos of the Maori are called **Tā moko**. They are artful lines and spirals, often on the face. They tell of a person's family and origin. Every Tā moko is unique. Many Maori wear it again with pride today.

gewusst: Some moas were taller than a grown person.
Maori art includes elaborate wood carvings on meeting houses.

teile.einleitung: In the Middle Ages, the first big banks arose in Italy. Merchants from Florence, Venice and Genoa invented things that we still use today, such as the bill of exchange and double-entry bookkeeping.
wichtigste: From 1252, Florence minted a gold coin, the Fiorino d'oro.
The florin became the leading currency in European trade.
The Church forbade lending money for interest.
Bankers hid their profit in the exchange rate of bills of exchange.
The Florentine banks Bardi and Peruzzi collapsed in the 1340s.
Luca Pacioli was the first to describe double-entry bookkeeping in print, in 1494.

abschnitte.text: In **1252**, **Florence** began to mint a gold coin: the **fiorino d'oro**, or **florin** for short. It contained about 3.5 grams of gold and stayed worth the same for a long time. That is why merchants all over Europe trusted it. The florin became the **leading currency** in trade. Venice followed in 1284 with the ducat.

abschnitte.titel: The ban on interest and the bill of exchange
abschnitte.text: The Church did not allow Christians to lend money for **interest**. This was regarded as **usury**. Bankers found a way: the **bill of exchange**. A merchant paid money in one city and received it back in another city in a different currency. The bank's profit was hidden in the **exchange rate** between the currencies. In addition, traders did not have to carry cash along dangerous roads.

abschnitte.titel: The crash of Bardi and Peruzzi
abschnitte.text: The Florentine banking houses of **Bardi** and **Peruzzi** were among the biggest of their time. They lent the English king **Edward III** a lot of money for the start of the **Hundred Years' War**. The king did not pay it back. In the **1340s** both banks collapsed. This shook the economy of Florence badly.

Italian merchants wrote down their business very precisely. They used **double-entry bookkeeping**: every amount is entered twice, once as an incoming sum and once as an outgoing sum in another account. This makes it easier to find mistakes. In **1494**, the Franciscan **Luca Pacioli** described this method in a printed book, the “Summa”. To this day, companies, including in Switzerland, keep their books this way.

gewusst: The word “bank” comes from the Italian “banco”, the table at which the money changers sat.
The word “bankrupt” comes from “banca rotta”, the broken bench.

teile.einleitung: The Hundred Years' War was a long conflict between England and France in the late Middle Ages. It lasted from 1337 to 1453, with long pauses, and was mainly about the French crown.
wichtigste: The fighting was between the kingdoms of England and France.
The war lasted from 1337 to 1453, so really 116 years.
Edward III of England laid claim to the French throne, through his mother Isabella.
English archers with the longbow won at Crécy in 1346 and Agincourt in 1415.
In 1340 the English fleet destroyed the French fleet at Sluys.
Burgundy allied itself at times with England but made peace with France in 1435.
In the end England kept only Calais, and that until 1558.

abschnitte.text: In 1328 the French king died without a son. King **Edward III** of England was, through his mother **Isabella**, a grandson of the French king **Philip IV**. So he thought the French throne was due to him. The French nobles, however, rejected succession through the female line and chose Philip VI. In addition there was a dispute over regions in France that belonged to the English kings. In 1337 the war began.

The English used many **archers** with the **longbow**. They could shoot quickly and far. England first won in 1340 in the sea battle at **Sluys** off the Flemish coast. In the **Battle of Crécy** in 1346, English archers defeated the French knights. In 1356 at Poitiers too the English won and took the French king prisoner.

After a long pause the war flared up again. In 1415 an English army under King **Henry V** won at **Agincourt** in the north of France against a superior French force. After that the English conquered large parts of northern France. The Duchy of **Burgundy** helped them in this, whose dukes were quarrelling with the French royal house.

In 1429 a French army with **Joan of Arc** relieved the besieged city of **Orléans**. Soon afterwards Charles VII was crowned king in Reims. In 1435 Burgundy made peace with France again. After that the French won back their country step by step. With the Battle of Castillon in 1453 the war ended.

Almost all English territories in France were lost. Only the port of **Calais** stayed English until **1558**. The long war brought hardship, hunger and destruction to many villages. At the same time, the feeling of being a people of their own grew in both countries. The name “Hundred Years' War” was invented only later by historians.

gewusst: During the war there were long truces in which no fighting took place for years.
At the time of the war the plague, the Black Death, also raged across Europe.

teile.einleitung: On 25 December 800 the Frankish king Charlemagne was crowned emperor in Rome by Pope Leo III. This event was very important for the history of Europe and is interpreted in different ways to this day.
wichtigste: Charlemagne was crowned on 25 December 800, on Christmas Day.
The coronation took place in the old St Peter's Basilica in Rome.
In 799 Charlemagne had received the fugitive Pope Leo III in Paderborn.
The Romans present proclaimed Charlemagne emperor.
The Byzantine Empire saw the coronation as presumption, as Empress Irene was then ruling in Constantinople.
Einhard wrote the best-known biography of Charlemagne.
In 813 Charlemagne had his son Louis crowned co-emperor.

abschnitte.text: In the year 799 Pope **Leo III** was attacked in Rome. He fled and sought help from the most powerful ruler in the West, the Frankish king **Charlemagne**. The two met in **Paderborn**. This meeting prepared the later imperial coronation. In the year 800 Charlemagne went to Rome to settle matters there.

On **25 December 800** a **Mass** took place in the old **St Peter's Basilica**. During it Leo III placed the crown on Charlemagne. According to the Frankish **Royal Frankish Annals**, the **Romans** present cheered Charlemagne as emperor. This shout is called an **acclamation** and, by Roman custom, was part of the raising of an emperor. The old building was replaced in the 16th century by the present St Peter's. By the reckoning of the time, the new year often began at Christmas.

In **Constantinople** an emperor still ruled who saw himself as the successor of the Roman emperors. The **Byzantine Empire** therefore regarded Charlemagne's coronation as **presumption**. People speak of the **problem of the two emperors**. In the year 800 Empress **Irene** was ruling there alone, from 797 to 802. In the West it was argued that the imperial throne was vacant, because a woman could not be emperor.

The best-known biography of Charlemagne was written by **Einhard**, who himself lived at Charlemagne's court. It is called “**Vita Karoli Magni**”. Einhard writes that Charlemagne was **surprised** by the coronation. Had he known the intention, he would not have gone to church that day. Many experts regard this as a modest presentation, because the coronation was probably arranged beforehand.

In **813**, shortly before his death, Charlemagne himself crowned his son **Louis** as **co-emperor**. Louis, later called “the Pious”, became sole ruler in 814. In Switzerland too, Charlemagne is remembered. According to a legend he is said to have founded the **Grossmünster** in **Zurich**. On the south tower sits a figure of him. The original stone figure stands today in the crypt, and a copy sits on the tower.

gewusst: Charlemagne lies buried in Aachen Cathedral, and his bones rest in a precious golden shrine.
Charlemagne is sometimes called the “Father of Europe” because his empire covered large parts of western Europe.

teile.einleitung: A half-timbered house has a frame of wooden beams that can be seen from outside. The panels between the beams are filled with other material. In Switzerland such houses are often called Riegelhäuser.
wichtigste: The frame of a half-timbered house is made of wooden beams.
The gaps were often filled with twigs and clay.
Straw was mixed into the clay so that it held better.
Upper storeys often jutted out further, so there was more room upstairs.
The wooden frame was built by the carpenter.
In Switzerland a half-timbered house is often called a Riegelhaus, and especially many stand in Thurgau.

abschnitte.text: In a half-timbered house it is not the walls that carry the house but a **frame of wooden beams**. There are upright beams, horizontal beams and sloping braces. The sloping braces make the frame stable so that it does not tip over. The panels between the beams are called **infill panels**. That is where the name half-timbered comes from.

The wooden frame was built by the **carpenter**. He sawed and dressed the beams and joined them without nails, using tenons and wooden pegs. Often the parts were first prepared on the spot and then put together. When the frame stood, people celebrated the **topping-out party**. Many old half-timbered houses have stood for several hundred years.

The panels were often filled with a lattice of **twigs** or rods. This lattice was coated with **clay**. **Straw** was mixed into the clay so that it held better and cracked less as it dried. Later bricks were also used. Finally the panels were often plastered white, while the beams stayed visible.

In the towns of the Middle Ages space was short. So the upper storeys were often allowed to jut out a little over the lower one. In this way there was **more room** upstairs without needing more ground. In some old towns the houses almost touch each other over the lane as a result.

In Switzerland a half-timbered house is often called a **Riegelhaus**. Especially many Riegelhäuser can be seen in the canton of **Thurgau**, but also in Zurich, Schaffhausen and Aargau. In the little town of **Stein am Rhein**, many old houses with brightly painted façades stand on the Town Hall Square. In Germany and Alsace too there are many half-timbered houses.

gewusst: The wooden beams of a half-timbered house were often joined with wooden pegs, without any iron nails at all.
Because the walls only fill and do not carry, a half-timbered house could sometimes be taken down and rebuilt in another place.

teile.einleitung: In the Middle Ages the feudal system ordered the life together of kings, nobles and knights. A lord granted land, and whoever received it owed him loyalty and help in return.
wichtigste: A fief was land that a lord lent out and did not give away.
The one who granted a fief was called lord, the one who received it a vassal.
The vassal swore loyalty to his lord and helped him in war.
Anyone who betrayed his lord could lose his fief.
Another word for the feudal system is feudalism.
The peasants worked the fields and gave up part of the harvest.

abschnitte.text: In the Middle Ages a lot of land belonged to the king. He could not administer it alone. So he passed parts of it on to others. This granted land was called a **fief**. In German the word, **Lehen**, is connected with **leihen**, to lend, because the land was only lent. The one who granted it was the **lord**, the one who received it the **vassal**.

In a solemn ceremony the vassal knelt down. He placed his folded hands in the hands of the lord. In this way he showed that he wanted to serve him. Then he swore an **oath of loyalty**. In return the lord promised protection. If the vassal betrayed his lord, the lord could take the fief away again.

The king granted large territories to **dukes** and **counts**. They passed parts of them on to knights and other followers. A vassal who received his fief not from the king but from another vassal was called a **subvassal**. In this way an order arose like a staircase with many steps.

At the very bottom stood the **peasants**. They worked the fields on the lords' land. They had to give up part of the harvest. Often they also had to do work for the lord. Many peasants were not free and were not allowed simply to leave their farm.

In the time of the Carolingians the fief was called **beneficium** in Latin, which means “good deed”. Later the word **feudum** prevailed. From it comes the word **feudalism**. Today it is used for the whole order of lords, vassals and peasants.

gewusst: Many castles in Switzerland too belonged to nobles who held their land as a fief from a higher lord.
In time many fiefs became hereditary, so that sons kept the land of their fathers.

teile.einleitung: In the Holy Roman Empire there was no king who simply inherited his office from his father. He was elected, and by a small group of powerful princes: the prince-electors.
wichtigste: The prince-electors elected the Roman-German king.
The German word “Kurfürst” comes from “küren”, which means to elect.
The Golden Bull of 1356 fixed seven prince-electors.
Three of them were archbishops: Mainz, Cologne and Trier.
The secular electors were the king of Bohemia, the Count Palatine of the Rhine, the duke of Saxony and the margrave of Brandenburg.

abschnitte.text: The old word **küren** means to elect. A **Kurfürst**, or prince-elector, was therefore a prince who was allowed to elect. The prince-electors decided who became **Roman-German king**. The man elected could later be crowned **emperor** by the pope. The word lives on today in **Kür**, for example in figure skating, where skaters choose their own programme.

For a long time it was not clear who exactly was allowed to elect. In 1356 Emperor **Charles IV** issued the **Golden Bull**. This document is so called because of its golden seal. It laid down that there are **seven prince-electors**. It also regulated that the election takes place in Frankfurt and that the majority decides.

Three of the seven prince-electors were **archbishops**: those of **Mainz**, **Cologne** and **Trier**. They are called ecclesiastical electors. The four secular electors were the **king of Bohemia**, the **Count Palatine of the Rhine**, the **duke of Saxony** and the **margrave of Brandenburg**. Later more electors were added, until the empire ended in 1806.

gewusst: The German sporting term “Kür” comes from the same old word as “Kurfürst”.
The Golden Bull owes its name to a seal made of gold.

teile.einleitung: The First Crusade was a great military expedition by knights from Europe to the Middle East. It began in 1096 and ended in 1099 with the conquest of Jerusalem. After that the first Crusader states arose there.
wichtigste: In 1095 Pope Urban II called for a crusade at the Council of Clermont in France.
The trigger was an appeal for help from the Byzantine Emperor Alexios I Komnenos.
The battle cry of the Crusaders was “Deus lo vult”, that is, “God wills it”.
Before the army of knights, Peter the Hermit set out with the People's Crusade.
In 1098 the County of Edessa and the Principality of Antioch arose.
In July 1099 the Crusaders conquered Jerusalem.
Baldwin I became the first King of Jerusalem in the year 1100.

abschnitte.titel: A call for help from Byzantium
abschnitte.text: The **Byzantine Empire** in the east was Christian and had its capital in Constantinople. In the year 1071 it lost the **Battle of Manzikert** against the **Seljuks**, a Turkish people. After that the Seljuks pushed far into Asia Minor, into present-day Turkey. So Emperor **Alexios I Komnenos** asked the pope in the west for soldiers. From this request grew a much greater undertaking.

In November 1095 **Pope Urban II** spoke at the **Council of Clermont** in central France. A council is a large assembly of clergy. The pope called on the knights to help the Christians in the east and to conquer Jerusalem. The listeners are said to have answered with “Deus lo vult”, which means “God wills it”. Those who went along sewed a cloth cross onto their clothes. That is where the word **crusade** comes from.

Even before the knights set out, many ordinary people set off in 1096. Their best-known leader was the preacher **Peter the Hermit**. The people were poorly equipped and hardly prepared for a war. On the way there were also attacks on Jewish communities, for example in the Rhineland. In Asia Minor the **People's Crusade** was defeated by the Seljuks.

The army of knights came from France, Lorraine and southern Italy. Well-known leaders were **Godfrey of Bouillon**, his brother **Baldwin** and the Norman **Bohemond of Taranto**. In 1098 Baldwin founded the **County of Edessa**, the first Crusader state. The Crusaders besieged the city of **Antioch** in Syria for about eight months, until it fell in June 1098. Bohemond kept Antioch and founded a principality there. In July 1099 the army conquered Jerusalem, and very many inhabitants were killed.

Godfrey of Bouillon became the first ruler in conquered Jerusalem. But he did not want to wear a royal crown where Christ had worn a crown of thorns. So he called himself **Advocate of the Holy Sepulchre**. After his death in the year 1100 his brother took the title of king. As **Baldwin I** he was crowned on Christmas Day 1100. The Crusader states lasted for almost 200 years.

gewusst: The First Crusade was the only one of the great crusades in which the Crusaders were able to conquer their goal, Jerusalem.
The word “crusade” comes from the cloth cross that the participants sewed onto their clothes.

teile.einleitung: Kievan Rus was a medieval empire in eastern Europe with its capital at Kyiv. It existed from the 9th to the 13th century. The present-day countries of Ukraine, Belarus and Russia see it as part of their history.
wichtigste: According to the Primary Chronicle, the East Slavs called Varangians from Scandinavia as princes.
Rurik is said to have settled in Novgorod around 862.
Around 988 Grand Prince Vladimir adopted Christianity from Byzantium.
Under Yaroslav the Wise the law collection “Russkaya Pravda” arose.
Yaroslav had St Sophia's Cathedral built in Kyiv.
An important trade route led from the Baltic Sea via the Dnieper to Constantinople.
In 1240 the Mongols conquered Kyiv.

abschnitte.text: The most important source for the early history is the **Primary Chronicle**, also called the Chronicle of Nestor. It arose in the early 12th century in Kyiv and is also called the “Tale of Bygone Years”. It reports that the East Slavs called **Varangians** as rulers. That is what Vikings from Scandinavia were called. Their leader **Rurik** is said to have settled in **Novgorod** around 862. Later Kyiv on the river Dnieper became the centre.

abschnitte.titel: From the Varangians to the Greeks
abschnitte.text: Through the land ran an important trade route. It was called the **route from the Varangians to the Greeks**. It joined the Baltic Sea with **Constantinople** by rivers and short overland paths. Merchants brought furs, wax and also slaves south. Kyiv lay very favourably on the **Dnieper** on this route and became rich.

Around 988 **Grand Prince Vladimir** was baptised. He adopted Christianity from the **Byzantine Empire** and married a sister of the emperor. So the Rus was shaped by Orthodox Christianity. The churches were decorated with domes and splendid pictures, the **icons**.

In the 11th century **Yaroslav the Wise** ruled. His time is regarded as the golden age of Kievan Rus. He had the first collection of laws written down, the **Russkaya Pravda**. He also built the **Cathedral of St Sophia** in Kyiv, named after the Hagia Sophia in Constantinople. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site today.

After Yaroslav's death the empire broke up into many small principalities, which often quarrelled with one another. In the 13th century the **Mongols** came from the east. In December 1240 they took Kyiv after a siege. With this the importance of Kyiv as the centre of the Rus came to an end.

gewusst: The Varangians, who may have given the Rus its name, were Vikings from Scandinavia.
Over the Dnieper merchants could travel from the Baltic Sea as far as Constantinople.

teile.einleitung: The Levant trade was, in the Middle Ages, the trade between Europe and the countries on the eastern Mediterranean. Through it spices, silk and other precious goods came from the Orient to Europe.
wichtigste: The Levant is the area on the eastern Mediterranean.
Spices from India came over the Red Sea to Egypt.
Alexandria was a main trading hub for pepper.
From there ships brought the goods to Venice.
With the commenda, financiers and merchants shared the business.

abschnitte.text: The word **Levant** means “land of the rising sun”, that is, the land where the sun rises. It refers to the coasts on the eastern Mediterranean. Goods from India and even more distant countries came there. **Pepper** was especially sought after. Spices travelled over the **Red Sea** to Egypt and then on to **Alexandria**. The ruling **Mamluks** earned well from the intermediate trade.

From Alexandria and other ports ships brought the goods to Europe. Above all **Venice** and **Genoa** became rich through this trade. From there the goods travelled on over the Alps to the north. Spices were very expensive in Europe because the route was long and dangerous.

A trading voyage needed a lot of money. So there was the **commenda**. A **financier** supplied the money, and a travelling merchant did business with it. The financier bore the risk of a loss, and the traveller contributed his labour. They shared the profit by a fixed formula.

gewusst: Because spices were so expensive, sailors later looked for a sea route of their own to India.

teile.einleitung: In South America the Incas built a huge road network through mountains, deserts and forests. On these paths people travelled on foot, and fast runners carried messages across the whole empire.
wichtigste: The Inca road network was many tens of thousands of kilometres long.
The centre was the capital Cusco, from where roads led to all parts of the empire.
The Incas knew no horses and no wheeled carts, so people went on foot.
Runners called chasquis passed on messages like in a relay.
Rest houses called tambos offered places to sleep and supplies.
Suspension bridges of woven grass led over deep gorges.
The Q'eswachaka bridge is still woven anew every year.

abschnitte.text: The empire of the **Incas** lay in the **Andes**, a high mountain range in South America. In the 15th and early 16th centuries it covered areas that today belong to Peru, Ecuador, Bolivia, Chile and Argentina. The Incas joined their empire together with a **road network** of many tens of thousands of kilometres. The paths led over mountains and through deserts and forests. The centre was the capital **Cusco**.

The Incas knew no **horses** and used no **wheeled carts**. So people went on foot. They carried loads themselves or had **llamas** carry them. In the steep mountains the Incas cut steps into the rock. In this way even very steep slopes could be crossed. The roads served mainly the state, that is, officials, soldiers and messengers.

For messages there were fast runners, the **chasquis**. Each ran only a short stretch and then passed the message on to the next runner, like in a **relay**. In this way messages travelled astonishingly fast through the whole empire. The Incas had no writing like ours. For numbers they used knotted cords, the **quipus**.

Along the roads stood **rest houses** called **tambos**. There travellers could spend the night. There were also **storehouses** with food, clothing and other goods. In this way soldiers and messengers were well supplied on their way. The people from the villages nearby had to look after the tambos and the roads.

Over deep gorges the Incas built **suspension bridges**. For this they wove thick ropes from **grass**. The **Q'eswachaka** bridge in Peru is still woven anew every year by the villagers, just as in the time of the Incas. Since 2014 the Inca road system, the **Qhapaq Ñan**, has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

gewusst: A well-known part of the old road network is the Inca Trail to Machu Picchu, where many people hike today.
In places the Inca roads led over passes that are higher than the highest mountains in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: In the Middle Ages the seasons ruled the daily life of the peasants. Each season had its own jobs, from sowing through the harvest to chopping wood in winter.
wichtigste: Peasants arranged their work according to the seasons and the weather.
Winter grain such as rye was sown in autumn.
In summer grass was made into hay as winter feed.
In autumn the pigs ate acorns and beechnuts in the forest.
In late autumn pigs were often slaughtered.
In the Swiss mountains the cattle were taken up to the alp in summer.
On St Martin's Day, 11 November, many peasants had to bring their dues.

abschnitte.text: In **spring** the peasants ploughed the fields, often with oxen. Then they sowed the **summer grain** such as oats or barley. In the garden they planted vegetables. The **winter grain**, which had already been sown in autumn, now grew on. The animals were allowed out to pasture again.

In **summer** the peasants mowed the grass and let it dry in the sun. This made **hay**, the feed for the animals in winter. Then came the **grain harvest** with the sickle. In the **Swiss mountains** the cattle were driven up to the **alp**, because up there plenty of fresh grass grew in summer. Cheese was made there too.

In **autumn** the **winter grain** such as **rye** was sown. It sprouted before winter and grew on the next spring. The **grapes** ripened, and the harvest is called the **grape harvest**. The pigs were driven into the forest. There they ate **acorns** and beechnuts and grew fat.

In **late autumn** the **pigs** were often slaughtered, because in winter there was little feed. The meat was smoked or salted so that it would keep. In **winter** there was no work in the fields. The peasants **chopped wood**, **mended tools**, spun wool and wove cloth. In this way they prepared for the new year.

Peasants had to bring their lords **dues**, for example grain, eggs or hens. An important rent day was **St Martin's Day** on **11 November**. By then the harvest was in, and people could pay. In **Sursee** in the canton of Lucerne, the **Gansabhauet**, the goose-cutting festival, is still celebrated on this day. The custom recalls this old time.

gewusst: Many month pictures in old calendars show a typical farming job for each month.
In Switzerland the cattle drive up to the alp in early summer and the drive down in autumn are still celebrated today.

teile.einleitung: Clovis I was a king of the Franks and lived around the year 500. He united many Frankish groups under his rule and so laid the foundation for later France.
wichtigste: Clovis came from the royal family of the Merovingians.
He became king at about 15 years old.
In the Battle of Tolbiac he fought against the Alamanni.
He turned to Christianity and was baptised in Reims.
In 507 he defeated the Visigoths in the Battle of Vouillé.
He made Paris his main seat.
Under him the Frankish law code, the Lex Salica, was produced.

abschnitte.text: Clovis was born around **466**. He belonged to the family of the **Merovingians**, which provided the kings of the Franks. Around 481 his father died, and Clovis became king of a small Frankish territory at **about 15 years old**. The **Franks** were a Germanic people. Present-day **France** is named after them.

Clovis enlarged his empire through wars and alliances. In 486 he defeated the last Roman ruler in Gaul. Later he fought in the **Battle of Tolbiac** against the **Alamanni**, who also lived in the area of present-day German-speaking Switzerland. In the year **507** he defeated the **Visigoths** in the **Battle of Vouillé**. After that almost the whole of Gaul belonged to him.

Clovis's wife **Clotilde** came from the people of the **Burgundians** and was a Catholic Christian. According to tradition, Clovis promised in the battle against the Alamanni to become a Christian if he won. He had himself baptised in **Reims**, probably around 500. It was important that he accepted the **Catholic** faith. In this way he won the support of the Church and of the Roman population in Gaul.

Clovis made **Paris** his **main seat**. Under him the law of the Franks was also written down, the **Lex Salica**. It laid down, for example, what punishments or fines had to be paid for an offence. Clovis died in the year **511** in Paris. His empire was divided among his sons, but remained a mighty Frankish kingdom.

gewusst: After Clovis, many French kings were crowned in Reims, in memory of his baptism.
The name Clovis has the same root as the French name Louis and the German name Ludwig.

teile.einleitung: In the Middle Ages only a few people could read and write. Anyone who was allowed to learn often went to a monastery school. The monastery school of St Gall was especially famous.
wichtigste: In monastery schools it was mainly boys who learnt, who often later became monks.
In women's monasteries girls also learnt.
Writing was practised on wax tablets with a stylus.
The children sang a lot and learnt songs for the church service.
Around 800 Charlemagne promoted schools in monasteries.
The monastery school of St Gall was one of the best in Europe.

abschnitte.text: In the **monastery schools** it was mainly **boys** who learnt. Many of them later became monks themselves. Some monasteries also taught sons of nobles who did not want to enter the monastery. In **women's monasteries** girls also learnt. The children of most peasants did not go to school at all, because they had to help with the work.

**Parchment** was too expensive to practise on. So the children wrote on a **wax tablet**. This is a wooden board with a layer of wax. With a **stylus**, a pointed stick, they scratched the letters into it. With the flat end of the stylus one could smooth the wax again and start afresh. Lessons were in **Latin**, the language of the Church.

In the monastery there was a lot of **singing**. The children learnt the songs and prayers for the church service by heart. Teachers in the Middle Ages were very strict. Anyone who did not pay attention often got **blows with the rod**. That was usual then, and today such a thing is forbidden in school.

Around the year 800 **Charlemagne** wanted more people to be able to read and write. So he promoted schools in monasteries and at churches. The monastery school of **St Gall** became one of the best in Europe over 1000 years ago. Learned monks taught there. One of the best known was **Notker**, who lived around the year 900. He was a teacher and wrote many songs.

gewusst: The Abbey Library of St Gall still keeps books that were used in the monastery school.
On a wax tablet one could write again and again, almost like on a slate.

teile.einleitung: A hilltop castle is a castle that stands raised up on a mountain, hill or rock. In Switzerland there are very many such castles, and some are museums today.
wichtigste: A hilltop castle stands on a mountain, hill or rock.
From above one saw enemies from far away.
Attackers had to fight uphill, which made defence easier.
Kyburg near Winterthur in the canton of Zurich is a museum today.
Thun Castle stands high above the old town and has a tower with four round corner turrets.
The three castles of Bellinzona are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

abschnitte.text: Castles are often classified by their position. A **hilltop castle** stands raised up on a mountain, hill or rock. The counterpart is the **lowland castle**, which stands on a plain and is often protected by moats of water. In a mountainous country such as **Switzerland**, hilltop castles are especially common. Many were built in the Middle Ages by noble families.

From a hilltop castle one could see far across the land. So one noticed **enemies** from far away. Attackers had to fight **uphill** and often came up only by a narrow path. The castle also showed the power of its owner, because everyone saw it from far off. One disadvantage was **water**: often one had to dig deep wells or collect rainwater in cisterns.

**Kyburg** stands on a hill near **Winterthur** in the **canton of Zurich**. In the Middle Ages it belonged to the counts of Kyburg and later to the Habsburgs. Today it is a **museum**. **Thun Castle** in the canton of Bern stands on the castle hill high above the old town. Its large tower has four round **corner turrets** and can be seen from far away.

In the Ticino town of **Bellinzona** there stand three famous castles at once: **Castelgrande**, **Montebello** and **Sasso Corbaro**. They guarded an important route to the Alpine passes. Walls joined the castles and shut off the valley. Since the year 2000 they have been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**. They can be visited today.

gewusst: Many hilltop castles in Switzerland are only ruins today, which one can discover on hikes.
The German word “Burg” is connected with “bergen”, that is, to protect.

teile.einleitung: Hernán Cortés was a Spanish conqueror, a so-called conquistador. Between 1519 and 1521 he conquered the empire of the Aztecs in Mexico with his troops and many native allies.
wichtigste: Cortés was born in 1485 in Medellín in Extremadura in Spain.
In 1519 he set out from Cuba for Mexico.
On the Gulf coast he founded the city of Veracruz.
He had his ships sunk so that his men could not turn back.
In the Noche Triste in 1520 the Spanish had to flee from the Aztec capital with great losses.
In 1521 he conquered the capital, which Cuauhtémoc had defended.
The conquered territory became the Spanish colony of New Spain.

abschnitte.text: Hernán Cortés was born in **1485** in Medellín. The place lies in **Extremadura**, a poor region in the west of Spain. Many **conquistadors**, that is, Spanish conquerors in America, came from this area. As a young man Cortés went to the Caribbean. He lived on **Cuba**, which was ruled by Spain.

In the year **1519** Cortés set out from Cuba for Mexico with a few ships. The governor **Diego Velázquez** tried at the last moment to prevent the voyage. On the Gulf coast Cortés founded the town of “Villa Rica de la Vera Cruz”, present-day **Veracruz**. By this he wanted to make himself legally independent of the governor. Then he had his ships made useless and sunk. So his men had only the way inland.

The capital of the Aztecs was called **Tenochtitlan** and lay on an island in a lake. Many peoples in the surrounding area were enemies of the Aztecs and allied themselves with Cortés. In the city the ruler **Moctezuma** was taken prisoner. In 1520 an uprising broke out. In the **Noche Triste**, the “Sad Night”, the Spanish fled across the causeways. Many drowned, also because they were carrying heavy gold.

Cortés returned with new troops and many native allies and besieged the city. The last ruler of the Aztecs, **Cuauhtémoc**, led the resistance. An imported disease, **smallpox**, also weakened the inhabitants badly. In 1521 the city fell. Cuauhtémoc was taken prisoner and executed in 1525 on Cortés's orders.

On the ruins of Tenochtitlan arose present-day **Mexico City**. The conquered territory became the Spanish colony of **New Spain**. Emperor **Charles V** appointed Cortés its governor in 1522. The conquest brought great suffering to the native people. Today Cortés is therefore seen very critically. He died in 1547 in Spain.

gewusst: At the time of the conquest Tenochtitlan was larger than most cities in Europe.
The Spanish had brought horses with them, animals that the people of Mexico had not known before.

teile.einleitung: Eleanor of Aquitaine was one of the most powerful women of the Middle Ages. She was Queen of France and later Queen of England and lived about 80 years, which was very rare at that time.
wichtigste: Eleanor was Queen of France and of England.
Aquitaine, her land, lay in the south-west of France.
With her first husband she went on a crusade.
Her second husband was King Henry II of England.
Her son was the famous King Richard the Lionheart.
She liked to bring singers and poets to her court.
When Richard was captured, she collected money for the ransom.

abschnitte.text: Eleanor was born around **1122**. Her father was Duke of **Aquitaine**, a large and rich region in the **south-west of France**. When he died, Eleanor inherited this land. So she was one of the richest women in Europe. In the same year, **1137**, she married the French heir to the throne, Louis. Soon afterwards he became king, and Eleanor became **Queen of France**.

Together with her first husband, King **Louis VII**, Eleanor went on a **crusade** to the Holy Land. This was the Second Crusade from 1147. The long journey was dangerous and tiring. The crusade was not a success, and the marriage of the two became more and more difficult. In the year **1152** it was dissolved.

Soon afterwards Eleanor married **Henry**, who in 1154 became King of **England** as **Henry II**. So she was a queen in a second country. Among her sons were the later kings **Richard the Lionheart** and John Lackland. Later, in an uprising of her sons, she sided against her husband. Henry then had her held under guard for many years.

Eleanor loved art and music. She liked to bring **singers and poets** to her court, for example **troubadours** from southern France, who performed love songs and stories. When her son Richard was travelling home from a crusade, he was taken prisoner in Austria. Eleanor, with great effort, collected a lot of money for the **ransom**. She died in the year **1204** at about **80 years** old.

gewusst: On his way home, Richard the Lionheart was held prisoner in Dürnstein Castle on the Danube.
Eleanor lies buried in Fontevraud Abbey in France, next to Henry II and Richard the Lionheart.

teile.einleitung: Travelling entertainers, or jugglers, were performers in the Middle Ages. At markets and festivals they showed tricks and made people marvel and laugh. Mostly they moved from place to place.
wichtigste: Entertainers showed tricks at the market.
Often they juggled with balls.
Some balanced on a rope high above the square.
Some spat fire.
Entertainers moved from place to place and had no fixed home.

abschnitte.text: When there was a **market** or a festival in a town, entertainers often came. They **juggled with balls**, rings or knives. Others did somersaults and leaps like acrobats. Some **balanced on a rope** high above the square. People were especially amazed when an entertainer **spat fire**.

Many entertainers could also make music. They played the flute, fiddle or drum and sang songs. Some told stories and news from other places. Others showed magic tricks or trained animals. In return the audience gave them a few coins or something to eat.

Entertainers mostly had **no fixed home**. They **moved from place to place**, often on foot or with a cart. They were counted among the **travelling people**. Many people liked their tricks but distrusted them all the same. Entertainers often had fewer rights than citizens who lived permanently in a town.

gewusst: Today jugglers who juggle and spit fire can be seen again at medieval markets.
The German word “gaukeln” means to pretend something, as in a magic trick.

teile.einleitung: The compass is a device that shows the compass direction. It was invented in China and later helped sailors on the open sea to find the right way.
wichtigste: The compass was invented in ancient China.
The compass needle is a small magnet and points north.
An early Chinese compass had the shape of a spoon.
Shen Kuo described in 1088 that the needle does not point exactly north.
Around 1100 Chinese texts mention the compass as an aid for sailors.
Today it is needed, for example, in orienteering.

abschnitte.text: The **compass needle** is a small **magnet**. The Earth has a **magnetic field**, and the needle lines up with it. That is why it always points **north**. On the compass are the four directions: **N** for north, **S** for south, **E** for east and **W** for west. If you know north, you can also find all the other directions.

The compass was invented in ancient **China**. Old reports describe a **spoon** made of lodestone that lay on a smooth plate. Its handle pointed south. At first lodestones were used more for fortune-telling. Later the compass came to Europe by way of Arabia.

The Chinese scholar **Shen Kuo** wrote about the magnetic needle in 1088 in his work “Dream Pool Essays”. He was one of the first to notice that it does not point exactly north. The **magnetic north pole** does not lie exactly at the geographic North Pole. This small deviation has to be taken into account in precise measurements.

On the open sea one sees no land. In fog or at night one cannot steer by the **sun** either. A Chinese text from the years around 1111 to 1117 mentions that sailors looked at the magnetic needle in cloudy weather. Later the compass also became indispensable for European **sailors** and explorers.

Today many mobile phones show the direction electronically. Even so, the compass is still important, for example when hiking in the mountains. In **orienteering** one finds the control points in the forest with a map and compass. This sport is also found in many Swiss schools.

gewusst: The first compass from China did not point north but south, with the handle of the spoon.
The magnetic north pole moves slowly and does not lie at the geographic North Pole.

teile.einleitung: Henry the Navigator was a Portuguese prince in the 15th century. He sent ships along the coast of Africa and is regarded as a pathfinder of the great voyages of discovery, although he himself hardly went to sea.
wichtigste: Henry was a son of the Portuguese King John I.
In 1415 he took part in the conquest of Ceuta in North Africa.
He himself hardly went to sea, but sent captains on voyages of discovery.
He often stayed at Sagres on the south-western tip of Portugal.
From about 1420 the Portuguese settled the Atlantic island of Madeira.
In 1434 Gil Eanes, on his orders, sailed round the dreaded Cape Bojador.
Henry died in November 1460.

abschnitte.text: Henry was born in 1394 and was a son of King **John I** of Portugal. Portugal is a small country on the Atlantic. Because it was open only towards the sea, the Portuguese looked for new ways to trade and wealth. Henry was not a king, but as a prince he had a lot of money and influence. He used these means for seafaring.

In the year **1415** Portugal conquered the city of **Ceuta** on the north coast of Africa. Henry took part in this campaign and distinguished himself. The conquest is regarded as the beginning of Portuguese expansion overseas. Later Henry went to sea mainly for such campaigns to North Africa.

His nickname is astonishing: Henry himself undertook **no voyages of discovery**. He paid for them and planned them, and his **captains** sailed off. He often stayed at **Sagres** on the south-western tip of Portugal and had a settlement built there. The story of a great “school of navigation” at Sagres is, however, regarded today as a legend.

Around 1419 Portuguese sailors reached the island of **Madeira** in the Atlantic and soon began to settle it. Later sugar cane was grown there. On the coast of West Africa lay **Cape Bojador**. Many sailors believed that beyond it began an impassable sea. **Gil Eanes** sailed round the cape in the year 1434 on Henry's orders and proved that this fear was unfounded.

Henry died in **November 1460** in Sagres. By then his ships had already sailed far along the coast of West Africa. Only after his death did the Portuguese reach the southern tip of Africa. Later **Vasco da Gama** found the sea route to India. With his voyages Henry had prepared the way for it.

gewusst: Henry got the nickname “the Navigator” only long after his death.
In Lisbon the great Monument to the Discoveries recalls Henry, and he stands right at the front.

teile.einleitung: The Frankish Empire was the most powerful empire in Western Europe in the early Middle Ages. It arose around 500 under King Clovis I and reached its greatest extent under Charlemagne. Later France and Germany emerged from it, and large parts of present-day Switzerland also belonged to it.
wichtigste: The Frankish Empire lasted from about the 5th to the 9th century.
The Frankish king Clovis I had himself baptised a Christian around 500.
Around 500 the Franks defeated the Alemanni, who also settled in present-day German-speaking Switzerland.
Charles Martel and Pepin held the office of mayor of the palace at the court of the Merovingian kings.
In 732 Charles Martel fought an Arab army at Tours and Poitiers.
In 751 Pepin the Younger became the first Carolingian king of the Franks.
In 843 the Frankish Empire was divided into three parts by the Treaty of Verdun.

abschnitte.text: The **Franks** were a Germanic tribe that lived on the Lower Rhine. After the end of the Western Roman Empire, King **Clovis I** of the family of the **Merovingians** united the Franks. Around 500 he defeated the Alemanni and had himself baptised a Christian. In this way he won the support of the Church and of the Roman population in Gaul.

Later the Merovingian kings lost power. The real rule was exercised by the **mayors of the palace**, the chief administrators at the royal court. The most famous was **Charles Martel**, who in 732 defeated an Arab army at the Battle of Tours and Poitiers. His son **Pepin the Younger** deposed the last Merovingian in 751 and became king himself.

With Pepin began the rule of the **Carolingians**, named after Charles Martel and Charlemagne. **Charlemagne** greatly extended the empire through many wars, as far as Italy, northern Germany and Spain. In the year 800 he was crowned emperor in Rome by the pope. The Frankish Empire now covered a large part of Western Europe.

After the death of Charlemagne's son Louis the Pious, his sons quarrelled over the inheritance. In the **Treaty of Verdun** the empire was divided into three parts in 843. Charles the Bald received the West Frankish Kingdom, Louis the German the East Frankish Kingdom and Lothair I the Middle Kingdom between them. The West Frankish Kingdom later became **France**, the East Frankish Kingdom **Germany**.

The regions of present-day Switzerland came under Frankish rule in the 6th century, after the Franks had also conquered the kingdom of the **Burgundians**. In German-speaking Switzerland lived the **Alemanni**, in western Switzerland the Burgundians, both under Frankish kings. In this period important monasteries arose such as the **Abbey of St Gallen** and the monastery of St John in Müstair. The language border between German and French in Switzerland goes back in part to this time.

The Frankish Empire combined Roman, Christian and Germanic traditions. It laid the foundations for the feudal system and for the order of the Middle Ages. The name France still recalls the Franks today. Charlemagne is often called the “Father of Europe”, because his empire joined large parts of Europe together.

begriffe.erklaerung: The first royal family of the Frankish Empire, named after an ancestor called Merovech.
The second Frankish royal family, to which Charlemagne belonged.
The chief administrator at the court of the Merovingian kings.
A Germanic tribe that settled, among other places, in present-day German-speaking Switzerland.

gewusst: According to tradition, Charlemagne founded the monastery of St John in Müstair, which is today a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The name France originally means “realm of the Franks”.
The Merovingian kings wore long hair as a sign of their dignity.

teile.einleitung: In the Middle Ages the Church was the most important institution in Europe, alongside kings and nobles. It determined belief, the calendar, education and often even politics. Its churches and monasteries still shape many towns and villages today, including in Switzerland.
wichtigste: The head of the Catholic Church in the Middle Ages was the pope in Rome.
Church services in the West were held in Latin.
The Investiture Controversy was about who may install bishops, the king or the pope.
In 1077 King Henry IV went to Canossa as a penitent to ask the pope for forgiveness.
With the ban the pope could exclude someone from the Church.
Monasteries were places of prayer, but also of education, medicine and farming.
Gothic churches can be recognised by pointed arches and tall windows.

abschnitte.text: Almost all people in western and central Europe belonged to the Catholic Church in the Middle Ages. At the top stood the **pope** in Rome, and beneath him came bishops, abbots and priests. The Church owned a lot of land and demanded the **tithe** from the peasants, that is, a tenth of the harvest. It also regulated everyday life: holidays, fasting seasons, baptism, marriage and burial all belonged to the Church.

For a long time kings and emperors installed bishops themselves, because bishops were also powerful lords of the land. Pope Gregory VII wanted to forbid this, and so the **Investiture Controversy** began. He laid King Henry IV under the **ban**, that is, exclusion from the Church. In the winter of 1077 Henry went as a penitent to **Canossa** in Italy and waited in the snow until the pope forgave him. Only in 1122 did emperor and pope agree in the Concordat of Worms.

In the West church services were celebrated in **Latin**, even though most people did not understand this language. Reading and writing were mainly skills of the clergy. Monks copied books by hand in monasteries and in this way preserved a great deal of knowledge from antiquity. From cathedral schools and monastery schools the first **universities** later arose.

Monks and nuns lived by fixed rules, the best known being the rule of Saint Benedict with the motto “Pray and work”. The **monastery of St Gall** was one of the most important monasteries in Europe. Its Abbey Library still holds very old manuscripts today and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The monastery of **Einsiedeln** has also been a well-known place of pilgrimage since the Middle Ages.

At first churches were built in the **Romanesque** style, with thick walls, small windows and round arches. From the 12th century **Gothic** appeared in France. Gothic churches have pointed arches, tall vaults and huge coloured glass windows through which a lot of light falls. In Switzerland the cathedral of Lausanne and the Bern Minster are well-known Gothic buildings.

begriffe.erklaerung: The head of the Catholic Church, who has his seat in Rome.
A punishment of the Church: one was excluded from the community of believers.
The solemn installation of a bishop in his office.
A place where monks or nuns live, pray and work together.
A building style of the Middle Ages with pointed arches and tall windows.

gewusst: The Plan of St Gall from the 9th century is the oldest surviving architectural drawing of a whole monastery.
The expression “to go to Canossa” still means today having to apologise humbly.
People often worked for over a hundred years on the building of great Gothic churches.

teile.einleitung: In the Middle Ages most people were peasants, about nine out of ten people lived in the countryside. They grew grain, kept animals and so fed the whole of society. Their lives were hard, because they also had to work for a lord and hand over dues.
wichtigste: Peasants were the largest group of the population in the Middle Ages.
Many peasants were unfree and, as serfs, were bound to their lord.
They had to hand over part of the harvest, for example the tithe.
They had to work for their lord for nothing, which is called labour service.
The plough was often pulled by an ox, and the grain was cut with a sickle.
Every day there was mostly porridge and bread, often made from rye.
Children also helped with the work from an early age.

abschnitte.text: In the Middle Ages there were three great estates: the clergy, who prayed, the nobility, who fought, and the **peasants**, who worked. The peasants were by far the largest group. Many were **serfs** or bondsmen, and they were not allowed to leave their village without permission. The land mostly belonged to a **landlord**, for example a nobleman or a monastery.

Peasants mainly grew grain such as **rye**, oats, barley and spelt. The plough was pulled by an **ox**, later also by horses. From the High Middle Ages the **three-field system** became established: one field carried winter grain, one carried summer grain and one was left fallow for a year so that the soil could recover. At harvest the grain was cut with a sickle and threshed with a flail.

Peasants had to hand over part of the harvest to their lord. The **tithe** was a tenth of the harvest and mostly went to the Church. In addition there was **labour service**: on certain days the peasants had to work on the lord's fields for nothing or do carting jobs. In return, the lord promised them protection.

Many farmhouses were built of wood and clay and had **thatched roofs**. In winter, people and animals often lived under one roof, and the animals helped to warm the house. People ate mostly **porridge** and bread, with vegetables such as turnips, cabbage and beans. Meat was rare, usually only on feast days.

Peasant children did not go to school. They helped with the work from an early age, minded geese and sheep, gathered wood or helped with the harvest. From their parents they learnt everything one had to know on the farm. Many children died young of illnesses, because there were hardly any doctors.

In some parts of present-day Switzerland, for example in Central Switzerland, the peasants were freer than elsewhere. They organised themselves into valley communities and used pastures and woods together as the **Allmend**, the common land. In the Alpine region, cattle farming with cheese and butter played a big part. In the **Peasants' War** of 1653, Swiss peasants rose up against the high dues demanded by their town authorities.

begriffe.erklaerung: An unfree peasant who was bound to his lord.
A due of a tenth of the harvest, mostly paid to the Church.
Work that peasants had to do for their lord without pay.
A way of farming in which one field was allowed to rest every third year.
Pastures and woods that belonged to everyone in a village together.

gewusst: A medieval peasant often harvested only three to four times as much grain as he had sown.
The word “Fron” originally means “lord”, so labour service was service for the lord.
In the Ballenberg open-air museum in the Bernese Oberland you can visit old farmhouses from all over Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: The Way of St James is a famous pilgrim route. It leads from all over Europe to Santiago de Compostela in Spain, where the apostle James is said to be buried. A Way of St James also runs through Switzerland.
wichtigste: Pilgrims are people who walk to a holy place.
The Way of St James ends at Santiago de Compostela in the north-west of Spain, in the region of Galicia.
It is named after the apostle James, one of the twelve apostles of Jesus.
The sign of the pilgrims of St James is the scallop shell.
In the Middle Ages most pilgrims travelled on foot and with a pilgrim's staff.
In Switzerland the route leads as far as Geneva and on through France.
Today pilgrims collect stamps in a pilgrim passport.

abschnitte.titel: A way to the tomb of James
abschnitte.text: **Pilgrims** are people who walk to a holy place in order to pray there. A particularly well-known destination is **Santiago de Compostela** in the north-west of **Spain**, in the region of **Galicia**. There the apostle **James** is said to be buried. He was one of the **twelve apostles** of Jesus. The name Santiago means “Saint James”. Even in the Middle Ages very many pilgrims were on their way there.

Most pilgrims went **on foot**. The journey often lasted many **months**, and on the way there were threats from illness, robbers and bad weather. Every pilgrim carried a **pilgrim's staff**. It helped with walking and with warding off dogs. Monasteries and **pilgrim hostels** offered food and a place to sleep. Many people made pilgrimages to thank God or to ask for forgiveness.

The sign of the pilgrims of St James is the **scallop shell**. In the Middle Ages pilgrims brought such a shell home from the coast of Galicia. With it they showed that they had been to Santiago. Today the shell can be seen on many **signposts**. It shows walkers where the path continues.

abschnitte.titel: The Way of St James in Switzerland
abschnitte.text: A Way of St James also runs through **Switzerland**. It begins at **Lake Constance** and leads via **Einsiedeln** with its famous monastery, on through Fribourg and Lausanne as far as **Geneva**. There the route leaves Switzerland towards **France**. After that it goes through France and over the Pyrenees to Spain. Many people today walk only individual sections.

Today very many people make the pilgrimage to Santiago every year, out of faith, for the joy of walking or to reflect. They carry a **pilgrim passport**. In churches and lodgings they receive **stamps** in it. In this way one can see where they have been. Anyone who walks at least the last 100 kilometres on foot can receive a certificate in Santiago, the **Compostela**.

gewusst: The Ways of St James in Spain are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
In 1987 the Way of St James was declared the first Cultural Route of the Council of Europe.

teile.einleitung: The Inquisition was a Church court procedure in the Middle Ages. Its aim was to track down people who departed from the official teaching of the Catholic Church, so-called heretics.
wichtigste: The word comes from the Latin “inquirere”, which means to investigate.
The aim was to track down heresy, that is, departures from Church teaching.
From the 1230s the popes often appointed Dominicans as inquisitors.
In 1252 Pope Innocent IV allowed torture with the bull “Ad extirpanda”.
Death sentences were carried out by the secular authorities, that is, princes or cities.
Bernard Gui wrote a well-known handbook for inquisitors in Toulouse.
In 1431 Joan of Arc was burnt after a Church trial in Rouen.

abschnitte.text: The word **Inquisition** comes from the Latin verb “**inquirere**”, which means **to investigate**. In this procedure a judge investigated suspects on his own initiative. So he did not wait for someone to bring a complaint. The search was for **heresy**. That is the name for a teaching that departs from the official teaching of the Church. People who believed such things were called **heretics**.

In the 13th century groups such as the **Cathars**, whom the Church rejected, spread in southern France and Italy. From the **1230s** the popes appointed their own **inquisitors**, who were answerable directly to them. They often chose **Dominicans** for this. These preaching friars were well educated and were thought especially suitable. Franciscans also worked as inquisitors.

The inquisitors questioned suspects and witnesses. With the bull “**Ad extirpanda**”, **Pope Innocent IV** allowed **torture** in **1252** in order to force confessions. Many accused people had to do **penance**, for example pray, go on pilgrimage or wear a mark on their clothing. Anyone who would not repent was handed over to the “secular arm”. The **secular authorities**, that is, princes or cities, then mostly carried out the death sentence.

One of the best-known inquisitors was **Bernard Gui**. He was a Dominican and worked in **Toulouse** in the early 14th century. He wrote the handbook “**Practica inquisitionis**”. In it he describes how interrogations should be conducted and how to recognise various groups. For historical research the book is an important source today.

A famous Church trial was the one against **Joan of Arc**. She had fought for France in the Hundred Years' War. A Church court under English influence condemned her, and in **1431** she was burnt in **Rouen**. In 1456 the verdict was overturned. In 1920 the Church declared her a saint. Today the Catholic Church itself takes a critical view of the Inquisition.

gewusst: The Spanish Inquisition arose only in 1478 and was an institution of its own under the supervision of the Spanish kings.
In the year 2000 Pope John Paul II publicly asked forgiveness for wrongs done in the name of the Church.

teile.einleitung: Humanism was an intellectual movement that began in Italy in the 14th century and spread across the whole of Europe in the 15th and 16th centuries. At the centre were man and his education. The humanists studied the writings of the ancient Greeks and Romans and in this way wanted to make people wiser and better.
wichtigste: At the centre of humanism were man and his education.
The motto of the humanists was “ad fontes”, which means “to the sources”.
The Italian poet Francesco Petrarch is regarded as the “father of humanism”.
Humanists learnt Latin and Greek especially eagerly.
Erasmus of Rotterdam lived for a long time in Basel and died there in 1536.
Thanks to its university and many printing houses, Basel was a centre of humanism.
The Zurich reformer Huldrych Zwingli was strongly influenced by Erasmus.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from the Latin **humanitas**, which means humanity and education. The humanists believed that through education man can develop his abilities. They cultivated especially the **studia humanitatis**, that is, language, poetry, history and philosophy. Humanism belongs closely to the **Renaissance**, the rebirth of ancient culture.
