The motto of the humanists was **“ad fontes”**, in English “to the sources”. They wanted to read the old texts in the original and not only in later copies or translations. So they learnt **Latin and Greek** eagerly. In old monastery libraries they searched for forgotten manuscripts of ancient writers.

The “father of humanism” is regarded as the Italian poet **Francesco Petrarch**, who lived in the 14th century. He collected old manuscripts and admired Roman writers such as Cicero. After the fall of Constantinople in 1453, many Greek scholars came to Italy and brought books and knowledge with them. Rich families such as the Medici in Florence supported scholars and artists.

The most famous humanist north of the Alps was **Erasmus of Rotterdam**. He lived for a long time in **Basel**, which had a university and many printing houses, and died there in 1536. In 1516 in Basel, with the printer Johann Froben, he published the **New Testament** anew in Greek. The University of Basel, the oldest in Switzerland, had already been founded in 1460.

In St Gallen **Joachim Vadian** was active, who was a doctor, scholar and mayor of his town. The Zurich reformer **Huldrych Zwingli** was strongly influenced by Erasmus and read the Bible in the Greek original. In this way humanism in Switzerland also prepared the way for the Reformation. In Basel, well-known artists also worked, such as Hans Holbein the Younger, who painted Erasmus several times.

The Englishman **Thomas More** wrote the book “Utopia” in 1516 about an invented, ideal state. The word **utopia** has since stood for an idea of a better world. Humanism shaped the schools in Europe, for example the grammar school with Latin and Greek. The idea that every person has a dignity of their own was also influenced by humanist thought.

begriffe.erklaerung: A movement that put man and his education at the centre.
Latin for “to the sources”, the motto of the humanists.
French for “rebirth”, the time in which ancient culture was rediscovered.
The idea of an ideal place or state that does not exist as such.

gewusst: Erasmus is buried in Basel Minster.
The exchange programme Erasmus, with which students in Europe study abroad, is named after Erasmus of Rotterdam.
Many humanists gave themselves Latin or Greek names, so Joachim von Watt called himself Vadianus.

teile.einleitung: Justinian I was emperor of the Eastern Roman or Byzantine Empire in the 6th century. He wanted to restore the old Roman Empire and had Roman law arranged in a great collection.
wichtigste: Justinian I reigned from 527 to 565, so in the 6th century.
His influential wife was Empress Theodora.
He had Roman law collected in the Corpus Juris Civilis.
In 532 the Nika riot in Constantinople threatened his rule.
His general Belisarius reconquered North Africa from the Vandals.
From 541 the so-called Justinianic Plague raged in the empire.
Around 552 monks secretly brought silkworm eggs into the empire.

abschnitte.text: The Roman Empire had split into a western and an eastern part. The West had fallen, but the **East** lived on. It is also called the **Byzantine Empire**, and its capital was **Constantinople**, today's Istanbul. **Justinian I** followed his uncle **Justin I** on the throne in **527**. He ruled until his death in **565**.

Justinian's wife **Theodora** came from a humble background and became **empress**. She advised him on important matters. In **532** the **Nika riot** broke out in Constantinople. The Blues and the Greens, two parties of spectators at the **chariot races**, rose together with the cry “**Nika**”, which means “Win!”. Justinian wanted to flee, but Theodora is said to have persuaded him to stay. The revolt was put down bloodily in the **Hippodrome**.

Justinian wanted to **restore the Roman Empire** and win back the lost territories of the West. His general **Belisarius** defeated the kingdom of the **Vandals** in North Africa in 533 and 534. After that he fought against the Ostrogoths in **Italy**. Parts of Spain were also conquered. The wars lasted a long time and cost a great deal of money.

Justinian's most important work was a huge **collection of laws**. He had Roman law collected and arranged. Later the work was called the **Corpus Juris Civilis**. It influences the law of many European countries to this day, including **Switzerland**. Many principles in Swiss civil law go back to Roman law.

In Constantinople Justinian had the **Hagia Sophia** rebuilt, a huge church with a mighty dome, consecrated in 537. From **541** the **plague** broke out in the empire. The **Justinianic Plague** killed very many people in the Mediterranean region and weakened the empire greatly. Around **552** **monks** smuggled eggs of **silkworms** in hollow canes from Asia into the empire. In this way Byzantium could make **silk** itself.

gewusst: The Hagia Sophia still stands in Istanbul today and for almost a thousand years was the largest church in Christendom.
In the church of San Vitale in Ravenna famous mosaics show Justinian and Theodora.

teile.einleitung: The Great Mosque of Djenné stands in the town of Djenné in the West African country of Mali. It is built entirely of mud and is regarded as the largest mud building in the world. Every year the people of the town repair it together.
wichtigste: The Great Mosque of Djenné is the largest mud building in the world.
It stands in the town of Djenné in Mali.
The present mosque was built around 1907.
Once a year people spread new mud on the walls.
The wooden beams in the walls serve as scaffolding for repairs.

abschnitte.text: **Djenné** lies in the inland delta of the river Niger in **Mali**. Even in the Middle Ages the town was an important trading place. Here traders exchanged gold, salt and other goods. Djenné was also a place of Islamic learning. A large mosque stood here early on. The **present mosque** was built **around 1907**, on the model of the older one.

The mosque is built of bricks made of **mud** that were dried in the sun. The walls are plastered with mud too. It is the **largest mud building in the world**. Many **wooden beams** of palm wood stick out of the walls. They serve as **scaffolding** on which one can climb when **repairing**. At the same time they are a decoration of the façade.

Rain softens the mud a little every year. So the mosque has to be looked after constantly. **Once a year** many people from the town come together and **spread new mud on the walls**. Children and women fetch water and carry mud, men climb on the beams and plaster the walls. The shared festival is very important for the town. The old town of Djenné is a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

gewusst: Without the yearly care with fresh mud, the mosque of Djenné would in time be destroyed by the rain.

teile.einleitung: The caravel was a small, nimble sailing ship. In the 15th century it became the most important ship of the Portuguese explorers, who sailed with it ever further south along the coast of Africa.
wichtigste: The caravel was a small, nimble sailing ship.
The Portuguese developed it further in the 15th century for voyages of discovery.
Typical were triangular sails, which are called lateen sails.
With lateen sails one could sail against the wind by tacking.
Because of its shallow draught it could sail close to coasts.
A caravel usually had two or three masts.
The Niña and the Pinta of Columbus were caravels.

abschnitte.text: The **caravel** was a small wooden sailing ship. The Portuguese developed it further in the 15th century because they wanted to explore unknown coasts. Their ship had to be nimble and able to react quickly to dangers. With caravels Portuguese sailors went south bit by bit along the west coast of Africa. In this way they prepared the sea route to India.

A typical Portuguese caravel carried **lateen sails**. These are triangular sails that come from the Mediterranean region. With them a ship can sail at an angle against the wind. This is called **tacking**: the ship sails in a zigzag and so still makes progress. This was important, because on the way back from Africa the sailors often had the wind against them.

The **draught** says how deep a ship reaches into the water. The hull of a caravel did not sit deep in the water. So it could sail close to coasts and even into river mouths without easily running aground. A caravel usually had **two or three masts**. Later, larger versions also carried four masts and in part square sails.

When **Christopher Columbus** sailed across the Atlantic in 1492, he had three ships with him. The **Niña** and the **Pinta** were caravels. The **Santa María**, by contrast, was larger and clumsier. She was a so-called **nao**. The small caravels were fast, while the nao offered more room for people and supplies.

For long trading voyages to India the caravel was too small. There one needed a lot of room for cargo, water and food. So the **carrack** became more important. It was a large ship with plenty of hold space. On these well-known routes nimbleness was less important than space.

gewusst: With triangular sails a ship can make progress in a zigzag even against the wind.
Two of the three ships of the first voyage of Columbus were caravels.

teile.einleitung: The Merovingians were the first great royal family of the Franks. From the 5th to the 8th century they ruled an empire that covered large parts of present-day France, Belgium and Germany.
wichtigste: The Merovingians are named after Merovech.
Long hair was the sign of their royal dignity.
Their empire was often divided into sub-kingdoms such as Austrasia and Neustria.
Dagobert I is regarded as the last Merovingian with real power.
The late kings are called shadow kings.
In 751 Pepin the Younger became king of the Franks.

abschnitte.text: The family is named after **Merovech**. He is said to have been an ancestor of Clovis and lived in the 5th century. Almost only legendary things are known about him. The kings wore their hair long. So they were called the “long-haired kings”. Anyone who was deposed often had his hair cut off.

In the year **1653** a rich grave was found during construction work in **Tournai** in present-day Belgium. It belonged to King **Childeric I**, the father of Clovis. In it lay weapons, jewellery and a **signet ring**. The ring bore the name of the king. So people knew who was buried here.

The Merovingians often divided their empire among several sons. In this way sub-kingdoms arose. **Austrasia** lay in the east on the Rhine, **Neustria** in the west with centres such as Paris and Soissons. The sub-kingdoms were often rivals. In the late 6th century the queens **Brunhilda** and **Fredegund** waged a bloody feud against each other lasting decades.

abschnitte.titel: Shadow kings and mayors of the palace
abschnitte.text: **Dagobert I**, who died in 639, still ruled with vigour. After him power passed more and more to the **mayors of the palace**. These were the chief stewards at court. The kings ruled only in name. They are therefore called **shadow kings**. The mayor of the palace **Charles Martel** defeated an Arab army between Tours and Poitiers in **732**.

Charles Martel's son **Pepin the Younger** wanted to be king himself. He first obtained the consent of the pope. In **751** he was raised to king of the Franks. The last Merovingian, **Childeric III**, was sent to a monastery. With this the time of the **Carolingians** began.

gewusst: The epithet “Martel” means “hammer”.
Parts of present-day Switzerland also belonged to the empire of the Merovingians.

teile.einleitung: In the Middle Ages the market square was the heart of a town. Here peasants and traders sold their goods, and here people met and learnt the news.
wichtigste: The market square was a large open space in the town.
The weekly market took place every week on a particular day.
A fair took place only once or a few times a year.
Peasants brought vegetables and eggs into the town.
People paid with coins, often of silver.
Goods were weighed with scales.

abschnitte.titel: In the middle of the town
abschnitte.text: The **market square** usually lay in the middle of the town. Often the town hall and a fountain stood there. On market day traders set up their **stalls**. People shopped, chatted and heard the news. So the market was also a meeting place.

The **peasants** came from the countryside into the town. They sold what grew on their farm: **vegetables**, **eggs**, cheese or grain. Bananas, cocoa, tomatoes and maize were not yet known in Europe in the Middle Ages. These plants came only later from distant countries.

A market that takes place every week is called a **weekly market**. It still exists in many Swiss towns today. A large market that took place only once or a few times a year was called a **fair**. Traders came there from far away. There was also entertainment, for example jugglers and musicians.

People paid with **coins**, mostly of silver. Sometimes goods were exchanged for goods. Many goods such as flour or salt were sold by weight. For this one needed **scales**. The town checked whether scales and weights were correct, so that nobody was cheated.

A **market crier** called out loudly how good and cheap his goods were. In this way he attracted buyers to his stall. Old markets still exist in Switzerland today. At the **Zibelemärit** in Bern every November it is above all **onions** that are sold. “Zibele” means onion in Bernese German, and everywhere there are braids of onions.

gewusst: Many towns arose in the first place around a market.
Market criers can still be found at some markets today.

teile.einleitung: The transatlantic slave trade was the trade in people who were taken by force from Africa and brought across the Atlantic to America. From the 15th to the 19th century, millions of Africans were captured, sold and forced to work in this way. It is one of the greatest crimes in history, and its consequences can still be felt today.
wichtigste: Around 12 to 13 million Africans were forced onto ships.
About 1.5 to 2 million people died during the crossing itself.
From the 1440s, Portugal was the first European sea power to begin taking people from West Africa by force.
The most important destination was Brazil.
In the triangular trade, goods went to Africa, enslaved people to America and plantation products to Europe.
In 1807, Britain banned its subjects from the slave trade.
In 1888, Brazil was the last country in the Americas to abolish slavery.

abschnitte.text: In the transatlantic slave trade, people were bought and sold like goods. **Enslaved** people had no rights, they belonged to an owner and had to work without pay. Their children also counted as slaves. From the **1440s**, the Portuguese were the first to take people by force from West Africa, followed later by Spain, England, France, the Netherlands and other countries.

The trade often ran in the shape of a triangle, which is why it is called the **triangular trade**. Ships brought goods such as cloth, weapons and alcohol from Europe to Africa. There they were exchanged for captured people, who were taken to America. With the proceeds from America, such as sugar, cotton, tobacco and coffee, the ships sailed back to Europe.

The crossing from Africa to America is usually called the **Middle Passage** by researchers, that is, the “middle leg” of the triangle. People lay chained close together below deck, often for weeks. There was too little water, food and fresh air, so diseases spread quickly. According to estimates, about 1.5 to 2 million people died on the crossing.

Most of those taken by force had to work on **plantations**, that is, on huge fields with a single crop. In the 17th and 18th centuries, especially many people were brought to the Caribbean for growing **sugar cane**. The most important destination was Brazil, where around 40 per cent of all those taken by force ended up. With the **asiento**, Spain granted licences to traders who were allowed to deliver enslaved people to the Spanish colonies.

Enslaved people resisted again and again, they fled or fought. In the French colony of Saint-Domingue, a great uprising led to the founding of **Haiti** in 1804. In Europe, **abolitionists** campaigned for a ban, including formerly enslaved people. Britain banned the slave trade in 1807, in 1815 European powers outlawed it at the **Congress of Vienna**, and in 1888 Brazil was the last country in the Americas to abolish slavery.

The slave trade changed Africa and America deeply. In many countries of the Americas, millions of descendants of those taken by force live today, and their culture shapes music, language and food. At the same time, inequality and **racism** from this period still have effects today. Merchants, banks and companies from Switzerland also profited from the slave trade and from plantations, which is now being researched and dealt with.

begriffe.erklaerung: When people belong to another person like property and have to work without rights or pay.
A very large field on which only one crop, such as sugar cane or cotton, is grown.
The dangerous crossing of the slave ships from Africa to America.
A permission from the Spanish crown to deliver enslaved people to its colonies.
The movement that demanded an end to slavery.

gewusst: On 23 August each year, UNESCO commemorates the slave trade and its abolition, because on that day in 1791 the uprising in Haiti began.
Haiti was the first state in the world to arise from a successful uprising of enslaved people.
More enslaved people were brought to Brazil than to any other country.

teile.einleitung: The manorial system was the most important order in the countryside in the Middle Ages. Most peasants did not own the land they farmed. It belonged to a landlord, to whom they had to give dues and work.
wichtigste: The peasants' land mostly belonged to a landlord.
The landlord could be a nobleman, a bishop or a monastery.
The landlord promised the peasants protection.
The peasants had to do unpaid work, the labour service.
The steward managed the manor farm for the landlord.
At carnival time peasants often had to hand over a hen.

abschnitte.text: A **landlord** owned a lot of land and the villages on it. This could be a **nobleman**, who often lived **in a castle**. But bishops and **monasteries** were landlords too. In Switzerland, for example, the monasteries of St Gallen and Einsiedeln had a great deal of land. The landlord gave the peasants land to farm and **promised them protection**.

For the land the peasants had to pay **dues**. They gave part of their harvest, for example grain, wine or cheese. In addition there were eggs or animals. Often a **hen** had to be handed over at **carnival time**, the so-called carnival hen. Many peasants were **bondsmen**. They were not allowed simply to leave their land and needed the lord's permission for many things.

Besides the dues, the peasants also had to **work without pay**. This work was called **labour service**. The old German word “fron” means “belonging to the lord”. The peasants ploughed the lord's fields, harvested his grain, felled wood or repaired roads. This time was then missing for their own fields.

At the centre stood the **manor farm**, the landlord's large farm. The peasants had to work for it, and there they brought their dues. Because the landlord could not be everywhere himself, he appointed a manager. He was called the **steward**, in German Meier. He collected the dues and kept an eye on the work. That is why Meier is still one of the most common family names in Switzerland today.

abschnitte.titel: The end of the manorial system
abschnitte.text: Many peasants were unhappy with the high dues. Again and again there were uprisings, in Switzerland for example the Peasants' War of 1653. In Switzerland the old dues were gradually abolished or bought out after 1798. In the 19th century the manorial system ended in most countries of Europe. Since then the land has mostly belonged to the peasants themselves.

gewusst: Many common Swiss family names such as Meier or Meyer come from the manager of a manor farm.
The German word “Fronleichnam” (Corpus Christi) contains the same old word “fron”, meaning “belonging to the lord”.

teile.einleitung: In the Middle Ages, most houses had no bathroom. To wash, people went to the bathhouse, where the bathkeeper provided warm water and did many other jobs as well.
wichtigste: In the bathhouse, people washed.
The man who ran it was called the bathkeeper (Bader).
The water was heated in cauldrons over the fire.
People bathed in large wooden tubs, often several people together.
Many bathhouses also had a steam bath.
The bathkeeper cut hair, shaved, pulled teeth and did cupping.

abschnitte.text: In the Middle Ages, houses had no **bathroom** and no running water. That is why people went to the **bathhouse**. In many towns there were several of them. People bathed in a **wooden tub**, a large vat made of wood. Often several people sat in it. Bathing was also a meeting place for a chat.

The water was heated in large **cauldrons** over the **fire**. This took a lot of **wood**. Many bathhouses also had a **steam bath**. There, water was poured onto hot stones, and steam rose, similar to a sauna. Afterwards you washed yourself off with warm water.

The bathhouse was run by the **bathkeeper**. He saw to the fire and the warm water. In addition he **cut hair** and **shaved beards**, so he was also a kind of barber. There were no dentists as there are today. If someone had a bad toothache, **the bathkeeper pulled the tooth**. He also treated small wounds.

A well-known treatment at the bathkeeper's was **cupping**. For this he placed warmed small **glasses** on the back. As they cooled, they sucked themselves tight to the skin. People believed that this helps against illnesses. Whether it really helps is disputed today.

From the 16th century, many bathhouses closed. One reason was that **wood** was getting more and more expensive. In addition, people feared that **diseases** spread in the baths. So for a long time people bathed less often. Only much later did houses get bathrooms of their own.

gewusst: The bathkeeper's trade was regarded for a long time as not very respectable, although it was very useful.
In Switzerland, warm springs such as those in Baden in Aargau were already popular in the Middle Ages.

teile.einleitung: The flagellants were religious groups in the Middle Ages who travelled through the countries in processions. They beat themselves in order to do penance for their sins. Most flagellants appeared during the great plague of about 1348.
wichtigste: In their processions the flagellants beat themselves.
The name comes from the Latin word for a whip.
Around 1260 flagellants appeared in greater numbers in Italy for the first time.
The flagellant processions reached their peak during the plague of 1348/1349.
According to their rule, a procession lasted 33 and a half days.
In 1349 Pope Clement VI banned the flagellant processions.

abschnitte.text: The flagellants believed that God punishes people because of their sins. So they wanted to do **penance**, that is, to atone for their faults. In their processions they **beat themselves** on the back with a whip. As they did so they sang songs and prayed aloud. The name comes from the Latin word for a **whip**.

Around **1260** flagellants appeared in greater numbers in **Italy** for the first time. At that time wars and unrest reigned there. The movement also spread to the north but soon disappeared again. Almost a hundred years later it came back, this time much bigger.

In 1348 and 1349 the **plague** raged in Europe, a serious illness from which very many people died. Many were very afraid and looked for explanations. Now the **flagellant processions** reached their **peak**. According to their rule, a procession lasted **33 and a half days**, for that many years Jesus is said to have lived. In some places the flagellants also stirred up feeling against Jews, who were falsely blamed for the plague.

The Church viewed the flagellants with concern. They travelled about without priests and did not keep to the order of the Church. In **1349** **Pope Clement VI** banned the flagellant processions. After that they quickly grew smaller. Individual groups, however, existed for a long time still.

gewusst: The duration of 33 and a half days was meant to recall the years of Jesus's life.
In scholarship the flagellants are also called Flagellanten, after the Latin word for a whip.

teile.einleitung: The Walk to Canossa is one of the best-known events of the Middle Ages. In January 1077 King Henry IV asked Pope Gregory VII for forgiveness outside the castle of Canossa in Italy. To this day people say “going to Canossa” when someone has to apologise humbly.
wichtigste: Henry IV wanted to have the excommunication lifted.
In the winter of 1076/77 he crossed the snow-covered Alps.
His wife Bertha of Savoy accompanied him.
Canossa Castle belonged to Margravine Matilda of Tuscany.
Henry is said to have waited three days in penitent's clothing outside the castle.
The princes elected Rudolf of Rheinfelden as anti-king.
In 1872 Bismarck said: “We shall not go to Canossa.”

abschnitte.titel: A quarrel between king and pope
abschnitte.text: In the 11th century the king and the pope quarrelled over who may appoint the **bishops**. This quarrel is called the **Investiture Controversy**. King **Henry IV** even wanted to depose Pope **Gregory VII**. In 1076 the pope replied with **excommunication**. With that Henry was shut out of the Church. Many princes therefore no longer wanted to obey him.

The princes threatened to elect a new king if the ban was not lifted soon. The pope was already on his way **to an assembly of princes in Augsburg**. Henry had to act quickly. In the winter of 1076/77 he crossed the **snow-covered Alps** with his wife **Bertha of Savoy** and his little son. The journey was dangerous and very cold.

When the pope heard that Henry was coming, he withdrew to the castle of **Canossa**. It belonged to the powerful **Margravine Matilda of Tuscany**. In **January 1077** Henry stood there in **penitent's clothing** in front of the gate. He is said to have waited for **three days**. Then the pope took him back into the Church. Henry was thereby freed from the ban.

The quarrel was not over with that. Still in the year 1077 the princes elected **Rudolf of Rheinfelden** as **anti-king**. He was Duke of Swabia, and his family had property on the High Rhine. There was fighting in which Rudolf died in 1080. Only in 1122 did emperor and pope settle the Investiture Controversy in the Concordat of Worms.

To this day people say **“going to Canossa”**. This means that someone has to **apologise humbly** or give way. A sentence by **Otto von Bismarck** is famous. In 1872, as Chancellor, he was in dispute with the Catholic Church and said in the Reichstag: **“We shall not go to Canossa.”** By this he meant that he did not want to give way to the pope.

gewusst: Of Canossa Castle in northern Italy only ruins stand today.
For Henry the walk to Canossa was also a clever move, because without the ban the pope could no longer depose him so easily.

teile.einleitung: Hildegard of Bingen was a famous nun and abbess in the 12th century. She wrote books on medicine and faith, composed songs and is still very well known today.
wichtigste: Hildegard was born in 1098 and died in 1179, so she lived in the 12th century.
She lived in present-day Germany and came into a monastery as a child.
She was a Benedictine and, as abbess, led her monastery.
Around 1150 she founded the monastery of Rupertsberg near Bingen on the Rhine.
Even as a child she spoke of visions.
She wrote about medicine and praised spelt in particular.
In 2012 Pope Benedict XVI declared her a saint and a Doctor of the Church.

abschnitte.text: Hildegard was born in **1098**. Even as a child she came into a **monastery** and was brought up there. Later she became a **Benedictine**, that is, a nun following the rule of Saint Benedict. The sisters chose her as **abbess**. An abbess is the head of a women's monastery. Hildegard died in **1179** and lived to over 80, which was very rare at that time.

abschnitte.titel: A monastery of her own on the Rhine
abschnitte.text: Around **1150** Hildegard founded a monastery of her own: the **Rupertsberg** near **Bingen on the Rhine**. Later she founded a second monastery in Eibingen on the other side of the river. Hildegard also travelled and gave sermons, which was unusual for a woman at that time. She wrote letters to popes, emperors and bishops.

Hildegard said that she had **visions** even as a child. These are special images that she saw inwardly. For a long time she kept this to herself. Only as an adult did she write down her visions. Her best-known book about them is called “**Scivias**”, which means “Know the ways”. The Church recognised her writings.

Today Hildegard is known above all for her **medicine**. She wrote about **plants**, animals and stones and about how they can help the sick. She praised **spelt** in particular. She wrote that it was good and easy to digest. That is why spelt is often linked with her today. Many recipes that bear her name today, however, do not come directly from her.

Hildegard also wrote poems and composed many **sacred songs**. Some are still sung today and recorded on CDs. For a long time she was venerated as a saint without officially being canonised. In the year **2012** **Pope Benedict XVI** officially declared her a **saint** and a **Doctor of the Church**. Only a few women bear this title.

gewusst: Hildegard invented a secret language of her own with letters of its own, the “Lingua ignota”.
About 70 songs by Hildegard survive, which is a great deal for the Middle Ages.

teile.einleitung: Charles Martel was the most powerful man in the Frankish Empire in the early 8th century. He was not a king but mayor of the palace, yet he governed the empire. His grandson was Charlemagne.
wichtigste: Charles Martel lived from about 690 to 741 and was mayor of the palace in the Frankish Empire.
His epithet “Martel” means “the Hammer”.
He was a son of Pepin of Herstal.
After his father's death he first had to fight for power.
He often rewarded his warriors with land from Church property.
After the death of King Theuderic IV in 737 he left the throne empty.

abschnitte.text: The epithet **Martel** comes from the Latin word “martellus”, which means **hammer**. Charles got it because of his many military successes. He led numerous campaigns and so strengthened the power of the Franks. Especially well known is his victory over an Arab army at Tours and Poitiers in the year 732. Later this victory was celebrated as the rescue of Europe, though historians see it more cautiously today.

abschnitte.titel: Mayor of the palace instead of king
abschnitte.text: In the Frankish Empire at that time the kings from the **Merovingian** family reigned. The real power, however, lay with the **mayor of the palace**. He was originally the steward of the royal court. Charles Martel was a son of the mayor of the palace **Pepin of Herstal**. After his father's death in 714 he first had to fight for power against relatives and opponents.

A ruler needed loyal warriors. Charles Martel rewarded his followers with land. He often took this land from **Church property**. So he seized estates of the Church and passed them on. This later brought him criticism from Church writers, who recorded history in the monasteries.

In the year 737 the Merovingian king **Theuderic IV** died. Charles Martel did not appoint a new king. He simply went on ruling but did not take the royal title himself. Only in 743, after Charles's death, was a Merovingian installed again. Charles's son **Pepin the Younger** became king himself in 751, and his son was **Charlemagne**.

gewusst: The ruling family of the Carolingians is named after Charles Martel.
For several years Charles Martel ruled the Frankish Empire entirely without a king.

teile.einleitung: The Cathars were a religious movement of the Middle Ages. In the 12th and 13th centuries they spread above all in southern France and northern Italy. The Church saw them as heretics and fought them.
wichtigste: The name comes from the Greek “katharoi”, the pure.
The Cathars held a dualism of good and evil.
For them the spiritual world came from a good God, the material world from an evil principle.
Their clergy were called Perfecti, the Perfect.
After the town of Albi they were also called Albigensians.
The Church fought them with a crusade and the Inquisition.

abschnitte.text: The name **Cathars** is derived from the Greek word “katharoi”. It means “the pure”. The Cathars wanted to lead a pure life that detaches itself from the material world. Their opponents, however, mostly used the name in a disparaging way. Incidentally, the German word **Ketzer** (heretic) also comes from the word Cathar.

The Cathars held a **dualism**. That means there are two opposing forces. According to their teaching, the spiritual comes from a good God. The material world with everything bodily, by contrast, comes from an evil principle. So they rejected many **sacraments** of the Church, that is, sacred rites such as the Mass with bread and wine.

Among the Cathars there were two groups. The **Perfecti**, the Perfect, served as clergy. They lived by strict rules, gave up property, ate no meat and travelled about preaching. The ordinary believers were called **credentes**. They lived a normal life and hoped to be taken into the community of the Perfect before their death.

The Cathars were especially numerous in the area around the town of **Albi** in Languedoc in southern France. So there they were also called **Albigensians**. The Church considered their teaching false. In 1209 Pope Innocent III called for the **Albigensian Crusade**, which lasted many years. After that the **Inquisition**, a Church court, pursued the last followers until the movement disappeared in the 14th century.

gewusst: The German word “Ketzer” comes from the name of the Cathars.
The Cathars rejected meat because they regarded the bodily as bad.

teile.einleitung: Bartolomeu Dias was a Portuguese navigator. In 1488 he became the first European to sail round the southern tip of Africa, showing that a sea route to India was possible.
wichtigste: Dias set out from Lisbon in 1487 with three ships.
He sailed with two caravels and a supply ship.
He was the first European to round the southern tip of Africa.
He called the cape the “Cape of Storms”.
King John II is said to have renamed it the “Cape of Good Hope”.
His crew forced him to turn back.
In 1500, his ship sank in a storm near the cape.

abschnitte.text: In the 15th century, Portugal was looking for a **sea route to India** in order to buy spices directly. In **1487**, **Bartolomeu Dias** set out from **Lisbon**, Portugal's most important port. He had **three ships**: two **caravels** and a **supply ship**. He left the supply ship behind on the coast along the way. With the caravels he sailed south along the coast of Africa.

On new coasts, Portuguese explorers put up **stone pillars**. They were called **“padrões”** and bore the coat of arms of Portugal and a **cross**. With them, Portugal showed that it claimed the area for itself. Dias also put up such pillars. Remains of them were found later.

abschnitte.titel: Round the southern tip of Africa
abschnitte.text: At the beginning of **1488**, the ships ran into violent storms and were driven far to the south. When Dias sailed north again, he noticed that the coast now ran to the east. He had rounded the **southern tip of Africa**. Because of the winds, he called the cape the **“Cape of Storms”**. King **John II** is said to have later given it the name **“Cape of Good Hope”**, because of the hope of a sea route to India.

Dias wanted to go on to India. But his **crew** was exhausted and supplies were running short. The sailors demanded to **turn back**, and Dias had to give way. Only **Vasco da Gama** reached India by this route, in 1498. In **1500**, Dias sailed with a large fleet towards India. Near the cape, his ship ran into a **storm** and sank.

gewusst: The southernmost point of Africa is not the Cape of Good Hope but Cape Agulhas.
Dias's voyage lasted about 16 months in all.

teile.einleitung: Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian painter, inventor and researcher of the Renaissance. He painted the Mona Lisa, probably the most famous picture in the world. Besides this he filled thousands of pages with drawings of flying machines, animals, plants and the human body.
wichtigste: Leonardo da Vinci lived from 1452 to 1519 and came from Italy.
“Da Vinci” means “from Vinci”, a small place in Tuscany.
He painted the Mona Lisa, which hangs today in the Louvre in Paris.
In Milan he painted the famous mural “The Last Supper”.
Leonardo wrote and drew with his left hand and often in mirror writing.
He planned flying machines modelled on birds but never flew in them himself.
He studied the bones and muscles of the human body very closely.

abschnitte.text: Leonardo was born in 1452 in the village of **Vinci** near Florence, hence his name. He had no family name in today's sense, because his parents were not married. As a teenager he was apprenticed in **Florence** to the artist Andrea del Verrocchio. There he learnt painting, drawing, sculpture and engineering.

Leonardo painted the **Mona Lisa** from about 1503. It probably shows Lisa del Giocondo, the wife of a merchant from Florence. Famous are her mysterious smile and the soft, smoky way of painting that is called **sfumato**. Today the picture hangs in the **Louvre** in Paris behind bulletproof glass, and every year millions of people come to see it.

In Milan Leonardo worked for Duke Ludovico Sforza. There, from about 1495 to 1498, he painted the mural **The Last Supper** in the monastery of Santa Maria delle Grazie. It shows Jesus with his twelve disciples at their last meal together. Leonardo tried out a new painting technique, so the paint soon began to flake. The picture later had to be restored often at great effort.

Leonardo watched closely how **birds** fly and, following them, drew flying machines with flapping wings. He also designed a parachute, bridges, war machines and canals. He never built or flew his flying machines; he mostly drew them. He recorded his ideas in **notebooks**, often in mirror writing, because he was left-handed.

Leonardo wanted to know how a person is built inside. He examined corpses and drew **bones**, muscles, the heart and even a child in the womb. His drawing **The Vitruvian Man** shows a man with outstretched arms and legs in a circle and a square. It shows the ideal proportions of the body and is world famous today.

Because Leonardo achieved great things in so many fields, he is called a **universal genius**. He is regarded as a typical person of the **Renaissance**, a time in which people wanted to observe nature closely and understand it anew. He spent his last years in France with King Francis I. He died in 1519 in Amboise on the Loire.

begriffe.erklaerung: A period from about 1400 in which art and science flourished in Europe.
Writing that can be read the right way round only when held up to a mirror.
A painting technique with very soft transitions, as if through a fine mist.
A person who is exceptionally gifted in very many fields.

gewusst: The Mona Lisa was stolen from the Louvre in 1911 and found again only over two years later in Florence.
Only about 15 to 20 paintings by Leonardo survive, but thousands of pages of notes.
At about 77 by 53 centimetres, the Mona Lisa is much smaller than many people think.

teile.einleitung: Constantinople was the capital of the Eastern Roman Empire for over 1000 years. The city on the Bosporus was rich, splendid and strongly fortified. Today it is called Istanbul and lies in Turkey.
wichtigste: The city used to be called Byzantium.
Emperor Constantine dedicated it as the new capital on 11 May 330.
Constantinople lies on the Bosporus between Europe and Asia.
From 330 to 1453 it was the capital of the Eastern Roman Empire.
The Theodosian Wall protected the city on the land side.
The Golden Horn served as a natural harbour.
With Greek fire, enemy ships were attacked.

abschnitte.text: The city used to be called **Byzantium**. Emperor **Constantine** made it his new capital and dedicated it on 11 May 330. After that it was called Constantinople, the city of Constantine. After the old name the Eastern Roman Empire is also called the **Byzantine Empire**. The city remained the capital from 330 to 1453, so for over 1100 years.

Constantinople lies on the **Bosporus**. This strait joins the Black Sea with the Sea of Marmara and so with the Mediterranean. The Bosporus separates **Europe** and **Asia**. Today's Istanbul lies on both sides. A long arm of the sea, the **Golden Horn**, served as a natural harbour. There the ships lay sheltered.

Constantinople had thick, multiple walls. The most important was the **Theodosian Wall** on the land side. It was built in the 5th century under Emperor **Theodosius II**. For many centuries it withstood numerous sieges. Many attackers failed against it.

Against enemy fleets Byzantium had a special weapon. **Greek fire** was an incendiary weapon that went on burning even on water. It was sprayed through tubes onto enemy ships. The recipe was strictly secret. How exactly it was made is still not known today.

In the year 1453 the **Ottomans** under Sultan Mehmed II conquered the city. With this the Eastern Roman Empire ended. The city became the capital of the Ottoman Empire. The great church **Hagia Sophia** became a mosque. Today the city is called **Istanbul** and is the largest city in Turkey.

gewusst: The recipe of Greek fire is still a mystery today.
Istanbul is one of the few large cities that lie on two continents.

teile.einleitung: At an imperial coronation a ruler was solemnly made emperor. In the Middle Ages it was usually the pope in Rome who crowned the emperor, who thereby became the highest secular ruler in the West.
wichtigste: The emperor was the highest secular ruler and stood above the kings.
Usually the pope crowned the emperor in Rome.
Charlemagne was crowned on 25 December 800 in the old St Peter's Basilica.
Otto the Great was crowned emperor in Rome in 962.
For a long time the German kings were first crowned in Aachen.
At the coronation the ruler was anointed with consecrated oil.

abschnitte.text: In the Middle Ages there were many **kings** in Europe. Above them stood the **emperor**. He was the highest **secular ruler** in the Christian West. The title went back to the emperors of the old **Roman Empire**. A king did not simply become emperor, however. This required an **imperial coronation**, and it was usually carried out by the **pope**.

The imperial coronation mostly took place in **Rome**, because the pope lived there. He placed the crown on the ruler's head. This showed that the emperor was also recognised by the **Church**. During the ceremony the ruler was anointed with **consecrated oil**. This was meant to show that **God** had chosen him as ruler. Kings often crossed the Alps to Rome with a great army.

The most famous imperial coronation is that of **Charlemagne**. He was crowned on **25 December 800**, that is, at **Christmas**. It happened in the old **St Peter's Basilica** in Rome. In its place stands **St Peter's** today. **Pope Leo III** placed the crown on his head. In this way the West had an emperor again for the first time in centuries.

In the year **962** **Otto I**, called **Otto the Great**, was crowned emperor in Rome. With him the **Holy Roman Empire** began. It lasted until 1806, and the area of present-day Switzerland also belonged to it for a long time. Its rulers were first elected king and only later, after the coronation by the pope, became emperor.

Before they became emperor, the German kings had themselves crowned. For many hundreds of years this happened in **Aachen Cathedral**. There the **throne of Charlemagne** still stands today. Later the kings were elected and crowned in **Frankfurt am Main**. The last imperial coronation by a pope was experienced by **Charles V** in 1530 in **Bologna**.

gewusst: The crown of the emperors of the Holy Roman Empire has survived and lies today in the Treasury in Vienna.
More than 30 kings sat on the throne of Charlemagne in Aachen at their coronation.

teile.einleitung: In the Middle Ages many monasteries had a garden of their own. There the monks grew vegetables, fruit and above all medicinal herbs, from which they made medicine for the sick.
wichtigste: Monks used medicinal herbs above all for medicine.
The name sage (Latin “salvia”) comes from the Latin “salvare”, to heal.
Camomile tea helped against stomach ache.
From the marigold an ointment for wounds was made.
Walahfrid Strabo wrote the garden poem “Hortulus” on the Reichenau.
The Plan of St Gall shows a herb garden next to the physician's house.

abschnitte.text: In the Middle Ages there were no pharmacies like today. Sick people often found help in the **monastery**. The monks made teas, ointments and poultices from **medicinal herbs**. With them they cared for the sick in the monastery and the surrounding area. In addition, vegetables and fruit for the kitchen grew in the monastery garden.

The **Plan of St Gall** was drawn over 1200 years ago. It shows a whole monastery with a **herb garden**, a vegetable garden and an orchard. On the plan the medicinal herb garden lies close to the **physician's house**. So the healing plants were quickly to hand. Today the plan is kept in the Abbey Library of St Gall.

**Walahfrid Strabo** was abbot on the island of **Reichenau** in Lake Constance. Around 840 he wrote a famous poem about his monastery garden. It is called “Hortulus”, which means little garden. In it he describes many plants and what they are good for, for example sage and mint. The toils of gardening also appear in it.

**Sage** is called “Salvia” in Latin. That comes from “salvare”, to heal or save. **Camomile** soothes stomach and skin, and its tea helped against stomach ache. The **marigold** has orange or yellow flowers, and its ointment helps with small wounds. **Mint** smells fresh and is still popular as a tea today. The purple-flowering **lavender** smells strongly and was also used against moths in clothing.

gewusst: Sage, camomile and mint are still popular tea herbs more than 1000 years after the first monastery gardens.
Many monasteries today again lay out herb gardens on old models.

teile.einleitung: In the High Middle Ages the population of Europe grew strongly. People needed more land for fields and pastures. So they cleared forests and also settled high-lying valleys. This is called the internal colonisation of land.
wichtigste: In the High Middle Ages the population grew, and more land was needed.
Forests were cleared to lay out fields and pastures.
Place names such as Rüti, Rüthi or Schwanden point to clearings.
From the 13th century the Walser settled high valleys from the Valais.
The Walser received special rights of freedom for this.

abschnitte.text: To gain new land, people had to remove forest. This is called **clearing**. The old German word for it is **reuten**. From it come Swiss place names such as **Rüti** or **Rüthi**. In **schwenden**, trees were left to die by peeling off their bark. Names such as **Schwanden** point to this. Such names bear witness to this day to the expansion of settlement in the High Middle Ages.

From the 13th century people from the **Upper Valais** migrated into high-lying valleys. They are called **Walser**. They settled, for example, **Davos** or the **Rheinwald** in Graubünden. There are also Walser settlements in Italy, Liechtenstein and Vorarlberg. The Walser made the harsh high valleys habitable.

Life in the high valleys was hard. So that settlers would come, the territorial lords gave them special **rights of freedom**. This is called **Walser law**. The Walser could pass on their land by inheritance and had a community of their own. In return they paid taxes and performed military service. To this day some Walser speak a dialect of their own.

gewusst: Place names such as Rüti tell us that forest was once cleared there.
In the Middle Ages Davos was settled by Walser from the Valais.

teile.einleitung: Iceland was settled in the 9th and 10th centuries, mainly by people from Norway. This period is called the Settlement. The settlers founded the Althing in 930, one of the oldest popular assemblies.
wichtigste: Before the Vikings, Irish monks lived on Iceland for a time.
Most settlers came from Norway, some from the British Isles.
Ingólfur Arnarson is regarded as the first permanent settler.
He built his farm where Reykjavík lies today.
Reykjavík means “Smoky Bay”.
The Book of Settlements names over 400 settlers and their farms.
Around 930 the Althing was founded.

abschnitte.text: Old accounts say that even before the Vikings, **Irish monks** lived on Iceland for a time. They sought solitude and peace for praying there. When the first settlers came from the north, the monks left again. Before that there were no permanent villages on the island.

From about **870**, settlers came to Iceland by ship. Most came from **Norway**, some also from the **British Isles**. **Ingólfur Arnarson** is regarded as the first permanent settler. He built his farm where **Reykjavík**, the capital of Iceland, lies today. The settlers brought sheep, cattle and **horses** with them. From these horses came the **Icelandic horse**, which is still found there today.

The name **Reykjavík** means **“Smoky Bay”**. The settlers saw steam rising there from **hot springs**. They took it for smoke. Iceland has many volcanoes and hot springs. Today Icelanders heat many houses with this **geothermal heat**.

A lot of what we know about the settlement comes from the **Book of Settlements**, in Icelandic “Landnámabók”. It was written in Iceland in the Middle Ages. It lists **over 400 settlers** with their farms and families. Some of the stories in it are more like legends than exact reports.

In **930** the Icelanders met for the first **Althing**. This was an assembly in the open air at **Þingvellir**. There they made **laws** and settled **disputes**. Iceland had no king at that time. The parliament of Iceland is still called the Althing today.

gewusst: The meeting place Þingvellir lies in a rift between two tectonic plates and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
To this day no horses may be imported into Iceland, so that the Icelandic horse stays pure.

teile.einleitung: The lord of the castle was the owner or master of a castle. He had power over the land and the people round about, but also many duties. Together with the lady of the castle he ran a large household with many servants.
wichtigste: In quarrels among his peasants, the lord of the castle often gave judgement as a judge.
The lady of the castle ran the household of the castle.
As a sign of her duties, the lady of the castle often wore a bunch of keys at her belt.
A castle steward managed the castle on behalf of the lord.
All the farmhands and maids together are called the household staff.
On the hunt the lord was often helped by a falcon.
Minstrels travelled from castle to castle as singers and musicians.

abschnitte.text: A lord of the castle usually had land with villages and peasants. The peasants had to pay him **dues**, for example part of their harvest. In return the lord was meant to protect them. When his peasants had a **quarrel**, he often gave judgement as a **judge**. Not every lord of the castle lived in his castle himself. Sometimes he appointed a **castle steward**, who managed the castle on his behalf.

The wife of the lord of the castle was the **lady of the castle**. She **ran the household**: she looked after supplies, the kitchen, clothing and the work of the servants. As a sign of these duties she often wore a **bunch of keys** at her belt. With it she could open storerooms and chests. When the lord was away, she often took over the whole management.

Many people worked in a castle. All the **farmhands** and **maids** together are called the **household staff**. A **maid** was a woman who worked as a servant, for example in the kitchen, in the stable or at the washing. Farmhands looked after the horses, chopped wood or carried water. In addition there were craftsmen, guards and sometimes a cook.

A favourite pastime of the nobility was **hunting**. In **falconry**, a trained **falcon** helped to catch small animals and birds. Hospitality was a duty of honour. For travelling guests the lord of the castle usually offered **food and a bed for the night**. Welcome indeed were the **minstrels**: singers and musicians who travelled from castle to castle and brought news.

gewusst: A falconer needed a lot of patience: it often took months until a falcon was well trained.
In Switzerland, many castles later housed bailiffs who governed a region on behalf of a town such as Bern or Zurich.

teile.einleitung: A farmhouse in the Middle Ages was mostly small and simple. People and animals often lived under one roof, and in the middle an open fire burned.
wichtigste: Many walls were made of a wooden frame with clay and twigs.
Cooking was done at an open hearth.
Many houses had no chimney, the smoke escaped through the roof.
Windows were closed with wooden shutters, because glass was expensive.
Often there were only one or two rooms.
The floor was mostly of stamped earth.
The animals in the stable warmed the house in winter.

abschnitte.text: Many farmhouses had a **wooden frame**. The gaps between were filled with woven **twigs** and coated with **clay**. The roof was often covered with straw or reeds, in the mountains also with wooden shingles or stone slabs. The **floor** was mostly of **stamped earth**. The houses were small and often had only **one or two rooms**.

In the middle of the house burned an **open hearth**. There people cooked in a cauldron, and the fire gave **warmth** and **light**. Many simple houses had no **chimney**. The smoke escaped through openings in the roof. So it was often smoky inside the house, and the beams turned black.

abschnitte.titel: People and animals under one roof
abschnitte.text: In many farmhouses the **stable** and the **living space** lay close together. The animals gave off **body heat**. In the cold winter this made the house a little warmer. In addition, one could keep a good eye on the animals. It did, however, smell strongly of the stable.

The whole family **slept, cooked and ate** in the same room. Poor peasants slept on a **straw sack**, a sack filled with straw. Often several people lay together, which kept them warm. There was little furniture, for example a table, benches and a chest. **Glass** was expensive, so the window openings were closed with **wooden shutters**.

gewusst: In the Ballenberg open-air museum near Brienz you can visit old farmhouses from all over Switzerland.
In smoke houses, meat and sausages were hung under the roof, where the smoke preserved them.

tmdczir.t: Persecutions of Jews at the Time of the Black Death

teile.einleitung: When around 1348 the plague, the Black Death, swept through Europe, Jews were falsely accused of having caused the epidemic. In many cities, including in Switzerland, serious persecutions took place.
wichtigste: It was claimed without proof that Jews had poisoned wells and so spread the plague.
In 1348 at Chillon Castle on Lake Geneva, Jews were tortured until they made false confessions.
In January 1349 many Jews were murdered in Basel.
On 14 February 1349 hundreds of Jews were murdered in Strasbourg.
In 1348 Pope Clement VI declared that the Jews were innocent of the plague.
Many survivors fled to eastern Europe, especially to the Kingdom of Poland.
The Erfurt Treasure, found in 1998, probably comes from a Jew who was murdered in 1349.

abschnitte.titel: The plague and a false accusation
abschnitte.text: From **1347** the **plague** spread in Europe. It was called the **Black Death**. A large part of the population died. Nobody knew at the time that bacteria cause the disease. Many looked for someone to blame. It was claimed without any proof that the **Jews** had **poisoned wells**. This lie spread quickly from city to city.

In the year **1348** at **Chillon Castle** on **Lake Geneva**, Jews were tortured until they made false **confessions**. These forced statements were sent to many cities. There they fuelled the persecutions. In **January 1349** many Jews were murdered in **Basel** on an island in the Rhine. In Zurich and other Swiss cities too, Jewish communities were wiped out.

In **Strasbourg** hundreds of Jews were murdered on **14 February 1349**, St Valentine's Day. Similar things happened in many cities in the empire, for example in Erfurt, Cologne or Mainz. Often it also played a part that the culprits wanted to be rid of their **debts** to Jewish moneylenders or to seize their property. These persecutions are called **pogroms**.

In **1348** **Pope Clement VI** declared that the Jews were **innocent** of the plague. He pointed out that Jews died of the plague just as others did. Besides, the epidemic raged even where no Jews lived at all. But many cities did not listen to him. After the pogroms many Jews fled to **eastern Europe**. The Kingdom of **Poland** in particular took them in, and large Jewish communities later arose there.

In the year **1998** construction workers in **Erfurt** in Germany found a treasure. It was hidden in a **house wall** and contained coins, silver tableware and jewellery, including a Jewish wedding ring. It probably belonged to a Jewish merchant who was murdered in 1349. Today the **Erfurt Treasure** is displayed in the Old Synagogue of Erfurt and recalls the victims.

gewusst: The Old Synagogue in Erfurt is one of the oldest surviving synagogues in Europe and has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2023.
The plague is caused by a bacterium that is often transmitted by fleas.

teile.einleitung: Castles were built of thick stone walls and were often icy cold in winter. The kemenate was a special room: it had a fireplace and could be heated.
wichtigste: The kemenate was a heatable living room in a castle.
The word comes from the Latin “caminata”, room with a chimney.
A chimney is a fireplace with a smoke flue.
Most rooms in a castle were cold, so the kemenate was popular in winter.
In the late Middle Ages some kemenates were heated with a tiled stove.

abschnitte.text: The **kemenate** was a living room in a castle that could be heated. The name comes from the Latin word “caminata”. That means **room with a chimney**. Often the women and children of the castle family stayed there. Here people spun, sewed, told stories and played. Later the word was used in general for a living room or bedroom.

Most rooms in a castle were cold and damp. **Stone walls** hold the cold for a long time. The windows were small and often had no glass, only wooden shutters. In winter many rooms were therefore uncomfortable. A heated room like the kemenate was something special and very popular.

A **chimney** is an open fireplace on the wall. The smoke rises through a shaft. In this way the room became warm without being full of smoke. In the late Middle Ages **tiled stoves** appeared. They are made of clay and store heat for a long time. In Switzerland too, beautiful tiled stoves can be found in old houses and castles, for example from Winterthur.

gewusst: In the kemenate people did not only keep warm but also worked: there they spun wool and sewed clothes.
A tiled stove still gives off warmth hours after the fire.

teile.einleitung: The Champagne fairs were the most important trade fairs in Europe in the Middle Ages. They took place in the County of Champagne in the north-east of France and brought together merchants from north and south.
wichtigste: The Champagne fairs flourished in the 12th and 13th centuries.
There were four fair towns: Troyes, Provins, Lagny and Bar-sur-Aube.
The yearly cycle comprised six fairs.
Above all, traders from Flanders and northern Italy met there.
The counts of Champagne protected the merchants with safe conduct.
Direct sea voyages by Italian galleys to Bruges contributed to the decline.
The troy ounce for precious metals probably goes back to the town of Troyes.

abschnitte.text: The fairs took place in four towns: **Troyes**, **Provins**, **Lagny** and **Bar-sur-Aube**. Troyes and Provins each had two fairs a year, Lagny and Bar-sur-Aube one each. This gave a cycle of **six fairs**, spread over the whole year. A merchant could do business somewhere in Champagne almost all year round. Each fair lasted several weeks.

Champagne lay conveniently between two rich trading regions. From **Flanders** in the north, traders brought fine **woollen cloth**. From **northern Italy**, for example from Genoa, Venice or Florence, came merchants with **spices**, silk and other goods from the Mediterranean and the Orient. At the fairs these goods were exchanged and sold.

The **counts of Champagne** deliberately promoted the fairs. They gave the merchants **safe conduct**: whoever travelled to the fair was under their protection. There were inspectors and courts of their own, which decided quickly in a dispute. Money changers were important too, because the traders brought coins from many countries. Here early forms of credit and of payment without cash developed.

Towards the end of the 13th century the fairs lost importance. Italian **galleys** now sailed directly across the sea to **Bruges** in Flanders. The traders no longer had to travel overland to Champagne. In addition, Champagne passed to the French crown, and wars and levies made trade harder. In the 14th century the fairs were only a shadow of their former selves.

gewusst: The troy ounce is still used today as a unit of measure for gold and silver.
Provins has preserved its medieval old town so well that it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

teile.einleitung: Erik the Red was a Viking who lived over 1000 years ago. He explored Greenland and founded the first settlements of Europeans there. We know a lot about him from old Icelandic sagas.
wichtigste: Erik the Red was born in Norway.
He got his nickname probably because of his red hair.
He was banished from Iceland for three years.
In this time he explored the large island in the west.
He called it “Greenland” to attract settlers.
He set out with about 25 ships to settle the land.
Around 985 he founded the settlements in Greenland.

abschnitte.text: Erik was born around 950 in **Norway**. He got his nickname **“the Red”** probably because of his **red hair**. While still a child he moved with his father to **Iceland**, because his father had to leave Norway after a serious quarrel. Erik grew up in Iceland and later founded a farm of his own.

In Iceland Erik too got into violent quarrels in which people lost their lives. So he was **banished** from Iceland for **three years**. That is, he was not allowed to return for that long. Erik used this time and sailed west. There he explored the coasts of a huge, icy island.

After his return to Iceland, Erik told of the new land. He called it **“Greenland”**. The name was meant to **attract settlers**, because a green land sounded better than an icy one. In fact, in some sheltered bays in the south there were green meadows for sheep and cattle. The greatest part of the island, however, is covered with ice.

Around **985** Erik set out with **about 25 ships**. Not all arrived, because some turned back or were lost on the way. The settlers founded two settlements in the south-west of Greenland. Erik lived on his farm **Brattahlíð**. His son **Leif Eriksson** later sailed even further west and around the year 1000 reached North America.

gewusst: The Viking settlements in Greenland lasted almost 500 years, then they disappeared.
Greenland is the largest island in the world.

teile.einleitung: Chain mail was the most important protection of a warrior in the Middle Ages. It consists of thousands of small iron rings that interlock like a fabric of metal.
wichtigste: A chain mail shirt consists of many small iron rings.
Each ring is linked with several others.
Underneath one wore a thickly padded shirt.
Chain mail protected well against sword cuts.
A simple chain mail shirt weighed about 15 kilograms.
In the late Middle Ages plate armour of large metal plates appeared.

abschnitte.text: A **chain mail shirt** consists of thousands of small **iron rings**. Each ring is linked with several others, usually with four neighbours. In this way a flexible armour is formed, almost like a fabric of metal. A smith needed many weeks to make a chain mail shirt. So it was expensive and valuable.

The iron rings held off the edge of a **sword** well. So chain mail protected very well against cuts. Against hard blows with a club or a hammer it helped less. The rings gave way, and the blow still struck the body. Here it was above all the padding underneath that helped.

Under the chain mail one wore a thickly **padded shirt** of cloth. It cushioned the blows and protected the skin from the rings. A simple chain mail shirt with short sleeves weighed about **15 kilograms**. That sounds like a lot, but the weight was spread over the shoulders and body. A practised warrior could move well in it.

In the late Middle Ages weapons became stronger, for example crossbows. So smiths developed armour made of large **steel plates**. It is called **plate armour**. It covered the whole body. In places such as the armpits, however, pieces of mail were often still worn, because they had to stay flexible.

gewusst: A chain mail shirt could consist of several tens of thousands of rings.
Even today some butchers wear gloves of chain mail so that they do not cut themselves with the knife.

teile.einleitung: The cog was the typical merchant ship of the Hanseatic League in the Middle Ages. With its thick, round hull it could carry many goods across the North Sea and the Baltic.
wichtigste: The cog is a wooden sailing ship.
It was the typical merchant ship of the Hanseatic League.
A typical cog had one mast with a large, square sail.
It carried goods such as salt, grain and cloth.
In 1962 an old cog was found in the Weser in Bremen.

abschnitte.text: The **cog** is a wooden sailing ship. It had a thick, round hull and a flat bottom. A typical cog had **one mast** with a large, **square sail**. The wind drove it across the sea. At the stern sat a rudder with which the ship was steered. At the front and back there were often raised structures that looked like small castles.

The **Hanseatic League** was an association of merchants and cities such as Lübeck, Hamburg and Bremen. For their trade they needed large ships. The cogs had plenty of room in their bellies. They carried goods such as **salt**, **grain**, cloth, timber and fish from port to port. In this way they joined cities on the North Sea and the Baltic.

In the year 1962, during construction work in the river **Weser** in **Bremen**, an old ship was found. It was a cog from the 14th century. Researchers carefully lifted out the parts and put them together again. The **Bremen cog** can be seen today in the German Maritime Museum in Bremerhaven. Replicas show how well the cog could sail.

gewusst: The Bremen cog lay in the mud of the Weser for over 500 years.
The cog is still the emblem of many old Hanseatic cities today.

teile.einleitung: Heraldry is the study of coats of arms. It describes how coats of arms are built up, what colours and figures they have and by what rules they are designed.
wichtigste: Coats of arms arose in the Middle Ages so that knights in full armour could be recognised.
Gold and silver count in heraldry as “metals”, red, blue, black and green as colours.
An important rule is: never metal on metal and never colour on colour.
Simple divisions such as a fess, a pale or a cross are called ordinaries.
A complete coat of arms has shield, helm and crest, often also supporters.
“Right” and “left” are determined from the point of view of the bearer of the shield.
The Swiss coat of arms shows a white cross on a red ground.

abschnitte.text: With a closed helmet a knight could no longer be recognised. So in the 12th century signs were painted on the **shield**. In this way friend and foe could see who was inside the armour. Soon coats of arms were also passed on to the children. Later towns, municipalities, cantons and families also bore coats of arms of their own. The name **heraldry** comes from the **heralds**, who knew coats of arms especially well.

In heraldry there are two **metals**: gold, usually painted as yellow, and silver, usually painted as white. In addition there are the **colours** red, blue, black and green. The most important rule is: never metal on metal and never colour on colour. A white cross may therefore stand on red, but not on yellow. In this way the coat of arms stays easy to recognise even from far away.

A shield can be divided with lines. From this come **ordinaries**, for example a horizontal **fess**, a vertical **pale** or a **cross**. Animals, plants and objects, by contrast, are called **common charges**. Lions, eagles, bears or towers were popular. The bear in the coat of arms of Bern is a well-known example of a common charge.

A complete coat of arms includes the **shield**, the **helm** and the **crest**. The crest was a figure of feathers, horns or animals on the helmet. Sometimes **supporters** hold the shield from both sides, for example two lions or angels. They are an ornament and not a compulsory part. Also important: “right” and “left” are determined from the point of view of the **bearer of the shield**. For the viewer, the heraldic right side is therefore on the left.

The **Swiss coat of arms** shows a free-standing white cross in a red shield. It probably goes back to the battle flag of the people of Schwyz. Every **canton** and almost every **municipality** also has a coat of arms of its own. They can be seen on town halls, on flags and on car number plates. In Switzerland many families also have a family coat of arms.

gewusst: The colour rule has a famous exception: the coat of arms of the Kingdom of Jerusalem showed golden crosses on silver, that is, metal on metal.
On Swiss number plates, next to the canton abbreviation, the canton's coat of arms can also be seen.

teile.einleitung: Avicenna, in Arabic Ibn Sina, was a Persian doctor and philosopher. His “Canon of Medicine” was one of the most important textbooks for centuries, in Europe too.
wichtigste: Avicenna is the Latin form of the name Ibn Sina.
He was born around 980 near Bukhara in present-day Uzbekistan.
He was famous above all as a doctor and philosopher.
His main work is the “Canon of Medicine” in five books.
In Europe the Canon served as a textbook until the 17th century.
His mother tongue was Persian, but he wrote mostly in Arabic.
His philosophical encyclopaedia is called “Kitab al-Shifa”, the “Book of Healing”.

abschnitte.text: Ibn Sina was born around the year **980** in the village of Afshana near **Bukhara**. The city lies today in **Uzbekistan**, and at that time it belonged to the empire of the **Samanids**. Even as a child he learnt very quickly. At about 18 he is said to have already been working as a doctor. In Europe he was called **Avicenna**.

His most important work is the **“Canon of Medicine”**. In **five books** he summed up the medical knowledge of the Greeks, Persians and Arabs. He described diseases, their signs and many **remedies**. In the 12th century the Canon was translated into **Latin**. At universities such as Montpellier and Leuven it was still used until the **17th century**.

Avicenna was also a great **philosopher**. His encyclopaedic work is called **“Kitab al-Shifa”**, which means **“Book of Healing”**. What is meant is the healing of the soul from ignorance. The book deals with **logic**, natural science, mathematics and the question of being. He relied heavily on Aristotle.

Avicenna's **mother tongue** was **Persian**. For science, however, he wrote mostly in **Arabic**, because that was then the language of scholars in the Islamic world, just as Latin was in Europe. Some works he also wrote in Persian. He lived at various princely courts in Persia and died in 1037 in Hamadan in present-day Iran.

gewusst: Avicenna wrote a great many works, and researchers count well over a hundred.
In Hamadan there is a large mausoleum for him today.

teile.einleitung: The Incas were a people in the Andes of South America who built the largest empire in the Americas in the 15th and early 16th centuries. It stretched from present-day Ecuador to Chile and had its capital in Cusco. The Incas are famous for their mountain city of Machu Picchu, their roads and their walls of precisely fitting stones.
wichtigste: The capital of the Inca Empire was Cusco in present-day Peru.
The empire lay in the Andes and was called Tawantinsuyu, Land of the Four Parts.
The Incas spoke Quechua.
With quipus, knotted cords, they recorded numbers.
Llamas served as pack animals and supplied wool.
The Incas built with precisely fitting stones without mortar.
In 1532 Francisco Pizarro captured the ruler Atahualpa at Cajamarca and conquered the empire.

abschnitte.text: The Inca Empire lay in the **Andes**, the longest mountain range in the world. It stretched across parts of the present-day countries of Peru, Ecuador, Bolivia, Chile, Argentina and Colombia. The Incas called their empire **Tawantinsuyu**, Land of the Four Parts, because it was divided into four great regions. In the centre lay the capital **Cusco**, at over 3000 metres above sea level.

At the top stood the **Sapa Inka**, who was revered as the son of the sun god Inti. Originally “Inca” was only the title of the ruler, and later the whole people were called that. The state was very well organised: officials counted people, supplies and animals and recorded everything with **quipus**, cords with knots. The people spoke **Quechua**, which millions of people in the Andes still speak today.

The Incas built a road network of tens of thousands of kilometres right across mountains and deserts. Suspension bridges of woven grass led over deep gorges. Messages were carried by **runners**, the chasquis, who took over from one another every few kilometres. In this way a message reached faraway places in just a few days.

On steep mountain slopes the Incas built **terraces** to gain fields. They grew maize, quinoa and many varieties of **potato**, which originally comes from the Andes. **Llamas** carried loads, and from the wool of llamas and alpacas the Incas wove cloth. In storehouses they kept food for bad years.

Typical of the Incas are walls of **precisely fitting stones** that hold together without mortar. The joints are often so fine that not even a knife blade fits in. These walls survived many earthquakes better than later buildings. The most famous Inca city is **Machu Picchu**, which lies high on a mountain in Peru and became internationally known in 1911 through the American Hiram Bingham.

When the Spanish arrived, the empire had been weakened by a civil war between the brothers Atahualpa and Huáscar. In 1532 **Francisco Pizarro**, with fewer than 200 men, captured the ruler **Atahualpa** at Cajamarca. Although the Incas filled a room with gold and silver as a ransom, the Spanish had Atahualpa killed in 1533. After that they conquered the empire, but the culture and language of the Incas live on in the Andes to this day.

begriffe.erklaerung: The language of the Incas, which is still spoken in the Andes today.
A knotted cord with which the Incas recorded numbers.
The title of the supreme ruler of the Inca Empire.
A flat step on a mountainside on which fields can be laid out.

gewusst: The Incas could freeze-dry potatoes by leaving them out in the frost at night and drying them in the sun by day.
Machu Picchu was never found by the Spanish and so stayed well preserved.
The word llama comes from Quechua.

teile.einleitung: In the year 1453 the Ottomans under Sultan Mehmed II conquered the city of Constantinople. With that the Byzantine Empire ended after more than 1000 years. Many historians see in it a turning point at the end of the Middle Ages.
wichtigste: Sultan Mehmed II conquered Constantinople in the year 1453.
The last Byzantine emperor was called Constantine XI.
The siege lasted just under two months.
Large cannons helped the Ottomans to break through the city walls.
To get round the boom chain in the harbour, the Ottomans dragged ships overland.
Mehmed II received the nickname “the Conqueror”.
Many Greek scholars fled to Italy.

abschnitte.text: In the 15th century hardly anything was left of the once great **Byzantine Empire** except the capital **Constantinople** and a few regions. All round, the **Ottomans** had built up a mighty empire. The young Sultan **Mehmed II** was determined to conquer the city. It was defended by Emperor **Constantine XI**, the last Byzantine emperor.

Constantinople was protected by enormous **city walls** that had survived many attacks. But Mehmed II had **large cannons** built. They fired heavy stone balls at the walls. The siege began in April **1453** and lasted **just under two months**. Again and again the cannons tore holes in the walls, which the defenders patched up roughly at night.

The harbour of the city, the **Golden Horn**, was protected by a heavy **boom chain**. Enemy ships could not get in. Mehmed II had a bold idea: he had **ships dragged overland**, on wooden tracks over a hill. In this way they got behind the chain into the harbour basin. The defenders now also had to protect this side and were under even greater strain.

On **29 May 1453** the Ottomans entered the city. Emperor Constantine XI lost his life in the fighting. Mehmed II received the nickname **“the Conqueror”**. He made the city the new **capital** of his empire. Many Greek **scholars** fled **to Italy** and brought old writings with them. This strengthened the study of antiquity there in the Renaissance.

gewusst: The great church of Hagia Sophia was turned into a mosque after the conquest.
Today the city is called Istanbul and is the largest city in Turkey.

teile.einleitung: King Arthur is a legendary figure from Britain. The stories about him, his Knights of the Round Table and the wizard Merlin were told all over Europe in the Middle Ages. Whether Arthur really existed is not certain.
wichtigste: The Arthurian legends come from Britain.
Arthur and his knights sat at the Round Table.
The young Arthur drew a sword from a stone.
His famous sword is called Excalibur.
The wizard Merlin advised King Arthur.
His castle was called Camelot, his wife Guinevere.
Many knights searched for the Holy Grail.

abschnitte.text: In the legend a sword is stuck in a stone. Only the true king can pull it out. Many strong knights try in vain. But the young **Arthur** manages it and becomes king. His most famous sword is called **Excalibur**. In some tales he received it from the **Lady of the Lake**.

King Arthur sat with his knights at a round table, the **Round Table**. At a round table there is no better place, and nobody is more important than anyone else. The Round Table stood in the castle of **Camelot**, the court of King Arthur. Among the best-known knights are **Lancelot**, **Gawain** and **Parzival**.
